Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr the same.

Al-Darimi, Abu Dawud in his *Marasil* (a collection of mursal reports, those in which the Companion is omitted from the chain), Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, Ibn Asakir and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* (*Shu'ab al-Iman*) transmitted from Ka'b, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Recite Hud on Friday."

He said: 'Hud, al-Waqi'ah, al-Mursalat, ʿAmma yatasa'aluna, and Idha al-shamsu kuwwirat have made me grey.'"

He said: 'Hud and its sisters have made me grey: al-Waqi'ah, al-Haqqah, ʿAmma yatasa'aluna, and Hal ata-ka hadithu al-ghashiyah.'"

He said: 'Hud and its sisters have made me grey: al-Waqi'ah, al-Haqqah, ʿAmma yatasa'aluna, and Hal ata-ka hadithu al-ghashiyah.'"

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Anas, who said: The Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Grey hair has come to you quickly." He said: "Hud and its sisters from al-Mufassal (the later short surahs of the Qur'an, from Surat Qaf to the end) have made me grey."

Al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan (good), al-Hakim, who graded it sahih (sound), Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Ba'th wa al-Nushur* transmitted through the route of Ikrimah from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Abu Bakr said: 'O Messenger of Allah, you have grown grey.' He said: 'Hud, al-Waqi'ah, al-Mursalat, ʿAmma yatasa'aluna, and Idha al-shamsu kuwwirat have made me grey.'"

Ibn Asakir transmitted through the route of Ata' from him that "the Companions said: 'O Messenger of Allah, grey hair has come to you quickly.' He said: 'Indeed, Hud and its sisters have made me grey.'"

Ata' said: "Its sisters are: Iqtaraba al-sa'ah (the Hour has drawn near), al-Mursalat, and Idha al-shamsu kuwwirat."

Al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* (*Dala'il al-Nubuwwah*, on the proofs of prophethood) transmitted from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: (p-646) "Umar ibn al-Khattab said: 'O Messenger of Allah, grey hair has come to you quickly.' He said: 'Hud and its sisters have made me grey: al-Waqi'ah, ʿAmma yatasa'aluna, and Idha al-shamsu kuwwirat.'"

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Hud and its sisters have made me grey: al-Waqi'ah, al-Haqqah, and Idha al-shamsu kuwwirat."

Both of them (al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh) also transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud: "that Abu Bakr said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what has made you grey?' He said: 'Hud and al-Waqi'ah.'"

In its chain is Amr ibn Thabit, who is matruk (abandoned, a narrator whose reports are rejected).

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted with a sahih chain from Uqbah ibn Amir: "that a man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, you have grown grey.' He said: 'Hud has made me grey, and Idha al-shamsu kuwwirat and its sisters.'"

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in *Nawadir al-Usul*, Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in *Zawa'id al-Zuhd*, Abu Ya'la, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn Asakir transmitted from Abu Juhayfah, who said: "They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we see that you have grown grey.' He said: 'Hud and its sisters have made me grey.'"

Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn Asakir transmitted from Imran ibn Husayn "that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was told by his Companions: 'Grey hair has come to you quickly.' He said: 'Hud and its sisters from al-Mufassal have made me grey.'"

Ibn Asakir transmitted from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Hud and its sisters, and what was done to the nations before, have made me grey."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

.

His saying: *Alif-Lam-Ra* (*al-Ra*). If it is recited as a list of letters, as in the rest of the openings of the surahs, then it has no grammatical position (*mahall*). If it is the name of the surah, then it is in the nominative (*raf'*) position, as a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate is what follows it, or as the predicate of an omitted subject. In this case, *kitab* ("a Book") is a predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "This is a Book." The same applies if *al-Ra* has no grammatical position. It is also permissible for *al-Ra* to be in the accusative (*nasb*) position, by supposing a verb suited to the context, such as *udhkur* ("mention") or *iqra'* ("recite"). In that case, *kitab* is the predicate of an omitted subject. The demonstrative referred to by the omitted subject is either to some part of the Qur'an or to the whole Qur'an.

The meaning of ﴿its verses have been made firm﴾ is that they have become firm and perfected, with no deficiency or contradiction, like a solidly built structure. It has been said that its meaning is that they were not abrogated (*nuskh*, the cancellation of a ruling by a later revelation), unlike the Torah and the Gospel. On this view, this description of the Book is according to what is predominant, namely, that it is firm and has not been abrogated. It has also been said that its meaning is: its verses were made firm with commands and prohibitions, and then detailed with promise and threat, reward and punishment. It has been said: Allah made them firm against falsehood, then detailed them with what is lawful and what is unlawful. It has been said: its whole was made firm, then its verses were detailed. It has been said: it was gathered in the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawh al-mahfuz*), then detailed through revelation. It has been said: they were strengthened with decisive proofs indicating that they are from Allah. It has been said: the meaning of making them firm is that there is no corruption in them, derived from the saying "I made the animal firm" (*ahkamtu al-dabbah*) when you put a bridle (*hakama*) on it to prevent it from bolting. ﴿Then detailed﴾ is conjoined to *uhkimat* (made firm), and its meaning is as explained above. The delay indicated by *thumma* ("then") is either temporal, if the detailing is interpreted as revelation in stages according to what is beneficial, or ranked (*rutbi*), if it is interpreted as other than that already mentioned. The sentences are in the nominative position, either as attributes of *kitab*, or as another predicate of the subject, or as a predicate of an omitted subject. In His saying ﴿from One who is All-Wise, All-Aware﴾ there is a *laff wa-nashr* (a rhetorical arrangement in which two items are mentioned and then each is assigned to its counterpart), since the meaning is: a Wise One made it firm, and an All-Aware One, who knows the positions of affairs, detailed it.

His saying: ﴿that you worship none but Allah﴾. It is an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*) from which the *lam* has been omitted. This is what al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*, but it is objected that it is not an action of the agent of the verb being explained. It has been said that *an* (that) is explanatory (*mufassirah*) of what is in the detailing of the sense of saying. It has been said that it is an independent statement, disconnected from what precedes it, related as speech of the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: the supposed meaning is: "It was made firm with [the aim] that you worship none but Allah."

Al-Zajjaj said: "It was made firm, then detailed, so that you would worship none but Allah. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) informed them that he is a warner and a bearer of good news, and said: ﴿Indeed, I am to you from Him a warner and a bearer of good news﴾." That is, he warns them and makes them fear His punishment if they disobey Him, and gives them good news of Paradise and Allah's pleasure if they obey Him. The pronoun in *minhu* refers to Allah, glorified is He: that is, "Indeed I am to you, from Allah, glorified is He, a warner and a bearer of good news." It has been said that it is part of Allah's speech, glorified is He, like His saying: ﴿and Allah warns you of Himself﴾.

His saying: ﴿and that you seek forgiveness from your Lord﴾ is conjoined to *an la ta'budu* ("that you worship none"), and the discussion of this *an* is like the discussion of the one before it.

His saying: ﴿then turn to Him in repentance﴾ is conjoined to *istaghfiru* ("seek forgiveness"). He placed the guidance to seeking forgiveness before repentance because it is a means to it. It has been said that repentance is among the completions of seeking forgiveness. It has been said that the meaning of *istaghfiru* is "repent," and the meaning of *tubu* is: sincerely repent and remain steadfast in it. It has been said: seek forgiveness for past sins, then repent of those to come. It has been said: seek forgiveness from polytheism, then return to Him in obedience.

Al-Farra' said: *thumma* here has the meaning of *wa* ("and"): that is, "and repent to Him," because seeking forgiveness is repentance and repentance is seeking forgiveness. It has been said that seeking forgiveness is mentioned first because forgiveness is the desired goal, and repentance is the means to it, and what is last in attainment is first in seeking. It has been said: seek forgiveness for minor sins and repent to Him for major sins.

Then He arranged two matters upon what preceded:

The first: ﴿He will let you enjoy a good provision﴾. The basic meaning of *imta'* (causing enjoyment) is prolongation, and from it comes *amta'a Allahu bika* ("may Allah prolong your enjoyment of Him through you"). So the meaning of the verse is: He will prolong your benefit in this world with good, pleasing benefits, such as abundance of provision and comfortable living, ﴿until a specified term﴾, that is, until a time determined by Allah, which is death. It has been said that it is the Resurrection, and it has been said that it is entry into Paradise. The first is preferable.

The second matter is His saying: ﴿and He will give every possessor of virtue his virtue﴾. That is, He will give everyone who has virtue in obedience and deed his virtue, that is, the reward for his virtue, either in this world, or in the Hereafter, or in both together. The pronoun in *fadlihi* refers to *kulli dhi fadl* ("every possessor of virtue"). It has been said that it refers to Allah, glorified is He, in the sense that Allah gives everyone whose good deeds are abundant his virtue, which He bestows upon His servants.

Then He threatened them for opposing the command, saying: ﴿But if you turn away﴾, that is, if you turn away and turn aside from sincerity in worship, seeking forgiveness, and repentance, ﴿then indeed I fear for you the punishment of a great Day﴾, which is the Day of Resurrection. He described it as great because of the terrors in it. It has been said: the great Day is the Day of Badr.

Then He, glorified is He, explained the punishment of the great Day by His saying: ﴿To Allah is your return﴾, that is, your return to Him by death, then resurrection, then recompense, not to anyone else. ﴿And He is Able over all things﴾. Among that is your punishment for not complying. This sentence confirms what precedes it.

Then Allah, glorified is He, informed that this warning, admonition, and threat did not benefit them, nor did their hearts soften to it. Rather, they persist in stubbornness and are determined in disbelief. So He said, introducing this information with the word of attention, which indicates astonishment at their condition, and that it is a matter intelligent people ought to pay attention to and understand: ﴿Unquestionably, they fold their chests﴾. It is said: *thana sadrahu 'an al-shay'* ("he folded his chest away from a thing") when he turned away from it and deviated from it. So there is in the statement a metonymy for turning away, since whoever turns away from something folds his chest away from it and withdraws his side from it. It has been said that its meaning is: they bend their chests over what is in them of disbelief and aversion from the truth, so there is in the statement a metonymy for concealing what they believe of disbelief, as was the habit of the hypocrites.

The second interpretation is preferable, and it is supported by His saying: ﴿that they may hide from Him﴾, that is, that they may hide from Allah, so He does not reveal it to His Messenger and the believers, or that they may hide from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then He repeated the word of attention, clarifying the time at which they fold their chests, and said: ﴿Unquestionably, when they cover themselves with their garments﴾. That is, they conceal themselves at the time of covering themselves with garments, which is wrapping oneself in them. They used to say: when we close our doors, cover ourselves with our garments, and fold our chests in enmity toward Muhammad, who will know about us? It has been said: the meaning of *hina yastaghshuna* ("when they cover themselves") is: when they retire to their beds and wrap themselves in their clothes. It has been said that it is literal: some of the disbelievers, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed by them, would fold their chests, turn their backs, and cover themselves with their garments, so as not to hear the speech of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

The sentence ﴿He knows what they conceal and what they reveal﴾ is a new sentence explaining that there is no benefit for them in concealment, because Allah, glorified is He, knows what they conceal within themselves or in their private talk, and what they show. So the apparent and the hidden are alike to Him, and secret and open are the same.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, He is Knower of what is within the chests﴾ gives the reason for what precedes it and confirms it. *Dhat al-sudur* ("what is within the chests") refers to the inner thoughts that the chests contain. It has been said that it means the hearts. The meaning is: He knows all inner thoughts, or He knows the hearts and their states in concealment and disclosure, so nothing of that is hidden from Him.

Then He affirmed His knowledge of all knowable things with what contains the utmost favor and the greatest kindness, saying: ﴿And there is no creature on earth but that upon Allah is its provision﴾. That is, the provision it needs of food suitable to living beings of their various kinds, as a bounty and kindness from Him. It was expressed in the form of obligation, as the word *'ala* indicates, in consideration of the promise of it that preceded from Him. *Min* here is extra, for emphasis. The connection of this statement to what precedes it is that Allah, glorified is He, since He does not neglect any living creature with regard to the provision He has apportioned to it, how could He neglect its states, sayings, and deeds? *Dabbah* is every living creature that crawls. ﴿And He knows its place of settling﴾, that is, the place where it settles on the earth, or its place of lodging in the loins, ﴿and its place of storage﴾, its place in the wombs and what is similar to them, such as the egg and the like.

Al-Farra' said: its place of settling is where it takes shelter by night and by day, and its place of storage is the place where it dies. The full range of opinions has already been discussed in Surat al-An'am. The reason for placing the settling place before the storage place, according to al-Farra's view, is clear. As for the first view, perhaps its justification is that the settling place is more fitting given the state the creature is in as a living creature.

The meaning is: there is no creature on earth but that Allah provides for it, wherever it is, from its places, after being a creature and before being a creature, and that is where it is in the womb and the like. Then He concluded the verse with His saying: ﴿All of it is in a clear Book﴾, that is, all of what has been mentioned of the creatures, their settling and storage places, and their provision, ﴿is in a clear Book﴾, which is the Preserved Tablet, meaning it is recorded in it.

Then He affirmed the proofs of His power by mentioning the creation of the heavens and the earth, and how the state was before their creation, saying: ﴿And He is the One who created the heavens and the earth in six days﴾. This has already been explained in Surat al-A'raf. It has been said: the days are intended as periods, that is, in six periods, as in His saying: ﴿and whoever turns his back to them that day﴾ [al-Anfal: 16]. It has been said: the amount of six days. It is not correct that the days here mean the known days, which are the opposite of nights, because at that time there was neither earth nor heaven, and the day is nothing but an expression for the duration of the sun's being above the earth. The creation of the heavens took place in two days, and the creation of the earths in two days, and what is on them of kinds of living beings, plants, and inanimate things in two days, as will come in Surat Ha-Mim al-Sajdah.

His saying: ﴿And His Throne was upon the water﴾, that is, before their creation His Throne was upon the water. This indicates that the creation of the Throne and the water preceded the creation of the heavens and the earths.

His saying: ﴿that He may test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾. The *lam* is connected to *khalaqa* ("He created"). That is, He created these creations so that He would test His servants by reflection, contemplation, and reasoning on His perfect power, and on resurrection and recompense, to see which of them is best in deed compared to others. Belief enters into deed, because it is one of the deeds of the heart. It has been said: the intended meaning of "best in deed" is most complete in intellect. It has been said: most ascetic regarding this world. It has been said: most thankful. It has been said: most God-fearing.

His saying: ﴿And if you, [O Muhammad], say, "Indeed, you will be resurrected after death," those who disbelieve will surely say, "This is not but obvious magic."﴾ Then, since testing includes the matter of resurrection, He followed this with its mention. The meaning is: if you tell them, O Muhammad, in accordance with what the nature of testing requires, "Indeed, you will be resurrected after death, and the doer of good will be rewarded for his good and the doer of evil for his evil," ﴿those who disbelieve﴾ among the people will say, "This that you say, O Muhammad, is nothing but falsehood, like the falsehood of magic, and a deception like its deception."

It is permissible that the reference of *hadha* ("this") is to the Qur'an, because it is what includes the information about resurrection.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read: *in hadha illa sahir* ("this is none but a sorcerer"), meaning the Prophet (ﷺ). *Inna* was read with a kasrah in His saying *innakum* ("indeed you") because it comes after the verb of saying.

Sibawayh recorded the fat-hah (opening vowel) on the basis that *qulta* ("you said") is taken to mean *dhakarta* ("you mentioned"), or on the basis that *la'* is in the sense of *'alla* ("perhaps"): that is, "And if you say, 'Perhaps you will be resurrected,'" with the hope being regarded from the perspective of the addressees: that is, let them expect that, and do not conclusively reject it by denying it.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on surah 11, verses 7–12 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And if We delay the punishment from them﴾, meaning the punishment mentioned in His saying: ﴿the punishment of a great day﴾. It is also said that it is the punishment of the Day of Resurrection and what follows it, and it is also said that it is the Day of Badr. ﴿Until a counted community﴾, meaning until a group of days that are few, because what counting can encompass is few. The word *ummah* (community) is derived from *umm*, which means intention (*al-qasd*), and by it is meant the appointed time for the infliction of the punishment. It is also said that *ummah* originally means a group of people. The time may be named after what occurs in it, as in your saying, "I was with so-and-so at the time of the afternoon prayer," meaning at that time. So the meaning, according to this, is: until the time when a counted community of people passes away. ﴿They will surely say, "What is holding it back?"﴾, meaning: what is preventing it from descending? They say this in haste, by way of mockery and denial. Allah answered them with His saying: ﴿Unquestionably, on the day it comes to them, it will not be averted from them﴾, meaning it will not be withheld from them, but will befall them without doubt. The word *yawma* (on the day) is in the accusative, governed by *maṣrūfan* (averted). ﴿And what they used to mock at encompassed them﴾, meaning the punishment they used to seek in haste, mocking, encompassed them. The phrase *yastahzi'ūna* (they mock) is used in place of *yastaʻjilūna* (they seek in haste), because their seeking in haste was a form of mockery on their part. He expressed it in the past tense to alert to the certainty of its occurrence, as if it had already encompassed them.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Zayd that he recited: ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. A Book whose verses have been made firm﴾, and said: "All of it is firm (*muḥkamah*)," meaning Surah Hud. ﴿Then detailed﴾, and he said: "Then he mentioned Muhammad (ﷺ), and judged between him and those who opposed him, and he recited the verse in full, like the two groups. Then he mentioned the people of Noah, then Hud. This was the detailing of it, and its beginning was firm." He said: "My father used to say this," meaning Zayd ibn Aslam.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Hasan regarding His saying: ﴿A Book whose verses have been made firm﴾: he said, "They were made firm by command and prohibition, and detailed by promise and threat."

These same compilers related from Mujahid regarding *fussilat* (detailed): he said, "It was explained."

These same compilers also related from Qatada regarding the verse: he said, "Allah made it firm against falsehood, then detailed it with His knowledge, so He made clear its lawful and unlawful, its obedience and disobedience." Regarding His saying: ﴿from One who is All-Wise, All-Aware﴾, he said, "meaning from the presence of One who is Wise." Regarding His saying: ﴿He will let you enjoy a good provision﴾, he said: "You are in that provision, so take it by obedience to Allah and recognition of His right, for Allah is a bestower of favours who loves the grateful, and the people of gratitude are in increase from Allah, and that is His decree which He has decreed." Regarding His saying: ﴿until a specified term﴾, he said, "meaning death." Regarding His saying: ﴿and He gives every person of merit his merit﴾, he said, "meaning in the Hereafter."

These same compilers also related from Mujahid regarding His saying: ﴿and He gives every person of merit his merit﴾, meaning in the Hereafter.

Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Hasan: "He gives every person of merit in Islam the excellence of degrees in the Hereafter."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Mas'ud regarding His saying: ﴿and He gives every person of merit his merit﴾: he said, "Whoever does an evil deed, one evil deed is recorded against him, and whoever does a good deed, ten good deeds are recorded for him. If he is punished for the evil deed he committed in this world, ten good deeds remain for him. If he is not punished for it in this world, one of the ten good deeds is taken and nine good deeds remain for him. Then he says, 'Destroyed is the one whose units outweigh his tens.'"

al-Bukhari and others related from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿Unquestionably, they fold up their breasts﴾, to the end of the verse: he said, "They used to be shy to relieve themselves, lest they expose themselves to the sky, and to have intercourse with their wives, lest they expose themselves to the sky. So this was revealed concerning them."

al-Bukhari said: "And from Ibn Abbas, *yastaghshūna* (they cover themselves) means they cover their heads."

al-Bukhari also related from Ibn Abbas in the interpretation of this verse, meaning: doubt concerning Allah and the doing of evil deeds. Similarly it was related from Mujahid, al-Hasan and others: that is, they used to fold up their breasts when they said something or did something, thinking that by this they were hiding from Allah. So He, glorified is He, informed them that when they cover their garments at the time of their sleep in the darkness of the night, ﴿He knows what they conceal﴾ of speech, ﴿and what they reveal﴾.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Abdullah ibn Shaddad ibn al-Hadi regarding His saying: ﴿Unquestionably, they fold up their breasts﴾: he said, "When one of the hypocrites passed by the Prophet (ﷺ), he would bend his chest and cover his garment so that he would not be seen, so this was revealed."

Ibn Jarir related from al-Hasan regarding His saying: ﴿Unquestionably, when they cover their garments﴾: he said, "In the darkness of the night, within the inner parts of their houses."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Abu Razin regarding the verse: he said, "One of them would bend his back and cover himself with his garment."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatada regarding the verse: he said, "They used to conceal their breasts so that they would not hear the Book of Allah."

He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Unquestionably, when they cover their garments, He knows what they conceal﴾. That is the most concealed state a son of Adam can be in, when he bends his back, covers himself with his garment, and hides his concern within himself, yet Allah is not hidden from Him in that.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, who said regarding the verse: "They conceal what is in their hearts. ﴿Unquestionably, when they cover their garments, He knows what they did by night and by day.﴾"

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And there is no creature (*dābbah*) on the earth﴾, to the end of the verse, he said: "meaning every creature."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid regarding His saying: ﴿And there is no creature on the earth﴾, to the end of the verse: he said, "meaning that whatever provision comes to it is from Allah, though He may not provide it until it dies of hunger; but whatever provision is due to it is from Allah."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And He knows its *mustaqarr* (place of settling)﴾, he said: "where it shelters," and ﴿its *mustawda'* (place of deposit)﴾, he said: "where it dies."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him: ﴿And He knows its place of settling﴾, he said: "its provision comes to it wherever it may be."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound) related from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "﴿*Mustaqarr*﴾ is in the wombs, and ﴿*mustawda'*﴾ is where it dies."

What supports this interpretation that Ibn Mas'ud gave is what al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim related in *Nawadir al-Usul*, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab*, from Ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "When the term of one of you is in a land, a need is made for him toward it, until he reaches the furthest point of his trace there, and he is taken. Then on the Day of Resurrection the earth will say: 'This is what you deposited with me.'"

Abd al-Razzaq in *al-Musannaf*, al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim (who graded it sound) and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa al-Sifat* related from Ibn Abbas that he was asked regarding His saying: ﴿And His Throne was upon the water﴾: "Upon what was the water?" He said: "Upon the back of the wind."

Many hadiths have been transmitted concerning the description of the Throne and concerning how the heavens and the earth were created, but this is not the place to mention them.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim in *al-Tarikh* and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Umar, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse: ﴿That He may test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾. It was asked: 'What is the meaning of that, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'That He may test you as to which of you is best in intellect (*'aql*).' Then he said: 'The best of you in intellect is the most scrupulous of you regarding the prohibitions of Allah, and the most active of you in obedience to Allah.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatada, who said: "Which of you is most complete in intellect."

He also related from Sufyan, who said: "Which of you is most abstinent in this world."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatada, who said: "When the verse was revealed: ﴿The reckoning of people has drawn near to them﴾ (21:1), some people said: 'The Hour has indeed drawn near,' so they desisted. The people desisted a little, then returned to their deeds, the deeds of evil. So Allah revealed: ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾ (16:1). Then some people of misguidance said: 'This is the command of Allah, it has come.' So the people desisted, then returned to their plotting, the evil plotting. So Allah revealed this verse: ﴿And if We delay the punishment from them until a counted community﴾."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and al-Hakim (who graded it sound) related from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿until a counted community﴾, he said: "until a counted term."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatada regarding ﴿They will surely say, "What is holding it back?"﴾: "meaning the people of hypocrisy."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi regarding His saying: ﴿And what they used to mock at encompassed them﴾: he said, "meaning the punishment they mocked befell them."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

.

His saying: *Alif-Lam-Ra* (*al-Ra*). If it is recited as a list of letters, as in the rest of the openings of the surahs, then it has no grammatical position (*mahall*). If it is the name of the surah, then it is in the nominative (*raf'*) position, as a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate is what follows it, or as the predicate of an omitted subject. In this case, *kitab* ("a Book") is a predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "This is a Book." The same applies if *al-Ra* has no grammatical position. It is also permissible for *al-Ra* to be in the accusative (*nasb*) position, by supposing a verb suited to the context, such as *udhkur* ("mention") or *iqra'* ("recite"). In that case, *kitab* is the predicate of an omitted subject. The demonstrative referred to by the omitted subject is either to some part of the Qur'an or to the whole Qur'an.

The meaning of ﴿its verses have been made firm﴾ is that they have become firm and perfected, with no deficiency or contradiction, like a solidly built structure. It has been said that its meaning is that they were not abrogated (*nuskh*, the cancellation of a ruling by a later revelation), unlike the Torah and the Gospel. On this view, this description of the Book is according to what is predominant, namely, that it is firm and has not been abrogated. It has also been said that its meaning is: its verses were made firm with commands and prohibitions, and then detailed with promise and threat, reward and punishment. It has been said: Allah made them firm against falsehood, then detailed them with what is lawful and what is unlawful. It has been said: its whole was made firm, then its verses were detailed. It has been said: it was gathered in the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawh al-mahfuz*), then detailed through revelation. It has been said: they were strengthened with decisive proofs indicating that they are from Allah. It has been said: the meaning of making them firm is that there is no corruption in them, derived from the saying "I made the animal firm" (*ahkamtu al-dabbah*) when you put a bridle (*hakama*) on it to prevent it from bolting. ﴿Then detailed﴾ is conjoined to *uhkimat* (made firm), and its meaning is as explained above. The delay indicated by *thumma* ("then") is either temporal, if the detailing is interpreted as revelation in stages according to what is beneficial, or ranked (*rutbi*), if it is interpreted as other than that already mentioned. The sentences are in the nominative position, either as attributes of *kitab*, or as another predicate of the subject, or as a predicate of an omitted subject. In His saying ﴿from One who is All-Wise, All-Aware﴾ there is a *laff wa-nashr* (a rhetorical arrangement in which two items are mentioned and then each is assigned to its counterpart), since the meaning is: a Wise One made it firm, and an All-Aware One, who knows the positions of affairs, detailed it.

His saying: ﴿that you worship none but Allah﴾. It is an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*) from which the *lam* has been omitted. This is what al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*, but it is objected that it is not an action of the agent of the verb being explained. It has been said that *an* (that) is explanatory (*mufassirah*) of what is in the detailing of the sense of saying. It has been said that it is an independent statement, disconnected from what precedes it, related as speech of the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: the supposed meaning is: "It was made firm with [the aim] that you worship none but Allah."

Al-Zajjaj said: "It was made firm, then detailed, so that you would worship none but Allah. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) informed them that he is a warner and a bearer of good news, and said: ﴿Indeed, I am to you from Him a warner and a bearer of good news﴾." That is, he warns them and makes them fear His punishment if they disobey Him, and gives them good news of Paradise and Allah's pleasure if they obey Him. The pronoun in *minhu* refers to Allah, glorified is He: that is, "Indeed I am to you, from Allah, glorified is He, a warner and a bearer of good news." It has been said that it is part of Allah's speech, glorified is He, like His saying: ﴿and Allah warns you of Himself﴾.

His saying: ﴿and that you seek forgiveness from your Lord﴾ is conjoined to *an la ta'budu* ("that you worship none"), and the discussion of this *an* is like the discussion of the one before it.

His saying: ﴿then turn to Him in repentance﴾ is conjoined to *istaghfiru* ("seek forgiveness"). He placed the guidance to seeking forgiveness before repentance because it is a means to it. It has been said that repentance is among the completions of seeking forgiveness. It has been said that the meaning of *istaghfiru* is "repent," and the meaning of *tubu* is: sincerely repent and remain steadfast in it. It has been said: seek forgiveness for past sins, then repent of those to come. It has been said: seek forgiveness from polytheism, then return to Him in obedience.

Al-Farra' said: *thumma* here has the meaning of *wa* ("and"): that is, "and repent to Him," because seeking forgiveness is repentance and repentance is seeking forgiveness. It has been said that seeking forgiveness is mentioned first because forgiveness is the desired goal, and repentance is the means to it, and what is last in attainment is first in seeking. It has been said: seek forgiveness for minor sins and repent to Him for major sins.

Then He arranged two matters upon what preceded:

The first: ﴿He will let you enjoy a good provision﴾. The basic meaning of *imta'* (causing enjoyment) is prolongation, and from it comes *amta'a Allahu bika* ("may Allah prolong your enjoyment of Him through you"). So the meaning of the verse is: He will prolong your benefit in this world with good, pleasing benefits, such as abundance of provision and comfortable living, ﴿until a specified term﴾, that is, until a time determined by Allah, which is death. It has been said that it is the Resurrection, and it has been said that it is entry into Paradise. The first is preferable.

The second matter is His saying: ﴿and He will give every possessor of virtue his virtue﴾. That is, He will give everyone who has virtue in obedience and deed his virtue, that is, the reward for his virtue, either in this world, or in the Hereafter, or in both together. The pronoun in *fadlihi* refers to *kulli dhi fadl* ("every possessor of virtue"). It has been said that it refers to Allah, glorified is He, in the sense that Allah gives everyone whose good deeds are abundant his virtue, which He bestows upon His servants.

Then He threatened them for opposing the command, saying: ﴿But if you turn away﴾, that is, if you turn away and turn aside from sincerity in worship, seeking forgiveness, and repentance, ﴿then indeed I fear for you the punishment of a great Day﴾, which is the Day of Resurrection. He described it as great because of the terrors in it. It has been said: the great Day is the Day of Badr.

Then He, glorified is He, explained the punishment of the great Day by His saying: ﴿To Allah is your return﴾, that is, your return to Him by death, then resurrection, then recompense, not to anyone else. ﴿And He is Able over all things﴾. Among that is your punishment for not complying. This sentence confirms what precedes it.

Then Allah, glorified is He, informed that this warning, admonition, and threat did not benefit them, nor did their hearts soften to it. Rather, they persist in stubbornness and are determined in disbelief. So He said, introducing this information with the word of attention, which indicates astonishment at their condition, and that it is a matter intelligent people ought to pay attention to and understand: ﴿Unquestionably, they fold their chests﴾. It is said: *thana sadrahu 'an al-shay'* ("he folded his chest away from a thing") when he turned away from it and deviated from it. So there is in the statement a metonymy for turning away, since whoever turns away from something folds his chest away from it and withdraws his side from it. It has been said that its meaning is: they bend their chests over what is in them of disbelief and aversion from the truth, so there is in the statement a metonymy for concealing what they believe of disbelief, as was the habit of the hypocrites.

The second interpretation is preferable, and it is supported by His saying: ﴿that they may hide from Him﴾, that is, that they may hide from Allah, so He does not reveal it to His Messenger and the believers, or that they may hide from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then He repeated the word of attention, clarifying the time at which they fold their chests, and said: ﴿Unquestionably, when they cover themselves with their garments﴾. That is, they conceal themselves at the time of covering themselves with garments, which is wrapping oneself in them. They used to say: when we close our doors, cover ourselves with our garments, and fold our chests in enmity toward Muhammad, who will know about us? It has been said: the meaning of *hina yastaghshuna* ("when they cover themselves") is: when they retire to their beds and wrap themselves in their clothes. It has been said that it is literal: some of the disbelievers, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed by them, would fold their chests, turn their backs, and cover themselves with their garments, so as not to hear the speech of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

The sentence ﴿He knows what they conceal and what they reveal﴾ is a new sentence explaining that there is no benefit for them in concealment, because Allah, glorified is He, knows what they conceal within themselves or in their private talk, and what they show. So the apparent and the hidden are alike to Him, and secret and open are the same.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, He is Knower of what is within the chests﴾ gives the reason for what precedes it and confirms it. *Dhat al-sudur* ("what is within the chests") refers to the inner thoughts that the chests contain. It has been said that it means the hearts. The meaning is: He knows all inner thoughts, or He knows the hearts and their states in concealment and disclosure, so nothing of that is hidden from Him.

Then He affirmed His knowledge of all knowable things with what contains the utmost favor and the greatest kindness, saying: ﴿And there is no creature on earth but that upon Allah is its provision﴾. That is, the provision it needs of food suitable to living beings of their various kinds, as a bounty and kindness from Him. It was expressed in the form of obligation, as the word *'ala* indicates, in consideration of the promise of it that preceded from Him. *Min* here is extra, for emphasis. The connection of this statement to what precedes it is that Allah, glorified is He, since He does not neglect any living creature with regard to the provision He has apportioned to it, how could He neglect its states, sayings, and deeds? *Dabbah* is every living creature that crawls. ﴿And He knows its place of settling﴾, that is, the place where it settles on the earth, or its place of lodging in the loins, ﴿and its place of storage﴾, its place in the wombs and what is similar to them, such as the egg and the like.

Al-Farra' said: its place of settling is where it takes shelter by night and by day, and its place of storage is the place where it dies. The full range of opinions has already been discussed in Surat al-An'am. The reason for placing the settling place before the storage place, according to al-Farra's view, is clear. As for the first view, perhaps its justification is that the settling place is more fitting given the state the creature is in as a living creature.

The meaning is: there is no creature on earth but that Allah provides for it, wherever it is, from its places, after being a creature and before being a creature, and that is where it is in the womb and the like. Then He concluded the verse with His saying: ﴿All of it is in a clear Book﴾, that is, all of what has been mentioned of the creatures, their settling and storage places, and their provision, ﴿is in a clear Book﴾, which is the Preserved Tablet, meaning it is recorded in it.

Then He affirmed the proofs of His power by mentioning the creation of the heavens and the earth, and how the state was before their creation, saying: ﴿And He is the One who created the heavens and the earth in six days﴾. This has already been explained in Surat al-A'raf. It has been said: the days are intended as periods, that is, in six periods, as in His saying: ﴿and whoever turns his back to them that day﴾ [al-Anfal: 16]. It has been said: the amount of six days. It is not correct that the days here mean the known days, which are the opposite of nights, because at that time there was neither earth nor heaven, and the day is nothing but an expression for the duration of the sun's being above the earth. The creation of the heavens took place in two days, and the creation of the earths in two days, and what is on them of kinds of living beings, plants, and inanimate things in two days, as will come in Surat Ha-Mim al-Sajdah.

His saying: ﴿And His Throne was upon the water﴾, that is, before their creation His Throne was upon the water. This indicates that the creation of the Throne and the water preceded the creation of the heavens and the earths.

His saying: ﴿that He may test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾. The *lam* is connected to *khalaqa* ("He created"). That is, He created these creations so that He would test His servants by reflection, contemplation, and reasoning on His perfect power, and on resurrection and recompense, to see which of them is best in deed compared to others. Belief enters into deed, because it is one of the deeds of the heart. It has been said: the intended meaning of "best in deed" is most complete in intellect. It has been said: most ascetic regarding this world. It has been said: most thankful. It has been said: most God-fearing.

His saying: ﴿And if you, [O Muhammad], say, "Indeed, you will be resurrected after death," those who disbelieve will surely say, "This is not but obvious magic."﴾ Then, since testing includes the matter of resurrection, He followed this with its mention. The meaning is: if you tell them, O Muhammad, in accordance with what the nature of testing requires, "Indeed, you will be resurrected after death, and the doer of good will be rewarded for his good and the doer of evil for his evil," ﴿those who disbelieve﴾ among the people will say, "This that you say, O Muhammad, is nothing but falsehood, like the falsehood of magic, and a deception like its deception."

It is permissible that the reference of *hadha* ("this") is to the Qur'an, because it is what includes the information about resurrection.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read: *in hadha illa sahir* ("this is none but a sorcerer"), meaning the Prophet (ﷺ). *Inna* was read with a kasrah in His saying *innakum* ("indeed you") because it comes after the verb of saying.

Sibawayh recorded the fat-hah (opening vowel) on the basis that *qulta* ("you said") is taken to mean *dhakarta* ("you mentioned"), or on the basis that *la'* is in the sense of *'alla* ("perhaps"): that is, "And if you say, 'Perhaps you will be resurrected,'" with the hope being regarded from the perspective of the addressees: that is, let them expect that, and do not conclusively reject it by denying it.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on surah 11, verses 7–12 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And if We delay the punishment from them﴾, meaning the punishment mentioned in His saying: ﴿the punishment of a great day﴾. It is also said that it is the punishment of the Day of Resurrection and what follows it, and it is also said that it is the Day of Badr. ﴿Until a counted community﴾, meaning until a group of days that are few, because what counting can encompass is few. The word *ummah* (community) is derived from *umm*, which means intention (*al-qasd*), and by it is meant the appointed time for the infliction of the punishment. It is also said that *ummah* originally means a group of people. The time may be named after what occurs in it, as in your saying, "I was with so-and-so at the time of the afternoon prayer," meaning at that time. So the meaning, according to this, is: until the time when a counted community of people passes away. ﴿They will surely say, "What is holding it back?"﴾, meaning: what is preventing it from descending? They say this in haste, by way of mockery and denial. Allah answered them with His saying: ﴿Unquestionably, on the day it comes to them, it will not be averted from them﴾, meaning it will not be withheld from them, but will befall them without doubt. The word *yawma* (on the day) is in the accusative, governed by *maṣrūfan* (averted). ﴿And what they used to mock at encompassed them﴾, meaning the punishment they used to seek in haste, mocking, encompassed them. The phrase *yastahzi'ūna* (they mock) is used in place of *yastaʻjilūna* (they seek in haste), because their seeking in haste was a form of mockery on their part. He expressed it in the past tense to alert to the certainty of its occurrence, as if it had already encompassed them.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Zayd that he recited: ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. A Book whose verses have been made firm﴾, and said: "All of it is firm (*muḥkamah*)," meaning Surah Hud. ﴿Then detailed﴾, and he said: "Then he mentioned Muhammad (ﷺ), and judged between him and those who opposed him, and he recited the verse in full, like the two groups. Then he mentioned the people of Noah, then Hud. This was the detailing of it, and its beginning was firm." He said: "My father used to say this," meaning Zayd ibn Aslam.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Hasan regarding His saying: ﴿A Book whose verses have been made firm﴾: he said, "They were made firm by command and prohibition, and detailed by promise and threat."

These same compilers related from Mujahid regarding *fussilat* (detailed): he said, "It was explained."

These same compilers also related from Qatada regarding the verse: he said, "Allah made it firm against falsehood, then detailed it with His knowledge, so He made clear its lawful and unlawful, its obedience and disobedience." Regarding His saying: ﴿from One who is All-Wise, All-Aware﴾, he said, "meaning from the presence of One who is Wise." Regarding His saying: ﴿He will let you enjoy a good provision﴾, he said: "You are in that provision, so take it by obedience to Allah and recognition of His right, for Allah is a bestower of favours who loves the grateful, and the people of gratitude are in increase from Allah, and that is His decree which He has decreed." Regarding His saying: ﴿until a specified term﴾, he said, "meaning death." Regarding His saying: ﴿and He gives every person of merit his merit﴾, he said, "meaning in the Hereafter."

These same compilers also related from Mujahid regarding His saying: ﴿and He gives every person of merit his merit﴾, meaning in the Hereafter.

Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Hasan: "He gives every person of merit in Islam the excellence of degrees in the Hereafter."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Mas'ud regarding His saying: ﴿and He gives every person of merit his merit﴾: he said, "Whoever does an evil deed, one evil deed is recorded against him, and whoever does a good deed, ten good deeds are recorded for him. If he is punished for the evil deed he committed in this world, ten good deeds remain for him. If he is not punished for it in this world, one of the ten good deeds is taken and nine good deeds remain for him. Then he says, 'Destroyed is the one whose units outweigh his tens.'"

al-Bukhari and others related from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿Unquestionably, they fold up their breasts﴾, to the end of the verse: he said, "They used to be shy to relieve themselves, lest they expose themselves to the sky, and to have intercourse with their wives, lest they expose themselves to the sky. So this was revealed concerning them."

al-Bukhari said: "And from Ibn Abbas, *yastaghshūna* (they cover themselves) means they cover their heads."

al-Bukhari also related from Ibn Abbas in the interpretation of this verse, meaning: doubt concerning Allah and the doing of evil deeds. Similarly it was related from Mujahid, al-Hasan and others: that is, they used to fold up their breasts when they said something or did something, thinking that by this they were hiding from Allah. So He, glorified is He, informed them that when they cover their garments at the time of their sleep in the darkness of the night, ﴿He knows what they conceal﴾ of speech, ﴿and what they reveal﴾.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Abdullah ibn Shaddad ibn al-Hadi regarding His saying: ﴿Unquestionably, they fold up their breasts﴾: he said, "When one of the hypocrites passed by the Prophet (ﷺ), he would bend his chest and cover his garment so that he would not be seen, so this was revealed."

Ibn Jarir related from al-Hasan regarding His saying: ﴿Unquestionably, when they cover their garments﴾: he said, "In the darkness of the night, within the inner parts of their houses."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Abu Razin regarding the verse: he said, "One of them would bend his back and cover himself with his garment."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatada regarding the verse: he said, "They used to conceal their breasts so that they would not hear the Book of Allah."

He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Unquestionably, when they cover their garments, He knows what they conceal﴾. That is the most concealed state a son of Adam can be in, when he bends his back, covers himself with his garment, and hides his concern within himself, yet Allah is not hidden from Him in that.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, who said regarding the verse: "They conceal what is in their hearts. ﴿Unquestionably, when they cover their garments, He knows what they did by night and by day.﴾"

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And there is no creature (*dābbah*) on the earth﴾, to the end of the verse, he said: "meaning every creature."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid regarding His saying: ﴿And there is no creature on the earth﴾, to the end of the verse: he said, "meaning that whatever provision comes to it is from Allah, though He may not provide it until it dies of hunger; but whatever provision is due to it is from Allah."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And He knows its *mustaqarr* (place of settling)﴾, he said: "where it shelters," and ﴿its *mustawda'* (place of deposit)﴾, he said: "where it dies."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him: ﴿And He knows its place of settling﴾, he said: "its provision comes to it wherever it may be."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound) related from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "﴿*Mustaqarr*﴾ is in the wombs, and ﴿*mustawda'*﴾ is where it dies."

What supports this interpretation that Ibn Mas'ud gave is what al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim related in *Nawadir al-Usul*, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab*, from Ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "When the term of one of you is in a land, a need is made for him toward it, until he reaches the furthest point of his trace there, and he is taken. Then on the Day of Resurrection the earth will say: 'This is what you deposited with me.'"

Abd al-Razzaq in *al-Musannaf*, al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim (who graded it sound) and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa al-Sifat* related from Ibn Abbas that he was asked regarding His saying: ﴿And His Throne was upon the water﴾: "Upon what was the water?" He said: "Upon the back of the wind."

Many hadiths have been transmitted concerning the description of the Throne and concerning how the heavens and the earth were created, but this is not the place to mention them.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim in *al-Tarikh* and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Umar, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse: ﴿That He may test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾. It was asked: 'What is the meaning of that, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'That He may test you as to which of you is best in intellect (*'aql*).' Then he said: 'The best of you in intellect is the most scrupulous of you regarding the prohibitions of Allah, and the most active of you in obedience to Allah.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatada, who said: "Which of you is most complete in intellect."

He also related from Sufyan, who said: "Which of you is most abstinent in this world."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatada, who said: "When the verse was revealed: ﴿The reckoning of people has drawn near to them﴾ (21:1), some people said: 'The Hour has indeed drawn near,' so they desisted. The people desisted a little, then returned to their deeds, the deeds of evil. So Allah revealed: ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾ (16:1). Then some people of misguidance said: 'This is the command of Allah, it has come.' So the people desisted, then returned to their plotting, the evil plotting. So Allah revealed this verse: ﴿And if We delay the punishment from them until a counted community﴾."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and al-Hakim (who graded it sound) related from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿until a counted community﴾, he said: "until a counted term."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatada regarding ﴿They will surely say, "What is holding it back?"﴾: "meaning the people of hypocrisy."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi regarding His saying: ﴿And what they used to mock at encompassed them﴾: he said, "meaning the punishment they mocked befell them."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

.

His saying: *Alif-Lam-Ra* (*al-Ra*). If it is recited as a list of letters, as in the rest of the openings of the surahs, then it has no grammatical position (*mahall*). If it is the name of the surah, then it is in the nominative (*raf'*) position, as a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate is what follows it, or as the predicate of an omitted subject. In this case, *kitab* ("a Book") is a predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "This is a Book." The same applies if *al-Ra* has no grammatical position. It is also permissible for *al-Ra* to be in the accusative (*nasb*) position, by supposing a verb suited to the context, such as *udhkur* ("mention") or *iqra'* ("recite"). In that case, *kitab* is the predicate of an omitted subject. The demonstrative referred to by the omitted subject is either to some part of the Qur'an or to the whole Qur'an.

The meaning of ﴿its verses have been made firm﴾ is that they have become firm and perfected, with no deficiency or contradiction, like a solidly built structure. It has been said that its meaning is that they were not abrogated (*nuskh*, the cancellation of a ruling by a later revelation), unlike the Torah and the Gospel. On this view, this description of the Book is according to what is predominant, namely, that it is firm and has not been abrogated. It has also been said that its meaning is: its verses were made firm with commands and prohibitions, and then detailed with promise and threat, reward and punishment. It has been said: Allah made them firm against falsehood, then detailed them with what is lawful and what is unlawful. It has been said: its whole was made firm, then its verses were detailed. It has been said: it was gathered in the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawh al-mahfuz*), then detailed through revelation. It has been said: they were strengthened with decisive proofs indicating that they are from Allah. It has been said: the meaning of making them firm is that there is no corruption in them, derived from the saying "I made the animal firm" (*ahkamtu al-dabbah*) when you put a bridle (*hakama*) on it to prevent it from bolting. ﴿Then detailed﴾ is conjoined to *uhkimat* (made firm), and its meaning is as explained above. The delay indicated by *thumma* ("then") is either temporal, if the detailing is interpreted as revelation in stages according to what is beneficial, or ranked (*rutbi*), if it is interpreted as other than that already mentioned. The sentences are in the nominative position, either as attributes of *kitab*, or as another predicate of the subject, or as a predicate of an omitted subject. In His saying ﴿from One who is All-Wise, All-Aware﴾ there is a *laff wa-nashr* (a rhetorical arrangement in which two items are mentioned and then each is assigned to its counterpart), since the meaning is: a Wise One made it firm, and an All-Aware One, who knows the positions of affairs, detailed it.

His saying: ﴿that you worship none but Allah﴾. It is an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*) from which the *lam* has been omitted. This is what al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*, but it is objected that it is not an action of the agent of the verb being explained. It has been said that *an* (that) is explanatory (*mufassirah*) of what is in the detailing of the sense of saying. It has been said that it is an independent statement, disconnected from what precedes it, related as speech of the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: the supposed meaning is: "It was made firm with [the aim] that you worship none but Allah."

Al-Zajjaj said: "It was made firm, then detailed, so that you would worship none but Allah. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) informed them that he is a warner and a bearer of good news, and said: ﴿Indeed, I am to you from Him a warner and a bearer of good news﴾." That is, he warns them and makes them fear His punishment if they disobey Him, and gives them good news of Paradise and Allah's pleasure if they obey Him. The pronoun in *minhu* refers to Allah, glorified is He: that is, "Indeed I am to you, from Allah, glorified is He, a warner and a bearer of good news." It has been said that it is part of Allah's speech, glorified is He, like His saying: ﴿and Allah warns you of Himself﴾.

His saying: ﴿and that you seek forgiveness from your Lord﴾ is conjoined to *an la ta'budu* ("that you worship none"), and the discussion of this *an* is like the discussion of the one before it.

His saying: ﴿then turn to Him in repentance﴾ is conjoined to *istaghfiru* ("seek forgiveness"). He placed the guidance to seeking forgiveness before repentance because it is a means to it. It has been said that repentance is among the completions of seeking forgiveness. It has been said that the meaning of *istaghfiru* is "repent," and the meaning of *tubu* is: sincerely repent and remain steadfast in it. It has been said: seek forgiveness for past sins, then repent of those to come. It has been said: seek forgiveness from polytheism, then return to Him in obedience.

Al-Farra' said: *thumma* here has the meaning of *wa* ("and"): that is, "and repent to Him," because seeking forgiveness is repentance and repentance is seeking forgiveness. It has been said that seeking forgiveness is mentioned first because forgiveness is the desired goal, and repentance is the means to it, and what is last in attainment is first in seeking. It has been said: seek forgiveness for minor sins and repent to Him for major sins.

Then He arranged two matters upon what preceded:

The first: ﴿He will let you enjoy a good provision﴾. The basic meaning of *imta'* (causing enjoyment) is prolongation, and from it comes *amta'a Allahu bika* ("may Allah prolong your enjoyment of Him through you"). So the meaning of the verse is: He will prolong your benefit in this world with good, pleasing benefits, such as abundance of provision and comfortable living, ﴿until a specified term﴾, that is, until a time determined by Allah, which is death. It has been said that it is the Resurrection, and it has been said that it is entry into Paradise. The first is preferable.

The second matter is His saying: ﴿and He will give every possessor of virtue his virtue﴾. That is, He will give everyone who has virtue in obedience and deed his virtue, that is, the reward for his virtue, either in this world, or in the Hereafter, or in both together. The pronoun in *fadlihi* refers to *kulli dhi fadl* ("every possessor of virtue"). It has been said that it refers to Allah, glorified is He, in the sense that Allah gives everyone whose good deeds are abundant his virtue, which He bestows upon His servants.

Then He threatened them for opposing the command, saying: ﴿But if you turn away﴾, that is, if you turn away and turn aside from sincerity in worship, seeking forgiveness, and repentance, ﴿then indeed I fear for you the punishment of a great Day﴾, which is the Day of Resurrection. He described it as great because of the terrors in it. It has been said: the great Day is the Day of Badr.

Then He, glorified is He, explained the punishment of the great Day by His saying: ﴿To Allah is your return﴾, that is, your return to Him by death, then resurrection, then recompense, not to anyone else. ﴿And He is Able over all things﴾. Among that is your punishment for not complying. This sentence confirms what precedes it.

Then Allah, glorified is He, informed that this warning, admonition, and threat did not benefit them, nor did their hearts soften to it. Rather, they persist in stubbornness and are determined in disbelief. So He said, introducing this information with the word of attention, which indicates astonishment at their condition, and that it is a matter intelligent people ought to pay attention to and understand: ﴿Unquestionably, they fold their chests﴾. It is said: *thana sadrahu 'an al-shay'* ("he folded his chest away from a thing") when he turned away from it and deviated from it. So there is in the statement a metonymy for turning away, since whoever turns away from something folds his chest away from it and withdraws his side from it. It has been said that its meaning is: they bend their chests over what is in them of disbelief and aversion from the truth, so there is in the statement a metonymy for concealing what they believe of disbelief, as was the habit of the hypocrites.

The second interpretation is preferable, and it is supported by His saying: ﴿that they may hide from Him﴾, that is, that they may hide from Allah, so He does not reveal it to His Messenger and the believers, or that they may hide from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then He repeated the word of attention, clarifying the time at which they fold their chests, and said: ﴿Unquestionably, when they cover themselves with their garments﴾. That is, they conceal themselves at the time of covering themselves with garments, which is wrapping oneself in them. They used to say: when we close our doors, cover ourselves with our garments, and fold our chests in enmity toward Muhammad, who will know about us? It has been said: the meaning of *hina yastaghshuna* ("when they cover themselves") is: when they retire to their beds and wrap themselves in their clothes. It has been said that it is literal: some of the disbelievers, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed by them, would fold their chests, turn their backs, and cover themselves with their garments, so as not to hear the speech of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

The sentence ﴿He knows what they conceal and what they reveal﴾ is a new sentence explaining that there is no benefit for them in concealment, because Allah, glorified is He, knows what they conceal within themselves or in their private talk, and what they show. So the apparent and the hidden are alike to Him, and secret and open are the same.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, He is Knower of what is within the chests﴾ gives the reason for what precedes it and confirms it. *Dhat al-sudur* ("what is within the chests") refers to the inner thoughts that the chests contain. It has been said that it means the hearts. The meaning is: He knows all inner thoughts, or He knows the hearts and their states in concealment and disclosure, so nothing of that is hidden from Him.

Then He affirmed His knowledge of all knowable things with what contains the utmost favor and the greatest kindness, saying: ﴿And there is no creature on earth but that upon Allah is its provision﴾. That is, the provision it needs of food suitable to living beings of their various kinds, as a bounty and kindness from Him. It was expressed in the form of obligation, as the word *'ala* indicates, in consideration of the promise of it that preceded from Him. *Min* here is extra, for emphasis. The connection of this statement to what precedes it is that Allah, glorified is He, since He does not neglect any living creature with regard to the provision He has apportioned to it, how could He neglect its states, sayings, and deeds? *Dabbah* is every living creature that crawls. ﴿And He knows its place of settling﴾, that is, the place where it settles on the earth, or its place of lodging in the loins, ﴿and its place of storage﴾, its place in the wombs and what is similar to them, such as the egg and the like.

Al-Farra' said: its place of settling is where it takes shelter by night and by day, and its place of storage is the place where it dies. The full range of opinions has already been discussed in Surat al-An'am. The reason for placing the settling place before the storage place, according to al-Farra's view, is clear. As for the first view, perhaps its justification is that the settling place is more fitting given the state the creature is in as a living creature.

The meaning is: there is no creature on earth but that Allah provides for it, wherever it is, from its places, after being a creature and before being a creature, and that is where it is in the womb and the like. Then He concluded the verse with His saying: ﴿All of it is in a clear Book﴾, that is, all of what has been mentioned of the creatures, their settling and storage places, and their provision, ﴿is in a clear Book﴾, which is the Preserved Tablet, meaning it is recorded in it.

Then He affirmed the proofs of His power by mentioning the creation of the heavens and the earth, and how the state was before their creation, saying: ﴿And He is the One who created the heavens and the earth in six days﴾. This has already been explained in Surat al-A'raf. It has been said: the days are intended as periods, that is, in six periods, as in His saying: ﴿and whoever turns his back to them that day﴾ [al-Anfal: 16]. It has been said: the amount of six days. It is not correct that the days here mean the known days, which are the opposite of nights, because at that time there was neither earth nor heaven, and the day is nothing but an expression for the duration of the sun's being above the earth. The creation of the heavens took place in two days, and the creation of the earths in two days, and what is on them of kinds of living beings, plants, and inanimate things in two days, as will come in Surat Ha-Mim al-Sajdah.

His saying: ﴿And His Throne was upon the water﴾, that is, before their creation His Throne was upon the water. This indicates that the creation of the Throne and the water preceded the creation of the heavens and the earths.

His saying: ﴿that He may test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾. The *lam* is connected to *khalaqa* ("He created"). That is, He created these creations so that He would test His servants by reflection, contemplation, and reasoning on His perfect power, and on resurrection and recompense, to see which of them is best in deed compared to others. Belief enters into deed, because it is one of the deeds of the heart. It has been said: the intended meaning of "best in deed" is most complete in intellect. It has been said: most ascetic regarding this world. It has been said: most thankful. It has been said: most God-fearing.

His saying: ﴿And if you, [O Muhammad], say, "Indeed, you will be resurrected after death," those who disbelieve will surely say, "This is not but obvious magic."﴾ Then, since testing includes the matter of resurrection, He followed this with its mention. The meaning is: if you tell them, O Muhammad, in accordance with what the nature of testing requires, "Indeed, you will be resurrected after death, and the doer of good will be rewarded for his good and the doer of evil for his evil," ﴿those who disbelieve﴾ among the people will say, "This that you say, O Muhammad, is nothing but falsehood, like the falsehood of magic, and a deception like its deception."

It is permissible that the reference of *hadha* ("this") is to the Qur'an, because it is what includes the information about resurrection.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read: *in hadha illa sahir* ("this is none but a sorcerer"), meaning the Prophet (ﷺ). *Inna* was read with a kasrah in His saying *innakum* ("indeed you") because it comes after the verb of saying.

Sibawayh recorded the fat-hah (opening vowel) on the basis that *qulta* ("you said") is taken to mean *dhakarta* ("you mentioned"), or on the basis that *la'* is in the sense of *'alla* ("perhaps"): that is, "And if you say, 'Perhaps you will be resurrected,'" with the hope being regarded from the perspective of the addressees: that is, let them expect that, and do not conclusively reject it by denying it.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on surah 11, verses 7–12 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And if We delay the punishment from them﴾, meaning the punishment mentioned in His saying: ﴿the punishment of a great day﴾. It is also said that it is the punishment of the Day of Resurrection and what follows it, and it is also said that it is the Day of Badr. ﴿Until a counted community﴾, meaning until a group of days that are few, because what counting can encompass is few. The word *ummah* (community) is derived from *umm*, which means intention (*al-qasd*), and by it is meant the appointed time for the infliction of the punishment. It is also said that *ummah* originally means a group of people. The time may be named after what occurs in it, as in your saying, "I was with so-and-so at the time of the afternoon prayer," meaning at that time. So the meaning, according to this, is: until the time when a counted community of people passes away. ﴿They will surely say, "What is holding it back?"﴾, meaning: what is preventing it from descending? They say this in haste, by way of mockery and denial. Allah answered them with His saying: ﴿Unquestionably, on the day it comes to them, it will not be averted from them﴾, meaning it will not be withheld from them, but will befall them without doubt. The word *yawma* (on the day) is in the accusative, governed by *maṣrūfan* (averted). ﴿And what they used to mock at encompassed them﴾, meaning the punishment they used to seek in haste, mocking, encompassed them. The phrase *yastahzi'ūna* (they mock) is used in place of *yastaʻjilūna* (they seek in haste), because their seeking in haste was a form of mockery on their part. He expressed it in the past tense to alert to the certainty of its occurrence, as if it had already encompassed them.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Zayd that he recited: ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. A Book whose verses have been made firm﴾, and said: "All of it is firm (*muḥkamah*)," meaning Surah Hud. ﴿Then detailed﴾, and he said: "Then he mentioned Muhammad (ﷺ), and judged between him and those who opposed him, and he recited the verse in full, like the two groups. Then he mentioned the people of Noah, then Hud. This was the detailing of it, and its beginning was firm." He said: "My father used to say this," meaning Zayd ibn Aslam.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Hasan regarding His saying: ﴿A Book whose verses have been made firm﴾: he said, "They were made firm by command and prohibition, and detailed by promise and threat."

These same compilers related from Mujahid regarding *fussilat* (detailed): he said, "It was explained."

These same compilers also related from Qatada regarding the verse: he said, "Allah made it firm against falsehood, then detailed it with His knowledge, so He made clear its lawful and unlawful, its obedience and disobedience." Regarding His saying: ﴿from One who is All-Wise, All-Aware﴾, he said, "meaning from the presence of One who is Wise." Regarding His saying: ﴿He will let you enjoy a good provision﴾, he said: "You are in that provision, so take it by obedience to Allah and recognition of His right, for Allah is a bestower of favours who loves the grateful, and the people of gratitude are in increase from Allah, and that is His decree which He has decreed." Regarding His saying: ﴿until a specified term﴾, he said, "meaning death." Regarding His saying: ﴿and He gives every person of merit his merit﴾, he said, "meaning in the Hereafter."

These same compilers also related from Mujahid regarding His saying: ﴿and He gives every person of merit his merit﴾, meaning in the Hereafter.

Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Hasan: "He gives every person of merit in Islam the excellence of degrees in the Hereafter."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Mas'ud regarding His saying: ﴿and He gives every person of merit his merit﴾: he said, "Whoever does an evil deed, one evil deed is recorded against him, and whoever does a good deed, ten good deeds are recorded for him. If he is punished for the evil deed he committed in this world, ten good deeds remain for him. If he is not punished for it in this world, one of the ten good deeds is taken and nine good deeds remain for him. Then he says, 'Destroyed is the one whose units outweigh his tens.'"

al-Bukhari and others related from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿Unquestionably, they fold up their breasts﴾, to the end of the verse: he said, "They used to be shy to relieve themselves, lest they expose themselves to the sky, and to have intercourse with their wives, lest they expose themselves to the sky. So this was revealed concerning them."

al-Bukhari said: "And from Ibn Abbas, *yastaghshūna* (they cover themselves) means they cover their heads."

al-Bukhari also related from Ibn Abbas in the interpretation of this verse, meaning: doubt concerning Allah and the doing of evil deeds. Similarly it was related from Mujahid, al-Hasan and others: that is, they used to fold up their breasts when they said something or did something, thinking that by this they were hiding from Allah. So He, glorified is He, informed them that when they cover their garments at the time of their sleep in the darkness of the night, ﴿He knows what they conceal﴾ of speech, ﴿and what they reveal﴾.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Abdullah ibn Shaddad ibn al-Hadi regarding His saying: ﴿Unquestionably, they fold up their breasts﴾: he said, "When one of the hypocrites passed by the Prophet (ﷺ), he would bend his chest and cover his garment so that he would not be seen, so this was revealed."

Ibn Jarir related from al-Hasan regarding His saying: ﴿Unquestionably, when they cover their garments﴾: he said, "In the darkness of the night, within the inner parts of their houses."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Abu Razin regarding the verse: he said, "One of them would bend his back and cover himself with his garment."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatada regarding the verse: he said, "They used to conceal their breasts so that they would not hear the Book of Allah."

He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Unquestionably, when they cover their garments, He knows what they conceal﴾. That is the most concealed state a son of Adam can be in, when he bends his back, covers himself with his garment, and hides his concern within himself, yet Allah is not hidden from Him in that.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, who said regarding the verse: "They conceal what is in their hearts. ﴿Unquestionably, when they cover their garments, He knows what they did by night and by day.﴾"

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And there is no creature (*dābbah*) on the earth﴾, to the end of the verse, he said: "meaning every creature."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid regarding His saying: ﴿And there is no creature on the earth﴾, to the end of the verse: he said, "meaning that whatever provision comes to it is from Allah, though He may not provide it until it dies of hunger; but whatever provision is due to it is from Allah."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿And He knows its *mustaqarr* (place of settling)﴾, he said: "where it shelters," and ﴿its *mustawda'* (place of deposit)﴾, he said: "where it dies."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him: ﴿And He knows its place of settling﴾, he said: "its provision comes to it wherever it may be."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound) related from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "﴿*Mustaqarr*﴾ is in the wombs, and ﴿*mustawda'*﴾ is where it dies."

What supports this interpretation that Ibn Mas'ud gave is what al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim related in *Nawadir al-Usul*, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab*, from Ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "When the term of one of you is in a land, a need is made for him toward it, until he reaches the furthest point of his trace there, and he is taken. Then on the Day of Resurrection the earth will say: 'This is what you deposited with me.'"
