This is the story of Lut (Lot), peace be upon him, and his people. He was the paternal cousin of Ibrahim (Abraham), peace be upon him. The towns of Lut were in the regions of al-Sham (Greater Syria), and Ibrahim was in the land of Palestine.

When Allah sent the angels with the punishment for the people of Lut, they passed by Ibrahim and stopped at his place. Whoever stopped at his place, he would treat generously as a guest. Their passing by him was to give him this good news mentioned here. He thought them to be guests, and they were Jibril (Gabriel), Mika'il (Michael), and Israfil (Raphael).

It has been said they were nine, and it has been said they were eleven. The good news they gave him was the news of a son, and it has been said it was the news of the destruction of the people of Lut. The first view is the better one. ﴿They said, "Peace."﴾ Salaman (peace) is in the accusative because it is governed by a verb that is understood: that is, "We greet you with peace." ﴿He said, "Peace."﴾ Its nominative case is because it is the predicate of an omitted subject: that is, "Your affair is peace." Or it is nominative because it is the subject, and the predicate is omitted, and the estimated meaning is: "Upon you is peace."

﴿So he did not delay⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿ ﻿﻿﻿—﻿that is, Ibrahim—﻿in bringing a roasted calf.﴾ Most of the grammarians say that "an" (that) here means "hatta" (until): that is, "So he did not delay until he brought." It has been said that it is in the accusative position after the removal of the preposition (ḥarf al-jarr), and the estimated meaning is: "So he did not delay in coming with a calf," meaning Ibrahim was not slow in bringing a calf. "Ma" is a negation. This is what Sibawayh said.

Al-Farra' said: "So his delay was not (his coming)," meaning his coming was not slow. It has also been said that "ma" is a relative pronoun and is the subject, and the predicate is "an ja'a bi-'ijlin ḥanidh" (that he came with a roasted calf). The estimated meaning is: "What Ibrahim delayed was his coming with a roasted calf."

Ḥanidh means roasted in general. It has been said it means roasted by the heat of stones without the fire touching it. It is said: "Hanadha ash-shāta yaḥnidhuhā" meaning he placed the sheep over heated stones to cook it, so it is ḥanidh. It has been said that the meaning of ḥanidh is fat. It has been said ḥanidh is samīṭ (skinned and roasted). It has also been said it is nadīj (well-cooked). It is a form (faʿīl) in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ūl). He brought them a calf because cattle was most of his wealth.

﴿When he saw their hands not reaching toward it⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿—﻿that is, they did not reach out to the calf as a person who wants to eat would reach out his hand—﻿he was suspicious of them.⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿ (p-665) It is said: "Nakirtahu, wa-ankartahu, wa-istankartahu," meaning when you find someone in a state other than what you are accustomed to. From this is the saying of the poet:

She disowned me, and what she disowned of the events
was nothing but gray hair and baldness.

So he combined the two dialects. Among the examples where the two dialects are combined is the saying of the poet:

When a land disowns me, or I disown it,
I went out with the falcon, and blackness was upon me.

It has also been said: "Ankartu" is used for what you see with your eye, and "nakirtu" for what you see with your heart. It has been said: He was suspicious of them because their custom was that when a guest came to them and did not eat their food, they thought he had come with evil intent.

﴿And he felt fear of them⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿—﻿that is, he sensed within himself a fear, meaning dread and alarm. It has been said the meaning of awjasa is that he concealed fear within himself. The first meaning is closer to the linguistic meaning. From this is the saying of the poet:

The messenger came with a letter urging him,
and the heart felt fear from its letter, alarmed.

It seems he thought they had come to him for a matter he disapproved of, or for the punishment of his people. ﴿They said, "Do not fear."⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿ They said this to him even though he had not spoken anything indicating fear; rather, he felt it within himself. Perhaps they inferred his fear from signs such as the effect of it appearing on his face. Or they said it to him after he said, following what he felt within himself of dread, a statement indicating fear, as in His saying in Surat al-Hijr: ﴿He said, "Indeed, we are fearful of you."﴾ [Al-Hijr: 52]. This was not mentioned here, being sufficient with what is there.

Then they gave the reason for prohibiting his fear by saying: ﴿Indeed, we have been sent to the people of Lut.﴾ That is, we have been sent to them specifically. It is possible that Ibrahim, peace be upon him, said a statement to which this would be the answer: ﴿He said, "What is your business, O messengers?" They said, "Indeed, we have been sent to a criminal people."﴾ [Al-Hijr: 57–58].

The clause ﴿and his wife was standing and she laughed⁠

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 11, verse 69–76 (part 2 of 2):

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatadah, who said: When Ibrahim sensed fear within himself, they (the angels) told him then what they had come for, and his wife laughed in wonder at the heedlessness of the people of Lut and at the punishment that had come upon them.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿فَضَحِكَتْ﴾ ("then she laughed"), who said: She menstruated, and she was ninety-eight years old.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid regarding His words ﴿فَضَحِكَتْ﴾, who said: She menstruated, and she was about ninety years old, while Ibrahim was one hundred years old.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ikrimah, who said: She menstruated.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Umar the same as this.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words ﴿ومِن وراءِ إسْحاقَ يَعْقُوبَ﴾ ("and after Ishaq, Ya'qub"), who said: He is the son's son.

Ibn al-Anbari, in his book al-Waqf wa al-Ibtida' (On Pausing and Starting), narrated from Hassan ibn Abjar, who said: I was with Ibn Abbas when a man from Hudhayl came. Ibn Abbas said to him: "What did so-and-so do?" He said: "He died and left four sons and three from among the descendants (al-waraʾ)." Ibn Abbas said: ﴿فَبَشَّرْناها بِإسْحاقَ ومِن وراءِ إسْحاقَ يَعْقُوبَ﴾ and said: "The son's son."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, Abu al-Shaykh and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated through several chains from Ibn Abbas that he used to forbid adding to the reply to the greeting beyond their saying: "ʿAlaykum al-salam wa rahmat Allah wa barakatuh," and he would recite this verse: ﴿رَحْمَةُ اللَّهِ وبَرَكاتُهُ عَلَيْكم أهْلَ البَيْتِ﴾ ("The mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you, O people of the household").

Al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn Umar something similar.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid regarding His words ﴿فَلَمّا ذَهَبَ عَنْ إبْراهِيمَ الرَّوْعُ﴾ ("When the fear had left Ibrahim"), who said: "Al-faraq" (the fright/alarm). ﴿يُجادِلُنا في قَوْمِ لُوطٍ﴾ ("he argued with us concerning the people of Lut"), who said: "He disputed with us."

Abd al-Razzaq and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatadah regarding the explanation of al-mujadalah (the arguing), who said: He said to them on that day: "What do you think if there are fifty Muslims among them?" They said: "If there are fifty among them, we will not punish them." He said: "Forty?" They said: "And forty." He said: "Thirty?" They said: "And thirty," until they reached ten. They said: "If there are ten among them, we will not punish them." He said: "What of a people among whom there are not ten, is there any good in them?" Qatadah said: In the town of Lut there were four thousand thousand people, or as much of that as Allah willed.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: When the angels came to Ibrahim, they said to Ibrahim: "If there are five among them who pray, the punishment will be lifted from them."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Amr ibn Maymun, who said: "Al-awwah" is "the compassionate."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Al-munib" is "the one who turns back (in repentance) to the obedience of Allah."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, who said: "Al-munib" is "the sincere."

(p. 667) When the angels left Abraham and went toward Lot's town, which was four farsakhs from Abraham, they came to Lot. When Lot saw them, and they were in the form of handsome young men without beards, ﴿he was distressed by them﴾, meaning their coming troubled him. It is said: sa'ahu yasu'uhu (it distressed him). The original form of "sī'a bihim" was "sū'iya bihim". The vowel of the waw was moved to the sin, the waw was changed to a ya', and when the hamza was lightened its vowel was placed on the ya'.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Amr read the sin with ishmam (a slight rounding toward a damma, the ishmam). ﴿And he was constrained for them in his heart﴾. Al-Azhari said: dhar' (ability, capacity) is used in the place of ṭāqa (strength). Its origin is that a camel stretches out its foreleg as it walks, according to the width of its stride, meaning it extends it. When more than its capacity is loaded onto it, its stride becomes constricted and it cannot do that. So constriction of the stride became a metaphor for little capacity and strength and for the severity of a matter. It was also said that it derives from dhara'ahu al-qay', meaning when vomiting overcomes a person and he cannot hold it in.

The meaning is that his chest was constricted when he saw the angels in that form, out of fear for them from his people, because he knew their wickedness and their committing the abomination of sodomy (liwāṭ). ﴿And he said: This is a difficult day﴾, meaning severe.

The poet said:
"And if you are not pleased with Bakr ibn Wa'il, there will be for you a day in Iraq that is grievous."
It is said: 'aṣīb, 'uṣayṣib and 'aṣawṣab (all meaning grievous), with intensive forms. That is, a day that is hateful, in which evil gathers. From this comes 'uṣba and 'iṣāba (a group whose word is united), and a man who is ma'ṣūb (whose frame is gathered).

﴿And his people came to him rushing﴾, meaning they came to Lot. The clause is in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative), describing the state of the subject.

The meaning of yuhra'ūna ilayhi is: they hasten toward him.

Al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and other lexicographers said: ihrā' is only hastening with trembling. It is said: ahra'a al-rajul ihrā'an, meaning he hastened while trembling from cold, anger or fever. Muhalhil said:
"They came rushing, while they were captives, their cheeks [trembling] in spite of their noses."

It was also said: yuhra'ūna means they run in a trot, and it was said: it is a walk between a trot and a run.

The meaning: when the report of the angels' coming in that form reached Lot's people, they hastened to him, as if they were being pushed, in pursuit of the abomination against his guests. ﴿And before this they used to do evil deeds﴾, meaning before the coming of the messengers at this time they used to commit evil deeds. It was also said: before Lot, they used to do evil deeds, meaning their custom was to mount men. When they came to Lot and aimed at his guests for that deed, Lot stood up to them, defending them. ﴿He said: O my people, these are my daughters, they are purer for you﴾, meaning marry them, and leave what you seek of the abomination with my guests. He had three daughters, and it is said two; they used to ask him to marry them to them, but he refused because of their wickedness. They had two prominent leaders whom they obeyed, and he intended to marry his two daughters to them. It was also said that by his words "these are my daughters" he meant women in general, because the prophet of a people is a father to them. A group said: this statement from him was by way of defense, and he did not intend the literal meaning.

The meaning of ﴿they are purer for you﴾ is: more lawful and cleaner. Tathahhur means keeping oneself clear of what is not lawful. The form "aṭhar" does not indicate comparison (superlative), but is like "Allahu akbar" (God is greatest). Al-Hasan and Isa ibn 'Umar read "aṭhara" with fatḥa (naṣb), and the rest read it with ḍamma (rafʿ). The reading with naṣb may be that the demonstrative ism al-ishara ("these") is the subject (mubtada'), its predicate is "my daughters", "hunna" is a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl, also called 'imād), and "aṭhar" is a ḥāl.

Al-Khalil, Sibawayh and al-Akhfash prohibited this, because the pronoun of separation, which is called 'imād, occurs only between two clauses in such a way that the sentence is not complete without what follows it, like: "kāna Zaydun huwa akhāka" (Zayd was your brother).

﴿So fear God and do not disgrace me regarding my guests﴾, meaning: fear God by abandoning what you want of the abomination with them, and do not humiliate me or bring shame upon me regarding my guests. The word ḍayf (guest) is used for one, two, or a group, because originally it is a verbal noun (maṣdar). The poet said:
"Do not let the time be without the blades of the slaughterer for the guest, and the guest has the greater right to visit."
It may be used in dual and plural forms, but the singular is more common.

It is said: khaziya al-rajul khazāyatan, meaning he felt shame, or was humbled, or was disgraced; and khazia khizyan, meaning he was exposed. The meaning of "regarding my guests" is "concerning the right of my guests", so the disgrace of the guest is a disgrace to the host. Then he rebuked them, saying: ﴿Is there not among you a man of sound judgment (rashīd)﴾, who would guide you to abandon this ugly deed and prevent you from it?

They answered him, turning away from what he advised them and directed them to, saying: ﴿You know that we have no need of your daughters, and you know what we want﴾. That is, we have no desire or need for them. Whoever needs something is as if he already has some right to it.

The meaning of what they attributed to him of knowledge is that he knew of them their eagerness for mounting males and their intense desire for them; from this standpoint they were as if they had no need for women. It is possible that they meant: we have no right to marry them, because no one marries them except a believer, and we will never believe. It was also said that they had earlier proposed to his daughters and he had refused them, and it was their custom that whoever proposed and was refused, the woman he proposed to would never become lawful to him. ﴿And you indeed know what we want﴾, namely mounting males.

Then, when he knew their determination in the abomination and that they would not leave what they had sought, ﴿he said: If only I had power against you﴾. The answer to "law" (if only) is omitted, and the estimate is: I would have repelled you from them and prevented you from them. This is from him, peace be upon him, by way of wishing: that is, if only I found a helper and supporter. He named what one is strengthened by "power". ﴿Or that I could take refuge in a strong pillar﴾. This is coordinated with what follows "law", because of the verbal sense it contains; the estimate is: if I were strong enough to repel you, or if I had taken refuge in a strong pillar.

It was also read as "aw ā'iya" with naṣb, coordinated with "quwwatan", as if he had said: if only I had power against you, or refuge in a strong pillar. By "the strong pillar" he meant the clan (al-'ashira), and that by which he and those with him would be protected from them. It was said: he meant by "power" his son, and by "the strong pillar" someone who would support him other than his son. It was also said: he meant by "power" his own strength in himself.

When the angels heard him say this statement, and found that his people had overcome him and he was unable to repel them, ﴿they said: O Lot, we are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you﴾. They first informed him that they were messengers of his Lord, then they gave him good news with their words: "they will never reach you". This clause clarifies what preceded it, because if they were sent from God to him, his enemy would not reach him and would not be able to overcome him. Then they ordered him to leave them, saying to him: ﴿So travel with your family during a part of the night﴾. [p. 668] Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read with waṣl (the hamza is elided: "fasri"), and the others read with qaṭʿ (the hamza is pronounced: "fa'sri"); these are two eloquent dialects.

God Most High said: ﴿By the night when it passes﴾ [al-Fajr: 4], and He said: ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra': 1]. A poet combined the two dialects, saying:
"The tribe of al-Nadir and the lady of the curtain traveled by night on it, and she had not been one who traveled."

It was said: asrā is for travel from the beginning of the night, and saraā is for travel from its end. "Qiṭʿ min al-layl" means a portion of it.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: "bi-qiṭʿin mina al-layl" means "with an hour of it". Al-Akhfash said: "with a dark part of the night". It was said: "with darkness of the night", and it was said: "after a quiet part of the night".

It is said: travel by night happens only at night, so what is the purpose of adding "a part of the night"? It is said: if he had not said "a part of the night", it would have been possible for the travel to be at its beginning before darkness gathered, and that is not intended. ﴿And let none of you look back﴾, meaning let him not look at what is behind him, or be occupied with what is behind him of wealth or other things.

It is said: the reason for the prohibition on looking back is so that they would not see the punishment of their people and the terror of what descended upon them, so that they would not pity them or be softened toward them; or so that they would not stop from the journey required of them by what would happen from looking back, for the one who looks back must have a pause in his journey. ﴿Except your wife﴾. It is read with naṣb according to the reading of the majority, and Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read with rafʿ as a substitution (badal). According to the first reading, "his wife" is excepted from "so travel with your family", meaning: travel with your family all together except your wife, so do not let her travel with them. ﴿Indeed, what will strike them will strike her﴾ of the punishment, which was their being pelted with stones, because she was an unbeliever. A group of scholars, including Abu 'Ubayd, denied the reading with rafʿ and said: this is not correct unless "yaltafit" is read with rafʿ and is a qualifier (na't), because the meaning becomes, when you substitute and read with jazm (jussive), that the wife was permitted to look back, and that is not the meaning.

Al-Nahhas said: this action by Abu 'Ubayd and others, in the manner of Abu 'Amr, despite his eminence and his standing in Arabic, does not necessarily have to be so. The reading with rafʿ as a substitution has a correct meaning, which is that it is an exception from the prohibition on looking back: that is, let none of you look back except your wife, for she will look back and perish. It was also said: the rafʿ as a substitution is from "aḥad" (anyone), and "al-iltifāt" (looking back) means lagging behind, not looking back at what is behind. It is as if he said: let none of you lag behind except your wife, for she will lag behind. The one forced to this distant interpretation is fleeing from the contradiction between the two readings.

The pronoun in ﴿indeed, what will strike them will strike her﴾ refers to the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), and the clause is the predicate of "inna". ﴿Indeed their appointed time is the morning﴾. This clause is a reduction of what preceded of the command to travel by night and the prohibition on looking back. The meaning: the appointed time of their punishment is the morning, which brings light after that night. The interrogative in ﴿Is not the morning near?﴾ is for a rhetorical denial, and the clause is an emphasis of the causal reason.

Isa ibn 'Umar read "alaysa al-ṣubuḥu" with ḍamma on the ba', and this is a dialect. It is likely that making the morning the time of their destruction is because souls are calmer at that time, and people are gathered in it, not yet dispersed to their work.

﴿So when Our command came﴾, meaning the time set for the punishment to fall upon them, or the command means the punishment itself, ﴿We made its uppermost part its lowest﴾, meaning the uppermost part of the towns of the people of Lot became the lowest. The meaning is that He overturned it in this form, so that its top became its bottom and its bottom became its top. This is because Gabriel put his wing beneath them and lifted them from the depths of the earth until he brought them close to the sky, then overturned them upon them. ﴿And We rained upon it stones of sijjīl﴾. It is said: amṭara is used for punishment and maṭara for mercy. It was also said that these are two dialects: it is said maṭarat al-samā' and amṭarat, meaning the sky rained. Al-Harawi related this.

Sijjīl is clay hardened by baking or otherwise. It was also said it is the very hard, solid stone. It was also said sijjīl means abundant. It was also said that sijjīl is a non-Arabic word, originally "sij" and "jīl", which are two words in Persian meaning stone and clay, which the Arabs arabicized and made into one word. It was also said it is from the language of the Arabs.

Al-Harawi mentioned that sijjīl is the name of the lowest heaven. Ibn 'Aṭiyya said: this is weak, because it is refuted by describing them as ﴿arranged in layers﴾. It was also said it is a sea suspended in the air between the sky and the earth. It was also said they are mountains in the sky.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is from "tasjīl" (writing) for them, meaning what was written for them of the punishment; so it has the meaning of sijjīn (the register), and from this is the saying of God Most High: ﴿And what will make you know what Sijjīn is? It is a written book﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 8–9]. It was also said it is from "asjaltuhu", when I gave it, so it is as if it were a punishment given to them. From this is the poet's saying:
"Whoever competes with me in giving will be matched by a noble man who fills the bucket up to the knot of the rope."

The meaning of "manḍūd" is that some of it was arranged upon some other, and it was said that some of it followed another, as one says: naḍḍadtu al-matā' when I placed some of the goods upon others, so it is manḍūd and naḍīd.

Al-Musawwama means marked, that is, one that has a sign. It was said: upon them were things like seal-rings. It was said: upon each stone was written the name of the one it was thrown at.

Al-Farra' said: they claimed that they were striped with red and black on white. That is their "taswīm" (marking). The meaning of ﴿with your Lord﴾ is in His treasuries. ﴿And they are not far from the wrongdoers﴾, meaning these described stones are not far from the wrongdoers, who are the people of Lot. Or it means: they are not far from any wrongdoer among the oppressors, among whom are the disbelievers of Quraysh and those who support them in disbelief against Muhammad, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace; for their wrongdoing they deserve it.

And it was said: "﴿And it is not far from the wrongdoers﴾," meaning the towns. Whoever disbelieved in the Prophet (ﷺ) is not far from them, for they lie between Syria and Madinah.

Regarding the rain of stones there are two opinions. The first is that it rained upon the cities when Jibril lifted them up. The second is that it rained upon those of its people who were not in the cities and were outside of them.

As for the masculine form of "far" (ba'id), it is either because "stones" is interpreted as "a stone," or because it is treated as agreeing with a masculine noun described: that is, "a far thing," or "a far place," or because it is a verbal noun (masdar) like "zafir" (roaring) and "sahil" (neighing), and verbal nouns are used as descriptions for both masculine and feminine alike.

Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari), Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿And when Our messengers came to Lut, he was distressed on their account and felt helpless for them﴾, that he said: he thought ill of his people, and was constrained for his guests. ﴿And he said, "This is a trying day"﴾: he means, "a hard one."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, regarding His words: ﴿They came rushing towards him﴾, he said: they hastened. ﴿And before this they had been doing evil deeds﴾, he said: they were approaching men.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh also narrated from him, saying: ﴿They came rushing towards him﴾: they were listening to him.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him also, regarding His words: ﴿These are my daughters﴾, he said: Lut did not offer his daughters to his people for illicit intercourse or for marriage. He only said, "These are your women," because the Prophet, when he is among a people, is their father. Allah the Exalted said in the Qur'an: ﴿and his wives are their mothers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 6], and he is their father in the recitation (qira'ah, a variant reading) of Ubayy.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, who said: his daughters were not his own, but they were from his community, and every prophet is the father of his community.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr something similar.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and Ibn Asakir narrated from al-Suddi something similar.

He said: In the recitation of Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud): "The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves, and he is a father to them, and his wives are their mothers."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, who said: He offered them his daughters in marriage, intending to protect his guests by marrying off his daughters.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi, regarding His words: ﴿And do not disgrace me concerning my guests﴾, he said: do not shame me.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Malik regarding ﴿Is there not among you a man of sound judgment?﴾, he said: a man who enjoins what is good and forbids what is evil.

Abu al-Shaykh and al-Bayhaqi, in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat, narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿Is there not among you a man of sound judgment?﴾, he said: one person who says, "There is no god but Allah."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ikrimah something similar.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi regarding ﴿And indeed you know what we desire﴾, he said: we only desire men. Lut said, ﴿If only I had power against you, or could take refuge in a mighty pillar﴾: he means, "in a mighty army to fight you."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿or could take refuge in a mighty pillar﴾, he said: a tribe.

It is established in al-Bukhari and others, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "May Allah have mercy on Lut; he used to take refuge in a mighty pillar." It is also narrated in non-authentic chains from other Companions.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿with a portion of the night﴾, he said: the middle of the night.

They also narrated from him, he said: in the darkness of the night.

Abd al-Razzaq narrated from Qatadah, he said: with a part of the night.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words: ﴿and let none of you look back﴾, he said: let none of you lag behind.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid regarding His words: ﴿and let none of you look back﴾, he said: let no one look behind him, ﴿except your wife﴾.

Abu Ubayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Harun, who said: in the reading (harf) of Ibn Mas'ud: "So travel with your family in a portion of the night, except your wife."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid regarding His words: ﴿So when Our command came, We turned it upside down﴾, he said: when they reached the morning, Jibril rushed at their town, uprooted it from its foundations, then inserted his wing beneath it, carried it upon the feathers of his wing with what was in it, then ascended with it to the sky until the people of the sky heard the barking of their dogs. Then he overturned it. The first thing to fall from it was its canopy, and so it did not strike a people except what struck them. Then Allah blinded their eyes, then their town was overturned, and stones of baked clay (sijjil) were rained down upon them.

The commentators have related many lengthy narrations and stories about the manner of the destruction of the people of Lut, and they differ greatly. There is no benefit in mentioning them, especially since between those who spoke of any of these things and the destruction of the people of Lut lies a long age, and for such a span a sound chain of transmission cannot readily be found. Most of this is taken from the People of the Book (Ahl al-Kitab, Jews and Christians), and their reliability in transmission is well known.

We have been commanded that we neither believe them nor disbelieve them. So understand this. This is the reason for our omitting many of these narrations found in the stories of the prophets and their peoples.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid regarding His words: ﴿And it is not far from the wrongdoers﴾, he said: by it he warns Quraysh that what befell that people might befall them.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi regarding the verse, he said: from among the wrongdoing Arabs, if they do not believe, so that they are punished by it.

Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, he said: from the wrongdoers of this Ummah.

(p. 667) When the angels left Abraham and went toward Lot's town, which was four farsakhs from Abraham, they came to Lot. When Lot saw them, and they were in the form of handsome young men without beards, ﴿he was distressed by them﴾, meaning their coming troubled him. It is said: sa'ahu yasu'uhu (it distressed him). The original form of "sī'a bihim" was "sū'iya bihim". The vowel of the waw was moved to the sin, the waw was changed to a ya', and when the hamza was lightened its vowel was placed on the ya'.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Amr read the sin with ishmam (a slight rounding toward a damma, the ishmam). ﴿And he was constrained for them in his heart﴾. Al-Azhari said: dhar' (ability, capacity) is used in the place of ṭāqa (strength). Its origin is that a camel stretches out its foreleg as it walks, according to the width of its stride, meaning it extends it. When more than its capacity is loaded onto it, its stride becomes constricted and it cannot do that. So constriction of the stride became a metaphor for little capacity and strength and for the severity of a matter. It was also said that it derives from dhara'ahu al-qay', meaning when vomiting overcomes a person and he cannot hold it in.

The meaning is that his chest was constricted when he saw the angels in that form, out of fear for them from his people, because he knew their wickedness and their committing the abomination of sodomy (liwāṭ). ﴿And he said: This is a difficult day﴾, meaning severe.

The poet said:
"And if you are not pleased with Bakr ibn Wa'il, there will be for you a day in Iraq that is grievous."
It is said: 'aṣīb, 'uṣayṣib and 'aṣawṣab (all meaning grievous), with intensive forms. That is, a day that is hateful, in which evil gathers. From this comes 'uṣba and 'iṣāba (a group whose word is united), and a man who is ma'ṣūb (whose frame is gathered).

﴿And his people came to him rushing﴾, meaning they came to Lot. The clause is in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative), describing the state of the subject.

The meaning of yuhra'ūna ilayhi is: they hasten toward him.

Al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and other lexicographers said: ihrā' is only hastening with trembling. It is said: ahra'a al-rajul ihrā'an, meaning he hastened while trembling from cold, anger or fever. Muhalhil said:
"They came rushing, while they were captives, their cheeks [trembling] in spite of their noses."

It was also said: yuhra'ūna means they run in a trot, and it was said: it is a walk between a trot and a run.

The meaning: when the report of the angels' coming in that form reached Lot's people, they hastened to him, as if they were being pushed, in pursuit of the abomination against his guests. ﴿And before this they used to do evil deeds﴾, meaning before the coming of the messengers at this time they used to commit evil deeds. It was also said: before Lot, they used to do evil deeds, meaning their custom was to mount men. When they came to Lot and aimed at his guests for that deed, Lot stood up to them, defending them. ﴿He said: O my people, these are my daughters, they are purer for you﴾, meaning marry them, and leave what you seek of the abomination with my guests. He had three daughters, and it is said two; they used to ask him to marry them to them, but he refused because of their wickedness. They had two prominent leaders whom they obeyed, and he intended to marry his two daughters to them. It was also said that by his words "these are my daughters" he meant women in general, because the prophet of a people is a father to them. A group said: this statement from him was by way of defense, and he did not intend the literal meaning.

The meaning of ﴿they are purer for you﴾ is: more lawful and cleaner. Tathahhur means keeping oneself clear of what is not lawful. The form "aṭhar" does not indicate comparison (superlative), but is like "Allahu akbar" (God is greatest). Al-Hasan and Isa ibn 'Umar read "aṭhara" with fatḥa (naṣb), and the rest read it with ḍamma (rafʿ). The reading with naṣb may be that the demonstrative ism al-ishara ("these") is the subject (mubtada'), its predicate is "my daughters", "hunna" is a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl, also called 'imād), and "aṭhar" is a ḥāl.

Al-Khalil, Sibawayh and al-Akhfash prohibited this, because the pronoun of separation, which is called 'imād, occurs only between two clauses in such a way that the sentence is not complete without what follows it, like: "kāna Zaydun huwa akhāka" (Zayd was your brother).

﴿So fear God and do not disgrace me regarding my guests﴾, meaning: fear God by abandoning what you want of the abomination with them, and do not humiliate me or bring shame upon me regarding my guests. The word ḍayf (guest) is used for one, two, or a group, because originally it is a verbal noun (maṣdar). The poet said:
"Do not let the time be without the blades of the slaughterer for the guest, and the guest has the greater right to visit."
It may be used in dual and plural forms, but the singular is more common.

It is said: khaziya al-rajul khazāyatan, meaning he felt shame, or was humbled, or was disgraced; and khazia khizyan, meaning he was exposed. The meaning of "regarding my guests" is "concerning the right of my guests", so the disgrace of the guest is a disgrace to the host. Then he rebuked them, saying: ﴿Is there not among you a man of sound judgment (rashīd)﴾, who would guide you to abandon this ugly deed and prevent you from it?

They answered him, turning away from what he advised them and directed them to, saying: ﴿You know that we have no need of your daughters, and you know what we want﴾. That is, we have no desire or need for them. Whoever needs something is as if he already has some right to it.

The meaning of what they attributed to him of knowledge is that he knew of them their eagerness for mounting males and their intense desire for them; from this standpoint they were as if they had no need for women. It is possible that they meant: we have no right to marry them, because no one marries them except a believer, and we will never believe. It was also said that they had earlier proposed to his daughters and he had refused them, and it was their custom that whoever proposed and was refused, the woman he proposed to would never become lawful to him. ﴿And you indeed know what we want﴾, namely mounting males.

Then, when he knew their determination in the abomination and that they would not leave what they had sought, ﴿he said: If only I had power against you﴾. The answer to "law" (if only) is omitted, and the estimate is: I would have repelled you from them and prevented you from them. This is from him, peace be upon him, by way of wishing: that is, if only I found a helper and supporter. He named what one is strengthened by "power". ﴿Or that I could take refuge in a strong pillar﴾. This is coordinated with what follows "law", because of the verbal sense it contains; the estimate is: if I were strong enough to repel you, or if I had taken refuge in a strong pillar.

It was also read as "aw ā'iya" with naṣb, coordinated with "quwwatan", as if he had said: if only I had power against you, or refuge in a strong pillar. By "the strong pillar" he meant the clan (al-'ashira), and that by which he and those with him would be protected from them. It was said: he meant by "power" his son, and by "the strong pillar" someone who would support him other than his son. It was also said: he meant by "power" his own strength in himself.

When the angels heard him say this statement, and found that his people had overcome him and he was unable to repel them, ﴿they said: O Lot, we are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you﴾. They first informed him that they were messengers of his Lord, then they gave him good news with their words: "they will never reach you". This clause clarifies what preceded it, because if they were sent from God to him, his enemy would not reach him and would not be able to overcome him. Then they ordered him to leave them, saying to him: ﴿So travel with your family during a part of the night﴾. [p. 668] Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read with waṣl (the hamza is elided: "fasri"), and the others read with qaṭʿ (the hamza is pronounced: "fa'sri"); these are two eloquent dialects.

God Most High said: ﴿By the night when it passes﴾ [al-Fajr: 4], and He said: ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra': 1]. A poet combined the two dialects, saying:
"The tribe of al-Nadir and the lady of the curtain traveled by night on it, and she had not been one who traveled."

It was said: asrā is for travel from the beginning of the night, and saraā is for travel from its end. "Qiṭʿ min al-layl" means a portion of it.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: "bi-qiṭʿin mina al-layl" means "with an hour of it". Al-Akhfash said: "with a dark part of the night". It was said: "with darkness of the night", and it was said: "after a quiet part of the night".

It is said: travel by night happens only at night, so what is the purpose of adding "a part of the night"? It is said: if he had not said "a part of the night", it would have been possible for the travel to be at its beginning before darkness gathered, and that is not intended. ﴿And let none of you look back﴾, meaning let him not look at what is behind him, or be occupied with what is behind him of wealth or other things.

It is said: the reason for the prohibition on looking back is so that they would not see the punishment of their people and the terror of what descended upon them, so that they would not pity them or be softened toward them; or so that they would not stop from the journey required of them by what would happen from looking back, for the one who looks back must have a pause in his journey. ﴿Except your wife﴾. It is read with naṣb according to the reading of the majority, and Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read with rafʿ as a substitution (badal). According to the first reading, "his wife" is excepted from "so travel with your family", meaning: travel with your family all together except your wife, so do not let her travel with them. ﴿Indeed, what will strike them will strike her﴾ of the punishment, which was their being pelted with stones, because she was an unbeliever. A group of scholars, including Abu 'Ubayd, denied the reading with rafʿ and said: this is not correct unless "yaltafit" is read with rafʿ and is a qualifier (na't), because the meaning becomes, when you substitute and read with jazm (jussive), that the wife was permitted to look back, and that is not the meaning.

Al-Nahhas said: this action by Abu 'Ubayd and others, in the manner of Abu 'Amr, despite his eminence and his standing in Arabic, does not necessarily have to be so. The reading with rafʿ as a substitution has a correct meaning, which is that it is an exception from the prohibition on looking back: that is, let none of you look back except your wife, for she will look back and perish. It was also said: the rafʿ as a substitution is from "aḥad" (anyone), and "al-iltifāt" (looking back) means lagging behind, not looking back at what is behind. It is as if he said: let none of you lag behind except your wife, for she will lag behind. The one forced to this distant interpretation is fleeing from the contradiction between the two readings.

The pronoun in ﴿indeed, what will strike them will strike her﴾ refers to the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), and the clause is the predicate of "inna". ﴿Indeed their appointed time is the morning﴾. This clause is a reduction of what preceded of the command to travel by night and the prohibition on looking back. The meaning: the appointed time of their punishment is the morning, which brings light after that night. The interrogative in ﴿Is not the morning near?﴾ is for a rhetorical denial, and the clause is an emphasis of the causal reason.

Isa ibn 'Umar read "alaysa al-ṣubuḥu" with ḍamma on the ba', and this is a dialect. It is likely that making the morning the time of their destruction is because souls are calmer at that time, and people are gathered in it, not yet dispersed to their work.

﴿So when Our command came﴾, meaning the time set for the punishment to fall upon them, or the command means the punishment itself, ﴿We made its uppermost part its lowest﴾, meaning the uppermost part of the towns of the people of Lot became the lowest. The meaning is that He overturned it in this form, so that its top became its bottom and its bottom became its top. This is because Gabriel put his wing beneath them and lifted them from the depths of the earth until he brought them close to the sky, then overturned them upon them. ﴿And We rained upon it stones of sijjīl﴾. It is said: amṭara is used for punishment and maṭara for mercy. It was also said that these are two dialects: it is said maṭarat al-samā' and amṭarat, meaning the sky rained. Al-Harawi related this.

Sijjīl is clay hardened by baking or otherwise. It was also said it is the very hard, solid stone. It was also said sijjīl means abundant. It was also said that sijjīl is a non-Arabic word, originally "sij" and "jīl", which are two words in Persian meaning stone and clay, which the Arabs arabicized and made into one word. It was also said it is from the language of the Arabs.

Al-Harawi mentioned that sijjīl is the name of the lowest heaven. Ibn 'Aṭiyya said: this is weak, because it is refuted by describing them as ﴿arranged in layers﴾. It was also said it is a sea suspended in the air between the sky and the earth. It was also said they are mountains in the sky.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is from "tasjīl" (writing) for them, meaning what was written for them of the punishment; so it has the meaning of sijjīn (the register), and from this is the saying of God Most High: ﴿And what will make you know what Sijjīn is? It is a written book﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 8–9]. It was also said it is from "asjaltuhu", when I gave it, so it is as if it were a punishment given to them. From this is the poet's saying:
"Whoever competes with me in giving will be matched by a noble man who fills the bucket up to the knot of the rope."

The meaning of "manḍūd" is that some of it was arranged upon some other, and it was said that some of it followed another, as one says: naḍḍadtu al-matā' when I placed some of the goods upon others, so it is manḍūd and naḍīd.

Al-Musawwama means marked, that is, one that has a sign. It was said: upon them were things like seal-rings. It was said: upon each stone was written the name of the one it was thrown at.

Al-Farra' said: they claimed that they were striped with red and black on white. That is their "taswīm" (marking). The meaning of ﴿with your Lord﴾ is in His treasuries. ﴿And they are not far from the wrongdoers﴾, meaning these described stones are not far from the wrongdoers, who are the people of Lot. Or it means: they are not far from any wrongdoer among the oppressors, among whom are the disbelievers of Quraysh and those who support them in disbelief against Muhammad, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace; for their wrongdoing they deserve it.

And it was said: "﴿And it is not far from the wrongdoers﴾," meaning the towns. Whoever disbelieved in the Prophet (ﷺ) is not far from them, for they lie between Syria and Madinah.

Regarding the rain of stones there are two opinions. The first is that it rained upon the cities when Jibril lifted them up. The second is that it rained upon those of its people who were not in the cities and were outside of them.

As for the masculine form of "far" (ba'id), it is either because "stones" is interpreted as "a stone," or because it is treated as agreeing with a masculine noun described: that is, "a far thing," or "a far place," or because it is a verbal noun (masdar) like "zafir" (roaring) and "sahil" (neighing), and verbal nouns are used as descriptions for both masculine and feminine alike.

Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari), Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿And when Our messengers came to Lut, he was distressed on their account and felt helpless for them﴾, that he said: he thought ill of his people, and was constrained for his guests. ﴿And he said, "This is a trying day"﴾: he means, "a hard one."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, regarding His words: ﴿They came rushing towards him﴾, he said: they hastened. ﴿And before this they had been doing evil deeds﴾, he said: they were approaching men.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh also narrated from him, saying: ﴿They came rushing towards him﴾: they were listening to him.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him also, regarding His words: ﴿These are my daughters﴾, he said: Lut did not offer his daughters to his people for illicit intercourse or for marriage. He only said, "These are your women," because the Prophet, when he is among a people, is their father. Allah the Exalted said in the Qur'an: ﴿and his wives are their mothers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 6], and he is their father in the recitation (qira'ah, a variant reading) of Ubayy.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, who said: his daughters were not his own, but they were from his community, and every prophet is the father of his community.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr something similar.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and Ibn Asakir narrated from al-Suddi something similar.

He said: In the recitation of Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud): "The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves, and he is a father to them, and his wives are their mothers."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, who said: He offered them his daughters in marriage, intending to protect his guests by marrying off his daughters.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi, regarding His words: ﴿And do not disgrace me concerning my guests﴾, he said: do not shame me.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Malik regarding ﴿Is there not among you a man of sound judgment?﴾, he said: a man who enjoins what is good and forbids what is evil.

Abu al-Shaykh and al-Bayhaqi, in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat, narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿Is there not among you a man of sound judgment?﴾, he said: one person who says, "There is no god but Allah."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ikrimah something similar.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi regarding ﴿And indeed you know what we desire﴾, he said: we only desire men. Lut said, ﴿If only I had power against you, or could take refuge in a mighty pillar﴾: he means, "in a mighty army to fight you."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿or could take refuge in a mighty pillar﴾, he said: a tribe.

It is established in al-Bukhari and others, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "May Allah have mercy on Lut; he used to take refuge in a mighty pillar." It is also narrated in non-authentic chains from other Companions.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿with a portion of the night﴾, he said: the middle of the night.

They also narrated from him, he said: in the darkness of the night.

Abd al-Razzaq narrated from Qatadah, he said: with a part of the night.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words: ﴿and let none of you look back﴾, he said: let none of you lag behind.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid regarding His words: ﴿and let none of you look back﴾, he said: let no one look behind him, ﴿except your wife﴾.

Abu Ubayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Harun, who said: in the reading (harf) of Ibn Mas'ud: "So travel with your family in a portion of the night, except your wife."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid regarding His words: ﴿So when Our command came, We turned it upside down﴾, he said: when they reached the morning, Jibril rushed at their town, uprooted it from its foundations, then inserted his wing beneath it, carried it upon the feathers of his wing with what was in it, then ascended with it to the sky until the people of the sky heard the barking of their dogs. Then he overturned it. The first thing to fall from it was its canopy, and so it did not strike a people except what struck them. Then Allah blinded their eyes, then their town was overturned, and stones of baked clay (sijjil) were rained down upon them.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi regarding the verse, he said: from among the wrongdoing Arabs, if they do not believe, so that they are punished by it.

Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, he said: from the wrongdoers of this Ummah.

Al-Khalil, Sibawayh and al-Akhfash prohibited this, because the pronoun of separation, which is called 'imād, occurs only between two clauses in such a way that the sentence is not complete without what follows it, like: "kāna Zaydun huwa akhāka" (Zayd was your brother).

﴿So fear God and do not disgrace me regarding my guests﴾, meaning: fear God by abandoning what you want of the abomination with them, and do not humiliate me or bring shame upon me regarding my guests. The word ḍayf (guest) is used for one, two, or a group, because originally it is a verbal noun (maṣdar). The poet said:
"Do not let the time be without the blades of the slaughterer for the guest, and the guest has the greater right to visit."
It may be used in dual and plural forms, but the singular is more common.

It is said: khaziya al-rajul khazāyatan, meaning he felt shame, or was humbled, or was disgraced; and khazia khizyan, meaning he was exposed. The meaning of "regarding my guests" is "concerning the right of my guests", so the disgrace of the guest is a disgrace to the host. Then he rebuked them, saying: ﴿Is there not among you a man of sound judgment (rashīd)﴾, who would guide you to abandon this ugly deed and prevent you from it?

They answered him, turning away from what he advised them and directed them to, saying: ﴿You know that we have no need of your daughters, and you know what we want﴾. That is, we have no desire or need for them. Whoever needs something is as if he already has some right to it.

The meaning of what they attributed to him of knowledge is that he knew of them their eagerness for mounting males and their intense desire for them; from this standpoint they were as if they had no need for women. It is possible that they meant: we have no right to marry them, because no one marries them except a believer, and we will never believe. It was also said that they had earlier proposed to his daughters and he had refused them, and it was their custom that whoever proposed and was refused, the woman he proposed to would never become lawful to him. ﴿And you indeed know what we want﴾, namely mounting males.

Then, when he knew their determination in the abomination and that they would not leave what they had sought, ﴿he said: If only I had power against you﴾. The answer to "law" (if only) is omitted, and the estimate is: I would have repelled you from them and prevented you from them. This is from him, peace be upon him, by way of wishing: that is, if only I found a helper and supporter. He named what one is strengthened by "power". ﴿Or that I could take refuge in a strong pillar﴾. This is coordinated with what follows "law", because of the verbal sense it contains; the estimate is: if I were strong enough to repel you, or if I had taken refuge in a strong pillar.

It was also read as "aw ā'iya" with naṣb, coordinated with "quwwatan", as if he had said: if only I had power against you, or refuge in a strong pillar. By "the strong pillar" he meant the clan (al-'ashira), and that by which he and those with him would be protected from them. It was said: he meant by "power" his son, and by "the strong pillar" someone who would support him other than his son. It was also said: he meant by "power" his own strength in himself.

When the angels heard him say this statement, and found that his people had overcome him and he was unable to repel them, ﴿they said: O Lot, we are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you﴾. They first informed him that they were messengers of his Lord, then they gave him good news with their words: "they will never reach you". This clause clarifies what preceded it, because if they were sent from God to him, his enemy would not reach him and would not be able to overcome him. Then they ordered him to leave them, saying to him: ﴿So travel with your family during a part of the night﴾. [p. 668] Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read with waṣl (the hamza is elided: "fasri"), and the others read with qaṭʿ (the hamza is pronounced: "fa'sri"); these are two eloquent dialects.

God Most High said: ﴿By the night when it passes﴾ [al-Fajr: 4], and He said: ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra': 1]. A poet combined the two dialects, saying:
"The tribe of al-Nadir and the lady of the curtain traveled by night on it, and she had not been one who traveled."

It was said: asrā is for travel from the beginning of the night, and saraā is for travel from its end. "Qiṭʿ min al-layl" means a portion of it.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: "bi-qiṭʿin mina al-layl" means "with an hour of it". Al-Akhfash said: "with a dark part of the night". It was said: "with darkness of the night", and it was said: "after a quiet part of the night".

It is said: travel by night happens only at night, so what is the purpose of adding "a part of the night"? It is said: if he had not said "a part of the night", it would have been possible for the travel to be at its beginning before darkness gathered, and that is not intended. ﴿And let none of you look back﴾, meaning let him not look at what is behind him, or be occupied with what is behind him of wealth or other things.

It is said: the reason for the prohibition on looking back is so that they would not see the punishment of their people and the terror of what descended upon them, so that they would not pity them or be softened toward them; or so that they would not stop from the journey required of them by what would happen from looking back, for the one who looks back must have a pause in his journey. ﴿Except your wife﴾. It is read with naṣb according to the reading of the majority, and Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read with rafʿ as a substitution (badal). According to the first reading, "his wife" is excepted from "so travel with your family", meaning: travel with your family all together except your wife, so do not let her travel with them. ﴿Indeed, what will strike them will strike her﴾ of the punishment, which was their being pelted with stones, because she was an unbeliever. A group of scholars, including Abu 'Ubayd, denied the reading with rafʿ and said: this is not correct unless "yaltafit" is read with rafʿ and is a qualifier (na't), because the meaning becomes, when you substitute and read with jazm (jussive), that the wife was permitted to look back, and that is not the meaning.

Al-Nahhas said: this action by Abu 'Ubayd and others, in the manner of Abu 'Amr, despite his eminence and his standing in Arabic, does not necessarily have to be so. The reading with rafʿ as a substitution has a correct meaning, which is that it is an exception from the prohibition on looking back: that is, let none of you look back except your wife, for she will look back and perish. It was also said: the rafʿ as a substitution is from "aḥad" (anyone), and "al-iltifāt" (looking back) means lagging behind, not looking back at what is behind. It is as if he said: let none of you lag behind except your wife, for she will lag behind. The one forced to this distant interpretation is fleeing from the contradiction between the two readings.

The pronoun in ﴿indeed, what will strike them will strike her﴾ refers to the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), and the clause is the predicate of "inna". ﴿Indeed their appointed time is the morning﴾. This clause is a reduction of what preceded of the command to travel by night and the prohibition on looking back. The meaning: the appointed time of their punishment is the morning, which brings light after that night. The interrogative in ﴿Is not the morning near?﴾ is for a rhetorical denial, and the clause is an emphasis of the causal reason.

Isa ibn 'Umar read "alaysa al-ṣubuḥu" with ḍamma on the ba', and this is a dialect. It is likely that making the morning the time of their destruction is because souls are calmer at that time, and people are gathered in it, not yet dispersed to their work.

﴿So when Our command came﴾, meaning the time set for the punishment to fall upon them, or the command means the punishment itself, ﴿We made its uppermost part its lowest﴾, meaning the uppermost part of the towns of the people of Lot became the lowest. The meaning is that He overturned it in this form, so that its top became its bottom and its bottom became its top. This is because Gabriel put his wing beneath them and lifted them from the depths of the earth until he brought them close to the sky, then overturned them upon them. ﴿And We rained upon it stones of sijjīl﴾. It is said: amṭara is used for punishment and maṭara for mercy. It was also said that these are two dialects: it is said maṭarat al-samā' and amṭarat, meaning the sky rained. Al-Harawi related this.

Sijjīl is clay hardened by baking or otherwise. It was also said it is the very hard, solid stone. It was also said sijjīl means abundant. It was also said that sijjīl is a non-Arabic word, originally "sij" and "jīl", which are two words in Persian meaning stone and clay, which the Arabs arabicized and made into one word. It was also said it is from the language of the Arabs.

Al-Harawi mentioned that sijjīl is the name of the lowest heaven. Ibn 'Aṭiyya said: this is weak, because it is refuted by describing them as ﴿arranged in layers﴾. It was also said it is a sea suspended in the air between the sky and the earth. It was also said they are mountains in the sky.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is from "tasjīl" (writing) for them, meaning what was written for them of the punishment; so it has the meaning of sijjīn (the register), and from this is the saying of God Most High: ﴿And what will make you know what Sijjīn is? It is a written book﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 8–9]. It was also said it is from "asjaltuhu", when I gave it, so it is as if it were a punishment given to them. From this is the poet's saying:
"Whoever competes with me in giving will be matched by a noble man who fills the bucket up to the knot of the rope."

The meaning of "manḍūd" is that some of it was arranged upon some other, and it was said that some of it followed another, as one says: naḍḍadtu al-matā' when I placed some of the goods upon others, so it is manḍūd and naḍīd.

Al-Musawwama means marked, that is, one that has a sign. It was said: upon them were things like seal-rings. It was said: upon each stone was written the name of the one it was thrown at.

Al-Farra' said: they claimed that they were striped with red and black on white. That is their "taswīm" (marking). The meaning of ﴿with your Lord﴾ is in His treasuries. ﴿And they are not far from the wrongdoers﴾, meaning these described stones are not far from the wrongdoers, who are the people of Lot. Or it means: they are not far from any wrongdoer among the oppressors, among whom are the disbelievers of Quraysh and those who support them in disbelief against Muhammad, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace; for their wrongdoing they deserve it.

And it was said: "﴿And it is not far from the wrongdoers﴾," meaning the towns. Whoever disbelieved in the Prophet (ﷺ) is not far from them, for they lie between Syria and Madinah.

Regarding the rain of stones there are two opinions. The first is that it rained upon the cities when Jibril lifted them up. The second is that it rained upon those of its people who were not in the cities and were outside of them.

As for the masculine form of "far" (ba'id), it is either because "stones" is interpreted as "a stone," or because it is treated as agreeing with a masculine noun described: that is, "a far thing," or "a far place," or because it is a verbal noun (masdar) like "zafir" (roaring) and "sahil" (neighing), and verbal nouns are used as descriptions for both masculine and feminine alike.

Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari), Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿And when Our messengers came to Lut, he was distressed on their account and felt helpless for them﴾, that he said: he thought ill of his people, and was constrained for his guests. ﴿And he said, "This is a trying day"﴾: he means, "a hard one."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, regarding His words: ﴿They came rushing towards him﴾, he said: they hastened. ﴿And before this they had been doing evil deeds﴾, he said: they were approaching men.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh also narrated from him, saying: ﴿They came rushing towards him﴾: they were listening to him.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him also, regarding His words: ﴿These are my daughters﴾, he said: Lut did not offer his daughters to his people for illicit intercourse or for marriage. He only said, "These are your women," because the Prophet, when he is among a people, is their father. Allah the Exalted said in the Qur'an: ﴿and his wives are their mothers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 6], and he is their father in the recitation (qira'ah, a variant reading) of Ubayy.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, who said: his daughters were not his own, but they were from his community, and every prophet is the father of his community.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr something similar.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and Ibn Asakir narrated from al-Suddi something similar.

He said: In the recitation of Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud): "The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves, and he is a father to them, and his wives are their mothers."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, who said: He offered them his daughters in marriage, intending to protect his guests by marrying off his daughters.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi, regarding His words: ﴿And do not disgrace me concerning my guests﴾, he said: do not shame me.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Malik regarding ﴿Is there not among you a man of sound judgment?﴾, he said: a man who enjoins what is good and forbids what is evil.

Abu al-Shaykh and al-Bayhaqi, in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat, narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿Is there not among you a man of sound judgment?﴾, he said: one person who says, "There is no god but Allah."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ikrimah something similar.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi regarding ﴿And indeed you know what we desire﴾, he said: we only desire men. Lut said, ﴿If only I had power against you, or could take refuge in a mighty pillar﴾: he means, "in a mighty army to fight you."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿or could take refuge in a mighty pillar﴾, he said: a tribe.

It is established in al-Bukhari and others, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "May Allah have mercy on Lut; he used to take refuge in a mighty pillar." It is also narrated in non-authentic chains from other Companions.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿with a portion of the night﴾, he said: the middle of the night.

They also narrated from him, he said: in the darkness of the night.

Abd al-Razzaq narrated from Qatadah, he said: with a part of the night.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words: ﴿and let none of you look back﴾, he said: let none of you lag behind.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid regarding His words: ﴿and let none of you look back﴾, he said: let no one look behind him, ﴿except your wife﴾.

Abu Ubayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Harun, who said: in the reading (harf) of Ibn Mas'ud: "So travel with your family in a portion of the night, except your wife."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid regarding His words: ﴿So when Our command came, We turned it upside down﴾, he said: when they reached the morning, Jibril rushed at their town, uprooted it from its foundations, then inserted his wing beneath it, carried it upon the feathers of his wing with what was in it, then ascended with it to the sky until the people of the sky heard the barking of their dogs. Then he overturned it. The first thing to fall from it was its canopy, and so it did not strike a people except what struck them. Then Allah blinded their eyes, then their town was overturned, and stones of baked clay (sijjil) were rained down upon them.

The commentators have related many lengthy narrations and stories about the manner of the destruction of the people of Lut, and they differ greatly. There is no benefit in mentioning them, especially since between those who spoke of any of these things and the destruction of the people of Lut lies a long age, and for such a span a sound chain of transmission cannot readily be found. Most of this is taken from the People of the Book (Ahl al-Kitab, Jews and Christians), and their reliability in transmission is well known.

We have been commanded that we neither believe them nor disbelieve them. So understand this. This is the reason for our omitting many of these narrations found in the stories of the prophets and their peoples.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid regarding His words: ﴿And it is not far from the wrongdoers﴾, he said: by it he warns Quraysh that what befell that people might befall them.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi regarding the verse, he said: from among the wrongdoing Arabs, if they do not believe, so that they are punished by it.

Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, he said: from the wrongdoers of this Ummah.

(p. 667) When the angels left Abraham and went toward Lot's town, which was four farsakhs from Abraham, they came to Lot. When Lot saw them, and they were in the form of handsome young men without beards, ﴿he was distressed by them﴾, meaning their coming troubled him. It is said: sa'ahu yasu'uhu (it distressed him). The original form of "sī'a bihim" was "sū'iya bihim". The vowel of the waw was moved to the sin, the waw was changed to a ya', and when the hamza was lightened its vowel was placed on the ya'.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Amr read the sin with ishmam (a slight rounding toward a damma, the ishmam). ﴿And he was constrained for them in his heart﴾. Al-Azhari said: dhar' (ability, capacity) is used in the place of ṭāqa (strength). Its origin is that a camel stretches out its foreleg as it walks, according to the width of its stride, meaning it extends it. When more than its capacity is loaded onto it, its stride becomes constricted and it cannot do that. So constriction of the stride became a metaphor for little capacity and strength and for the severity of a matter. It was also said that it derives from dhara'ahu al-qay', meaning when vomiting overcomes a person and he cannot hold it in.

The meaning is that his chest was constricted when he saw the angels in that form, out of fear for them from his people, because he knew their wickedness and their committing the abomination of sodomy (liwāṭ). ﴿And he said: This is a difficult day﴾, meaning severe.

The poet said:
"And if you are not pleased with Bakr ibn Wa'il, there will be for you a day in Iraq that is grievous."
It is said: 'aṣīb, 'uṣayṣib and 'aṣawṣab (all meaning grievous), with intensive forms. That is, a day that is hateful, in which evil gathers. From this comes 'uṣba and 'iṣāba (a group whose word is united), and a man who is ma'ṣūb (whose frame is gathered).

﴿And his people came to him rushing﴾, meaning they came to Lot. The clause is in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative), describing the state of the subject.

The meaning of yuhra'ūna ilayhi is: they hasten toward him.

Al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and other lexicographers said: ihrā' is only hastening with trembling. It is said: ahra'a al-rajul ihrā'an, meaning he hastened while trembling from cold, anger or fever. Muhalhil said:
"They came rushing, while they were captives, their cheeks [trembling] in spite of their noses."

It was also said: yuhra'ūna means they run in a trot, and it was said: it is a walk between a trot and a run.

The meaning: when the report of the angels' coming in that form reached Lot's people, they hastened to him, as if they were being pushed, in pursuit of the abomination against his guests. ﴿And before this they used to do evil deeds﴾, meaning before the coming of the messengers at this time they used to commit evil deeds. It was also said: before Lot, they used to do evil deeds, meaning their custom was to mount men. When they came to Lot and aimed at his guests for that deed, Lot stood up to them, defending them. ﴿He said: O my people, these are my daughters, they are purer for you﴾, meaning marry them, and leave what you seek of the abomination with my guests. He had three daughters, and it is said two; they used to ask him to marry them to them, but he refused because of their wickedness. They had two prominent leaders whom they obeyed, and he intended to marry his two daughters to them. It was also said that by his words "these are my daughters" he meant women in general, because the prophet of a people is a father to them. A group said: this statement from him was by way of defense, and he did not intend the literal meaning.

The meaning of ﴿they are purer for you﴾ is: more lawful and cleaner. Tathahhur means keeping oneself clear of what is not lawful. The form "aṭhar" does not indicate comparison (superlative), but is like "Allahu akbar" (God is greatest). Al-Hasan and Isa ibn 'Umar read "aṭhara" with fatḥa (naṣb), and the rest read it with ḍamma (rafʿ).
