Then, after frightening them with punishment, he commanded them to seek forgiveness and repent, saying: ﴿And seek forgiveness of your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance. Indeed, my Lord is Merciful and Loving﴾. The explanation of seeking forgiveness, together with the ordering of repentance after it, has passed at the beginning of the surah, and the explanation of "al-Rahim" has passed. What is meant here is that He is greatly merciful to the penitent. "Al-Wadud" is the one who loves.

In al-Sihah it is said: "waddadtu al-rajul awuddu wuddan": when I loved the man. Al-wadud is the loving one, and al-widd, al-wudd and al-wadd are love. The meaning here is that He does to His servants what one who is most loving does to one he loves: kindness toward him, bringing good to him, and warding off evil from him.

In this is a reason for what preceded it, the command to seek forgiveness and repent.

The sentence ﴿They said: O Shu'ayb, we do not understand much of what you say﴾ is a fresh statement like the preceding sentences. The meaning: you bring us things for which we have no prior knowledge, such as reports of unseen matters like resurrection and rising, and we do not understand that, meaning we do not comprehend it as we comprehend visible, present matters. So the negation of understanding in this case is literal, not figurative. It is also said: they said this turning away from hearing him and holding his speech in contempt, though it was understood by them and known to them; so the negation of understanding is not literal but figurative. It is said: faqiha yafqahu means "he understood, with understanding and comprehension"; and al-Kisa'i related fuqhanan; and it is said faqaha fiqhan means "he became a faqih."

﴿And indeed, we see you among us as weak﴾: that is, you have no strength by which you can prevent yourself from us and by which you can oppose us. It is said the meaning is that he was weak in his body; this was said by Ali ibn Isa. It is also said that he had been afflicted in his sight.

An-Nahhas said: The lexicographers related that Himyar would say to a blind man "da'if" (weak): that is, he has become weak through the loss of his sight, just as he is called "darir" (harmed): that is, he has been harmed by the loss of his sight. It is said that "da'if" means "contemptible," which is close to the first statement.

﴿And had it not been for your clan, we would have stoned you﴾. The clan (rahṭ) of a man is his kinsfolk upon whom he relies and by whom he is strengthened; and from it is "al-rahit," the hole of the jerboa, because it is secured by it and its young is hidden in it. "Al-rahṭ" applies to three up to ten. They made his clan a barrier against inflicting harm upon him, though they were few while the disbelievers were numerous and gathered; because they were upon their religion, they left him out of respect for them, not out of fear of them.

Then they confirmed what they had described him with of weakness by saying: ﴿And you are not mighty against us﴾, so that we would restrain from you for the sake of your might among us; rather, we left stoning you because of the might of your clan over us. The meaning of "we would have stoned you" is that we would have killed you by stoning, for they, when they killed a person, stoned him with stones. It is also said the meaning of "we would have stoned you" is "we would have reviled you." From it is the saying of al-Ja'di:

"We reviled one another with bitter speech, until we became as if we were two horses racing."

The word "rajm" is also applied to cursing, and from it is "al-shaytan al-rajim" (the accursed Satan).

The clause "﴿Qāla yā qawmi a-rahṭī aʿazzu ʿalaykum mina llāh﴾" [He said: "O my people, is my clan more honourable to you than God?"] is a resumed statement (mustaʾnafah), and he said "aʿazzu ʿalaykum mina llāh" and did not say "aʿazzu ʿalaykum minnī" because the negation of honour from himself and its affirmation for his people, as indicated by the placing of the pronoun before the negative particle, is a belittling of him, and belittling the prophets of God is belittling God, Mighty and Majestic. Thus their speech implied that his clan was more honourable to them than God. So he disapproved of this from them, marvelled at it, and obliged them with something from which they had no escape or way out, in the form of a question. In this there is what is not hidden of the strength of argument, clarity of disputation, and silencing of the opponent. For this reason Shuʿayb was named "khaṭīb al-anbiyāʾ" (the orator of the prophets). The pronoun in "wa-ttakhadhtumūhu" refers to God, glorified is He.

The meaning: "You have taken God, Mighty and Majestic, [as something to be cast aside] because of your lack of regard for His prophet whom He sent to you, ﴿and have put Him behind your backs﴾", i.e., cast away and placed behind the back, not caring for Him. It was also said the meaning is: "You have taken the command of God, which He commanded me to convey to you, and which is what I brought you, and put it behind your backs." It is said: "I made his command a back (bi-ẓahr)" when one neglects it. "Ẓihriyyan" is a relative form derived from "ẓahr," and the kasra is to alter the relative form. ﴿Indeed my Lord is encompassing of what you do﴾, nothing of your sayings and deeds is hidden from Him.

﴿And O my people, act according to your position; indeed I am acting. You will soon know﴾: when he saw their persistence in disbelief and their determination upon the religion of their fathers, and that admonition had no effect on them, he threatened them that he would act to the utmost of their ability and the limit of their capacity. It is said: "makuna makānatan" when one becomes firmly established to the utmost degree. He informed them that he was acting according to what is possible for him and what God decrees for him. Then he intensified the threat and warning by saying: ﴿You will soon know﴾, i.e., the outcome of what you are in of worshipping other than God and harming His servants. A similar expression occurred earlier in al-Anʿām. ﴿Who will receive a punishment that disgraces him﴾: "man" is in a position of object of "taʿlamūn" (you will know), i.e., you will soon know who it is that will receive the disgracing punishment that results in humiliation, shame and disgrace. ﴿And who is a liar﴾ is conjoined to "man yaʾtīhi," and the meaning: "You will soon know who is the one punished and who is the liar?" In it there is an allusion to their lying in their saying: ﴿Had it not been for your clan, we would have stoned you, and you are not mighty against us﴾. It was also said: "man" is a subject (mubtadaʾ) and what follows it is its relative clause, and the predicate is omitted, the estimation being: "Whoever is a liar, he will know his lie and taste the evil of his affair."

Al-Farrāʾ said: The reason "huwa" came in "man huwa kādhib" is that they do not say "man qāʾimun" (who is standing); they say "man qāma," "man yaqūmu," and "man al-qāʾim," so they added "huwa" so that it would form a clause standing in place of a verb (faʿala and yafʿalu).

Al-Naḥḥās said: What indicates the opposite of this is the saying of the poet:

*"Man rasūlī ilā al-Thurayyā, fa-innī / ḍiqtu dhar'an bi-hajrihā wa-l-kitābi"*
(Who will be my messenger to the Pleiades? For I have become constricted with distress from her separation and from the letter.)

﴿And wait; indeed I am with you among the watchers﴾, i.e., await, for I am with you awaiting what God will decide between us.

﴿And when Our command came, We saved Shuʿayb and those who believed with him﴾, i.e., when Our punishment came, or Our command to punish them came, We saved Shuʿayb and his followers who believed in him ﴿by a mercy from Us﴾ toward them because of their faith, or by a mercy from Us toward them, which is their guidance to faith. (p-672) ﴿And the cry seized those who wronged﴾, others, for what they took of people's wealth without right, and who wronged themselves by their insistence upon disbelief: the Cry with which Gabriel shouted at them until their souls left their bodies. In al-Aʿrāf it says: ﴿So the quake seized them﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 7:78, 91], and likewise in al-ʿAnkabūt.

We have already stated that the "rajfah" is the earthquake, and that it follows the Cry, due to the agitation of the air that leads to it. ﴿So they became in their homes prostrate﴾, i.e., dead.

Its explanation, and the explanation of ﴿as if they had never dwelt therein﴾, has been given shortly before, and likewise the explanation of ﴿Away with Madyan, as Thamūd were taken away﴾.

Al-Kisāʾī reported that Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī recited "kamā baʿudat Thamūd" with a ḍammah on the ʿayn.

Al-Mahdawī said: Whoever puts a ḍammah on the ʿayn in "baʿudat" has a dialect in which it is used for both good and bad; whereas "baʿidat" with a kasra, according to the reading of the majority, is used specifically for evil, and here it means a curse.

Ibn Jarīr and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed I see you in prosperity﴾, he said: cheap prices; ﴿and indeed I fear for you the punishment of an encompassing day﴾, he said: high prices.

Ibn Jarīr reported from him regarding ﴿baqiyyatu llāh﴾, he said: God's provision.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Qatādah: ﴿The remainder of God is better for you﴾, he says: your portion from your Lord is better for you.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Mujāhid: he said: obedience to God.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from al-Aʿmash regarding His saying: ﴿Does your prayer command you?﴾, he said: your recitation.

Ibn ʿAsākir reported from al-Aḥnaf that Shuʿayb was the most prayerful of the prophets.

Ibn Jarīr and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Zayd regarding His saying: ﴿or that we do with our wealth what we please﴾, he said: He forbade them from clipping these dinars and dirhams, and they said: "They are only our wealth; we do with them what we please. If we wish, we clip them; if we wish, we burn them; if we wish, we throw them away."

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn al-Mundhir reported similar from Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb.

Both reported similarly from Zayd ibn Aslam as well.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Ibn Saʿd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abū al-Shaykh and ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported similarly from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab as well.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed you are the forbearing, the upright﴾, he said: they say, "Indeed you are not forbearing nor upright."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Qatādah: a mockery of him.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk regarding His saying: ﴿and He provided me from Himself with good provision﴾, he said: the lawful.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Qatādah regarding His saying: ﴿And I do not intend to oppose you in what I forbid you from﴾, he said: he says, "I would not forbid you from a matter and then commit it myself."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Mujāhid regarding His saying: ﴿And to Him I turn in repentance﴾, he said: to Him I return.

Abū Nuʿaym in al-Ḥilyah reported "from ʿAlī, who said: I said, 'O Messenger of God, advise me.' He said: 'Say: God is my Lord, then be steadfast.' I said: 'My Lord is God, and my success is only by God; upon Him I rely and to Him I turn in repentance.' He said: 'May knowledge be pleasant for you, Abū al-Ḥasan; you have drunk knowledge in gulps and quaffed it deeply.'" In its chain is Muḥammad ibn Yūsuf al-Kudaymī.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Qatādah: ﴿Let not my opposition lead you to sin﴾: let not my separation from you bring you to it.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Mujāhid: he said: "my opposition" is my enmity.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from al-Suddī: he said: let not my enmity move you.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq and Ibn Jarīr reported from Qatādah regarding His saying: ﴿And the people of Lot are not far from you﴾, he said: they were only recent people, close after Noah and Thamūd.

Abū al-Shaykh and Ibn ʿAsākir reported from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr: ﴿And indeed we see you among us as weak﴾, he said: he was blind, and he became blind from his weeping out of love for God, Mighty and Majestic.

al-Wāḥidī and Ibn ʿAsākir reported from Shaddād ibn Aws, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Shuʿayb (peace be upon him) wept out of love for God until he became blind."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim (who authenticated it), al-Khaṭīb and Ibn ʿAsākir reported through several chains from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His saying: ﴿And indeed we see you among us as weak﴾, he said: he was blind in sight.

Abū al-Shaykh reported similarly from Abū Ṣāliḥ.

Abū al-Shaykh reported from Sufyān regarding His saying: ﴿And indeed we see you among us as weak﴾, he said: he was blind, and he was called "the orator of the prophets."

Abū al-Shaykh reported from al-Suddī: he said: its meaning is, "You are only one."

Abū al-Shaykh reported from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib that he delivered a sermon and recited this verse concerning Shuʿayb, ﴿And indeed we see you among us as weak﴾, and said: he was blind, so they attributed weakness to him. ﴿Had it not been for your clan, we would have stoned you﴾. ʿAlī said: "By God, besides whom there is no god, they did not fear the majesty of their Lord; they feared only the tribe."

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Mujāhid regarding His saying: ﴿And you have taken Him behind your backs as something cast away﴾, he said: you have cast away His command. Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Qatādah, who said regarding the verse: "You do not fear Him."

Abū al-Shaykh reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, who said: "You belittled Him."

And We sent to Madyan their brother Shu'ayb. That is, the people of Shu'ayb, and Shu'ayb was their brother in lineage. They were named Madyan after their father, who was Madyan ibn Ibrahim; and it is said they were named after their city.

An-Nahhas said: Madyan is not declined, because it is the name of a city. This matter has already been discussed in Surat al-A'raf more fully than here. The explanation of ﴿O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him﴾ has already passed at the beginning of the surah. This sentence is a fresh statement, as if it were said: What did Shu'ayb say to them when Allah sent him to them? Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, was called the orator of the prophets for the excellence of his argumentation with his people. He first commanded them to worship Allah, glorified is He, who is the God alone, having no partner. Then he forbade them from diminishing the measure and the balance, because they, along with their disbelief, were people of fraud (tatfif). When the seller came to them with food, they took more by measure; likewise, when what was weighed reached them, they took more by weight. And when they sold, they sold with a lesser measure (p-670) and a lesser weight.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, I see you in prosperity﴾ is a reason for the prohibition: that is, do not diminish the measure and the balance, for indeed I see you in prosperity, meaning in wealth and abundance of provision. So do not change Allah's blessing upon you by disobeying Him and harming His servants. In this blessing there is what suffices you from taking people's wealth without right. Then after this reason he mentioned another reason, saying: ﴿And indeed, I fear for you the punishment of an encompassing day﴾. In this reason there is a reminder to them of the punishment of the Hereafter, just as the first reason contained a reminder of the bounties of this world. The day is described as encompassing, and what is meant is the punishment, because the punishment occurs on the day. The meaning of the encompassing of the day's punishment over them is that none of them will escape it, and they will find no refuge or place of escape from it. The day is the Day of Resurrection; it is also said that it is the day of retribution against them in this world by the Blast.

Then he emphasized the prohibition against diminishing the measure and the weight with his words: ﴿And O my people, give full measure and weight with justice﴾. Al-iyfa' is completion, and al-qist is justice, which is the absence of excess and deficiency. Although exceeding the full measure is virtue and good, it is beyond what the name of justice conveys. The prohibition against deficiency, though it entails giving full measure, combines the two indications into an eloquent emphasis and a fine reinforcement. Then he increased this emphasis, saying: ﴿And do not deprive people of their things﴾. The explanation of this has passed in Surat al-A'raf. It includes a general prohibition against bakhs (defrauding), and "things" is broader than what is measured and weighed; so defrauding by cheating in measure and weight enters into this first and foremost. It is also said that bakhs means only the unjust levy (maks).

Then he said: ﴿And do not act corruptly on the earth, spreading corruption﴾. Its explanation has also passed in al-Baqarah. Acting corruptly on the earth (al-'uthiy) includes everything that causes harm to people in it, so the diminishing of measure and balance in the context enters it. He restricted it by the circumstantial phrase "spreading corruption" in order to exclude what has the form of acting corruptly on the earth but whose aim is reform, as happened with al-Khidr in the ship.

﴿The remainder from Allah is better for you﴾: that is, what Allah leaves for you of lawful provision after giving full rights with justice is more beneficial and blessed than what you leave for yourselves through fraud, defrauding and corruption on the earth. Ibn Jarir and other exegetes mentioned this meaning.

Mujahid said: "The remainder from Allah" is His obedience.
Al-Rabi' said: His counsel.
Al-Farra' said: His watchfulness.

He restricted this by saying ﴿if you are believers﴾, because this benefits only the believer and not the disbeliever; or the intended meaning of "believers" here is those who affirmed Shu'ayb.

﴿And I am not a guardian over you﴾: I do not guard you from falling into sins such as fraud, defrauding and others; or it means I do not keep watch over your deeds, and I will call you to account for them and recompense you for them.

The sentence ﴿They said: O Shu'ayb, does your prayer command you that we abandon what our fathers worshipped, or that we not do with our wealth what we please?﴾ is a fresh statement, an answer to an assumed question, as if it were said: What did they say to Shu'ayb? The reading "ṣalātuka" is in the singular. "An natruka" is in the position of an accusative. Al-Kisa'i said its position is genitive by the implied preposition "bi". Their intent by "what our fathers worshipped" is the idols they worshipped. The interrogation is for denial against him and for mockery of him, because prayers in their view are not among the good things said to one who does them when one wants to soften his heart and tame his harshness, as one says to someone who was very generous in charity when he does something not fitting to right conduct: "Your charity has commanded you to this!" It is said that the prayer here means recitation; it is said it means religion; it is said it means his followers, and from this is the "musalli" who follows the forerunner. This was their answer to Shu'ayb concerning his command to them to worship Allah alone. And their saying: ﴿or that we do with our wealth what we please﴾ is their answer to him concerning his command to them to give full measure and weight, and his prohibition against diminishing them, and against defrauding people and against corruption on the earth. This sentence is conjoined to what is in "what our fathers worshipped."

The meaning is: Does your prayer command you that we abandon what our fathers worshipped, and command you that we abandon doing with our wealth what we will, by taking and giving, increasing and decreasing?

It was read: "naf'ala fi amwalina ma nashā'", with the second-person in both. An-Nahhas said: then "aw" in this reading is for conjunction with the first "an", and the estimate is: "Does your prayer command you that you do with our wealth what you will?"

It was also read: "naf'ala" with a nun and "ma tashā'" with a second-person, and its meaning: Does your prayer command you that we do with our wealth what you will, and that we leave what we will and what is mutually agreed among us?

Then they described him with two great attributes, saying: ﴿Indeed, you are the forbearing, the rightly guided﴾, in the manner of mockery of him, for they believe he is contrary to these two. Or they mean: "Indeed, you are the forbearing, the rightly guided [in yourself and in your own estimation]." Their meaning: this which you forbid us and command us contradicts what you hold in yourself of forbearance and rectitude. It is said they said this not in mockery but that it was truly so in their view, and they denied his command and prohibition to them, as contrary to forbearance and rectitude in their belief.

The explanation of forbearance (ḥilm) and rectitude (rushd) has already passed.

The sentence ﴿He said: O my people, tell me, if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord﴾ is a fresh statement like the sentences before it. The meaning: Inform me, if I am upon a clear proof from my Lord regarding what I have commanded you and forbidden you; ﴿and He has provided me from Himself﴾: that is, from His bounty and the treasuries of His dominion; ﴿with good provision﴾: that is, abundant, wide, lawful, good. He, peace be upon him, was a man of much wealth. It is said he meant by "provision" prophethood; it is said wisdom; it is said knowledge; it is said success (tawfiq). The answer to the condition is omitted, indicated by the context: its estimate is "Shall I abandon your command and your prohibition?" or "Will you say about me what you say, intending by it mockery and derision?"

﴿And I do not intend to oppose you in what I forbid you from﴾: that is, I do not intend by my prohibition to you against defrauding and defrauding people that I oppose you by doing what I forbade you, doing it apart from you. It is said: "khalafahu ila kadha" when one intends it while turning away from it, and "khalaftuhu 'an kadha" in the reverse of that.

﴿I intend only reform﴾: that is, I intend by command and prohibition only reform for you and the removal of corruption in your religion and your dealings.

﴿As far as I am able﴾: as far as my capacity reaches and my power is enabled.

﴿And my success is only through Allah﴾: that is, I have not become one granted success, a guide, a prophet, a rightly-guiding one, except by Allah's support, His empowering me to it, and His granting it to me.

﴿Upon Him I rely﴾ in all my affairs, among which is your command and your prohibition.

﴿And to Him I turn penitently﴾: that is, I return in every matter that befalls me and I entrust all my affairs to what He chooses for me of His decree and destiny. It is said the meaning is: and to Him I return in the Hereafter. It is also said that inabah means supplication, and the meaning is: and to Him I supplicate.

His statement: (p-671) ﴿And O my people, let not my opposition cause you to incur [the punishment]﴾.

Az-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, let not my opposition cause you to incur the punishment's striking you, as it struck those before you. It is said the meaning is: let not my opposition move you; and al-shiqaq is enmity, and from it is the saying of al-Akhtal:

"Is there none who will convey from me a message? How did you find the taste of enmity?"

And ﴿that there befall you﴾ is in the position of an accusative as the second object of "yajrimannakum". ﴿Like what befell the people of Nuh﴾ by drowning; ﴿or the people of Hud﴾ by the wind; ﴿or the people of Salih﴾ by the Blast. The explanation of "yajrimannakum" and of shiqaq has already passed. ﴿And the people of Lut are not far from you﴾. It may mean: their place is not far from your place; or their time is not far from your time; or they are not far from you in the cause that brings their punishment, which is absolute disbelief. The word "ba'id" is singular for the same reason as in ﴿and it is not far from the wrongdoers﴾.

Then, after frightening them with punishment, he commanded them to seek forgiveness and repent, saying: ﴿And seek forgiveness of your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance. Indeed, my Lord is Merciful and Loving﴾. The explanation of seeking forgiveness, together with the ordering of repentance after it, has passed at the beginning of the surah, and the explanation of "al-Rahim" has passed. What is meant here is that He is greatly merciful to the penitent. "Al-Wadud" is the one who loves.

In al-Sihah it is said: "waddadtu al-rajul awuddu wuddan": when I loved the man. Al-wadud is the loving one, and al-widd, al-wudd and al-wadd are love. The meaning here is that He does to His servants what one who is most loving does to one he loves: kindness toward him, bringing good to him, and warding off evil from him.

In this is a reason for what preceded it, the command to seek forgiveness and repent.

The sentence ﴿They said: O Shu'ayb, we do not understand much of what you say﴾ is a fresh statement like the preceding sentences. The meaning: you bring us things for which we have no prior knowledge, such as reports of unseen matters like resurrection and rising, and we do not understand that, meaning we do not comprehend it as we comprehend visible, present matters. So the negation of understanding in this case is literal, not figurative. It is also said: they said this turning away from hearing him and holding his speech in contempt, though it was understood by them and known to them; so the negation of understanding is not literal but figurative. It is said: faqiha yafqahu means "he understood, with understanding and comprehension"; and al-Kisa'i related fuqhanan; and it is said faqaha fiqhan means "he became a faqih."

﴿And indeed, we see you among us as weak﴾: that is, you have no strength by which you can prevent yourself from us and by which you can oppose us. It is said the meaning is that he was weak in his body; this was said by Ali ibn Isa. It is also said that he had been afflicted in his sight.

An-Nahhas said: The lexicographers related that Himyar would say to a blind man "da'if" (weak): that is, he has become weak through the loss of his sight, just as he is called "darir" (harmed): that is, he has been harmed by the loss of his sight. It is said that "da'if" means "contemptible," which is close to the first statement.

﴿And had it not been for your clan, we would have stoned you﴾. The clan (rahṭ) of a man is his kinsfolk upon whom he relies and by whom he is strengthened; and from it is "al-rahit," the hole of the jerboa, because it is secured by it and its young is hidden in it. "Al-rahṭ" applies to three up to ten. They made his clan a barrier against inflicting harm upon him, though they were few while the disbelievers were numerous and gathered; because they were upon their religion, they left him out of respect for them, not out of fear of them.

Then they confirmed what they had described him with of weakness by saying: ﴿And you are not mighty against us﴾, so that we would restrain from you for the sake of your might among us; rather, we left stoning you because of the might of your clan over us. The meaning of "we would have stoned you" is that we would have killed you by stoning, for they, when they killed a person, stoned him with stones. It is also said the meaning of "we would have stoned you" is "we would have reviled you." From it is the saying of al-Ja'di:

"We reviled one another with bitter speech, until we became as if we were two horses racing."

The word "rajm" is also applied to cursing, and from it is "al-shaytan al-rajim" (the accursed Satan).

The clause "﴿Qāla yā qawmi a-rahṭī aʿazzu ʿalaykum mina llāh﴾" [He said: "O my people, is my clan more honourable to you than God?"] is a resumed statement (mustaʾnafah), and he said "aʿazzu ʿalaykum mina llāh" and did not say "aʿazzu ʿalaykum minnī" because the negation of honour from himself and its affirmation for his people, as indicated by the placing of the pronoun before the negative particle, is a belittling of him, and belittling the prophets of God is belittling God, Mighty and Majestic. Thus their speech implied that his clan was more honourable to them than God. So he disapproved of this from them, marvelled at it, and obliged them with something from which they had no escape or way out, in the form of a question. In this there is what is not hidden of the strength of argument, clarity of disputation, and silencing of the opponent. For this reason Shuʿayb was named "khaṭīb al-anbiyāʾ" (the orator of the prophets). The pronoun in "wa-ttakhadhtumūhu" refers to God, glorified is He.

The meaning: "You have taken God, Mighty and Majestic, [as something to be cast aside] because of your lack of regard for His prophet whom He sent to you, ﴿and have put Him behind your backs﴾", i.e., cast away and placed behind the back, not caring for Him. It was also said the meaning is: "You have taken the command of God, which He commanded me to convey to you, and which is what I brought you, and put it behind your backs." It is said: "I made his command a back (bi-ẓahr)" when one neglects it. "Ẓihriyyan" is a relative form derived from "ẓahr," and the kasra is to alter the relative form. ﴿Indeed my Lord is encompassing of what you do﴾, nothing of your sayings and deeds is hidden from Him.

﴿And O my people, act according to your position; indeed I am acting. You will soon know﴾: when he saw their persistence in disbelief and their determination upon the religion of their fathers, and that admonition had no effect on them, he threatened them that he would act to the utmost of their ability and the limit of their capacity. It is said: "makuna makānatan" when one becomes firmly established to the utmost degree. He informed them that he was acting according to what is possible for him and what God decrees for him. Then he intensified the threat and warning by saying: ﴿You will soon know﴾, i.e., the outcome of what you are in of worshipping other than God and harming His servants. A similar expression occurred earlier in al-Anʿām. ﴿Who will receive a punishment that disgraces him﴾: "man" is in a position of object of "taʿlamūn" (you will know), i.e., you will soon know who it is that will receive the disgracing punishment that results in humiliation, shame and disgrace. ﴿And who is a liar﴾ is conjoined to "man yaʾtīhi," and the meaning: "You will soon know who is the one punished and who is the liar?" In it there is an allusion to their lying in their saying: ﴿Had it not been for your clan, we would have stoned you, and you are not mighty against us﴾. It was also said: "man" is a subject (mubtadaʾ) and what follows it is its relative clause, and the predicate is omitted, the estimation being: "Whoever is a liar, he will know his lie and taste the evil of his affair."

Al-Farrāʾ said: The reason "huwa" came in "man huwa kādhib" is that they do not say "man qāʾimun" (who is standing); they say "man qāma," "man yaqūmu," and "man al-qāʾim," so they added "huwa" so that it would form a clause standing in place of a verb (faʿala and yafʿalu).

Al-Naḥḥās said: What indicates the opposite of this is the saying of the poet:

*"Man rasūlī ilā al-Thurayyā, fa-innī / ḍiqtu dhar'an bi-hajrihā wa-l-kitābi"*
(Who will be my messenger to the Pleiades? For I have become constricted with distress from her separation and from the letter.)

﴿And wait; indeed I am with you among the watchers﴾, i.e., await, for I am with you awaiting what God will decide between us.

﴿And when Our command came, We saved Shuʿayb and those who believed with him﴾, i.e., when Our punishment came, or Our command to punish them came, We saved Shuʿayb and his followers who believed in him ﴿by a mercy from Us﴾ toward them because of their faith, or by a mercy from Us toward them, which is their guidance to faith. (p-672) ﴿And the cry seized those who wronged﴾, others, for what they took of people's wealth without right, and who wronged themselves by their insistence upon disbelief: the Cry with which Gabriel shouted at them until their souls left their bodies. In al-Aʿrāf it says: ﴿So the quake seized them﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 7:78, 91], and likewise in al-ʿAnkabūt.

We have already stated that the "rajfah" is the earthquake, and that it follows the Cry, due to the agitation of the air that leads to it. ﴿So they became in their homes prostrate﴾, i.e., dead.

Its explanation, and the explanation of ﴿as if they had never dwelt therein﴾, has been given shortly before, and likewise the explanation of ﴿Away with Madyan, as Thamūd were taken away﴾.

Al-Kisāʾī reported that Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī recited "kamā baʿudat Thamūd" with a ḍammah on the ʿayn.

Al-Mahdawī said: Whoever puts a ḍammah on the ʿayn in "baʿudat" has a dialect in which it is used for both good and bad; whereas "baʿidat" with a kasra, according to the reading of the majority, is used specifically for evil, and here it means a curse.

Ibn Jarīr and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed I see you in prosperity﴾, he said: cheap prices; ﴿and indeed I fear for you the punishment of an encompassing day﴾, he said: high prices.

Ibn Jarīr reported from him regarding ﴿baqiyyatu llāh﴾, he said: God's provision.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Qatādah: ﴿The remainder of God is better for you﴾, he says: your portion from your Lord is better for you.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Mujāhid: he said: obedience to God.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from al-Aʿmash regarding His saying: ﴿Does your prayer command you?﴾, he said: your recitation.

Ibn ʿAsākir reported from al-Aḥnaf that Shuʿayb was the most prayerful of the prophets.

Ibn Jarīr and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Zayd regarding His saying: ﴿or that we do with our wealth what we please﴾, he said: He forbade them from clipping these dinars and dirhams, and they said: "They are only our wealth; we do with them what we please. If we wish, we clip them; if we wish, we burn them; if we wish, we throw them away."

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn al-Mundhir reported similar from Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb.

Both reported similarly from Zayd ibn Aslam as well.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Ibn Saʿd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abū al-Shaykh and ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported similarly from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab as well.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed you are the forbearing, the upright﴾, he said: they say, "Indeed you are not forbearing nor upright."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Qatādah: a mockery of him.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk regarding His saying: ﴿and He provided me from Himself with good provision﴾, he said: the lawful.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Qatādah regarding His saying: ﴿And I do not intend to oppose you in what I forbid you from﴾, he said: he says, "I would not forbid you from a matter and then commit it myself."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Mujāhid regarding His saying: ﴿And to Him I turn in repentance﴾, he said: to Him I return.

Abū Nuʿaym in al-Ḥilyah reported "from ʿAlī, who said: I said, 'O Messenger of God, advise me.' He said: 'Say: God is my Lord, then be steadfast.' I said: 'My Lord is God, and my success is only by God; upon Him I rely and to Him I turn in repentance.' He said: 'May knowledge be pleasant for you, Abū al-Ḥasan; you have drunk knowledge in gulps and quaffed it deeply.'" In its chain is Muḥammad ibn Yūsuf al-Kudaymī.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Qatādah: ﴿Let not my opposition lead you to sin﴾: let not my separation from you bring you to it.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Mujāhid: he said: "my opposition" is my enmity.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from al-Suddī: he said: let not my enmity move you.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq and Ibn Jarīr reported from Qatādah regarding His saying: ﴿And the people of Lot are not far from you﴾, he said: they were only recent people, close after Noah and Thamūd.

Abū al-Shaykh and Ibn ʿAsākir reported from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr: ﴿And indeed we see you among us as weak﴾, he said: he was blind, and he became blind from his weeping out of love for God, Mighty and Majestic.

al-Wāḥidī and Ibn ʿAsākir reported from Shaddād ibn Aws, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Shuʿayb (peace be upon him) wept out of love for God until he became blind."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim (who authenticated it), al-Khaṭīb and Ibn ʿAsākir reported through several chains from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His saying: ﴿And indeed we see you among us as weak﴾, he said: he was blind in sight.

Abū al-Shaykh reported similarly from Abū Ṣāliḥ.

Abū al-Shaykh reported from Sufyān regarding His saying: ﴿And indeed we see you among us as weak﴾, he said: he was blind, and he was called "the orator of the prophets."

Abū al-Shaykh reported from al-Suddī: he said: its meaning is, "You are only one."

Abū al-Shaykh reported from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib that he delivered a sermon and recited this verse concerning Shuʿayb, ﴿And indeed we see you among us as weak﴾, and said: he was blind, so they attributed weakness to him. ﴿Had it not been for your clan, we would have stoned you﴾. ʿAlī said: "By God, besides whom there is no god, they did not fear the majesty of their Lord; they feared only the tribe."

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Mujāhid regarding His saying: ﴿And you have taken Him behind your backs as something cast away﴾, he said: you have cast away His command. Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Qatādah, who said regarding the verse: "You do not fear Him."

Abū al-Shaykh reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, who said: "You belittled Him."

And We sent to Madyan their brother Shu'ayb. That is, the people of Shu'ayb, and Shu'ayb was their brother in lineage. They were named Madyan after their father, who was Madyan ibn Ibrahim; and it is said they were named after their city.

An-Nahhas said: Madyan is not declined, because it is the name of a city. This matter has already been discussed in Surat al-A'raf more fully than here. The explanation of ﴿O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him﴾ has already passed at the beginning of the surah. This sentence is a fresh statement, as if it were said: What did Shu'ayb say to them when Allah sent him to them? Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, was called the orator of the prophets for the excellence of his argumentation with his people. He first commanded them to worship Allah, glorified is He, who is the God alone, having no partner. Then he forbade them from diminishing the measure and the balance, because they, along with their disbelief, were people of fraud (tatfif). When the seller came to them with food, they took more by measure; likewise, when what was weighed reached them, they took more by weight. And when they sold, they sold with a lesser measure (p-670) and a lesser weight.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, I see you in prosperity﴾ is a reason for the prohibition: that is, do not diminish the measure and the balance, for indeed I see you in prosperity, meaning in wealth and abundance of provision. So do not change Allah's blessing upon you by disobeying Him and harming His servants. In this blessing there is what suffices you from taking people's wealth without right. Then after this reason he mentioned another reason, saying: ﴿And indeed, I fear for you the punishment of an encompassing day﴾. In this reason there is a reminder to them of the punishment of the Hereafter, just as the first reason contained a reminder of the bounties of this world. The day is described as encompassing, and what is meant is the punishment, because the punishment occurs on the day. The meaning of the encompassing of the day's punishment over them is that none of them will escape it, and they will find no refuge or place of escape from it. The day is the Day of Resurrection; it is also said that it is the day of retribution against them in this world by the Blast.

Then he emphasized the prohibition against diminishing the measure and the weight with his words: ﴿And O my people, give full measure and weight with justice﴾. Al-iyfa' is completion, and al-qist is justice, which is the absence of excess and deficiency. Although exceeding the full measure is virtue and good, it is beyond what the name of justice conveys. The prohibition against deficiency, though it entails giving full measure, combines the two indications into an eloquent emphasis and a fine reinforcement. Then he increased this emphasis, saying: ﴿And do not deprive people of their things﴾. The explanation of this has passed in Surat al-A'raf. It includes a general prohibition against bakhs (defrauding), and "things" is broader than what is measured and weighed; so defrauding by cheating in measure and weight enters into this first and foremost. It is also said that bakhs means only the unjust levy (maks).

Then he said: ﴿And do not act corruptly on the earth, spreading corruption﴾. Its explanation has also passed in al-Baqarah. Acting corruptly on the earth (al-'uthiy) includes everything that causes harm to people in it, so the diminishing of measure and balance in the context enters it. He restricted it by the circumstantial phrase "spreading corruption" in order to exclude what has the form of acting corruptly on the earth but whose aim is reform, as happened with al-Khidr in the ship.

﴿The remainder from Allah is better for you﴾: that is, what Allah leaves for you of lawful provision after giving full rights with justice is more beneficial and blessed than what you leave for yourselves through fraud, defrauding and corruption on the earth. Ibn Jarir and other exegetes mentioned this meaning.

Mujahid said: "The remainder from Allah" is His obedience.
Al-Rabi' said: His counsel.
Al-Farra' said: His watchfulness.

He restricted this by saying ﴿if you are believers﴾, because this benefits only the believer and not the disbeliever; or the intended meaning of "believers" here is those who affirmed Shu'ayb.

﴿And I am not a guardian over you﴾: I do not guard you from falling into sins such as fraud, defrauding and others; or it means I do not keep watch over your deeds, and I will call you to account for them and recompense you for them.

The sentence ﴿They said: O Shu'ayb, does your prayer command you that we abandon what our fathers worshipped, or that we not do with our wealth what we please?﴾ is a fresh statement, an answer to an assumed question, as if it were said: What did they say to Shu'ayb? The reading "ṣalātuka" is in the singular. "An natruka" is in the position of an accusative. Al-Kisa'i said its position is genitive by the implied preposition "bi". Their intent by "what our fathers worshipped" is the idols they worshipped. The interrogation is for denial against him and for mockery of him, because prayers in their view are not among the good things said to one who does them when one wants to soften his heart and tame his harshness, as one says to someone who was very generous in charity when he does something not fitting to right conduct: "Your charity has commanded you to this!" It is said that the prayer here means recitation; it is said it means religion; it is said it means his followers, and from this is the "musalli" who follows the forerunner. This was their answer to Shu'ayb concerning his command to them to worship Allah alone. And their saying: ﴿or that we do with our wealth what we please﴾ is their answer to him concerning his command to them to give full measure and weight, and his prohibition against diminishing them, and against defrauding people and against corruption on the earth. This sentence is conjoined to what is in "what our fathers worshipped."

The meaning is: Does your prayer command you that we abandon what our fathers worshipped, and command you that we abandon doing with our wealth what we will, by taking and giving, increasing and decreasing?

It was read: "naf'ala fi amwalina ma nashā'", with the second-person in both. An-Nahhas said: then "aw" in this reading is for conjunction with the first "an", and the estimate is: "Does your prayer command you that you do with our wealth what you will?"

It was also read: "naf'ala" with a nun and "ma tashā'" with a second-person, and its meaning: Does your prayer command you that we do with our wealth what you will, and that we leave what we will and what is mutually agreed among us?

Then they described him with two great attributes, saying: ﴿Indeed, you are the forbearing, the rightly guided﴾, in the manner of mockery of him, for they believe he is contrary to these two. Or they mean: "Indeed, you are the forbearing, the rightly guided [in yourself and in your own estimation]." Their meaning: this which you forbid us and command us contradicts what you hold in yourself of forbearance and rectitude. It is said they said this not in mockery but that it was truly so in their view, and they denied his command and prohibition to them, as contrary to forbearance and rectitude in their belief.

The explanation of forbearance (ḥilm) and rectitude (rushd) has already passed.

The sentence ﴿He said: O my people, tell me, if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord﴾ is a fresh statement like the sentences before it. The meaning: Inform me, if I am upon a clear proof from my Lord regarding what I have commanded you and forbidden you; ﴿and He has provided me from Himself﴾: that is, from His bounty and the treasuries of His dominion; ﴿with good provision﴾: that is, abundant, wide, lawful, good. He, peace be upon him, was a man of much wealth. It is said he meant by "provision" prophethood; it is said wisdom; it is said knowledge; it is said success (tawfiq). The answer to the condition is omitted, indicated by the context: its estimate is "Shall I abandon your command and your prohibition?" or "Will you say about me what you say, intending by it mockery and derision?"

﴿And I do not intend to oppose you in what I forbid you from﴾: that is, I do not intend by my prohibition to you against defrauding and defrauding people that I oppose you by doing what I forbade you, doing it apart from you. It is said: "khalafahu ila kadha" when one intends it while turning away from it, and "khalaftuhu 'an kadha" in the reverse of that.

﴿I intend only reform﴾: that is, I intend by command and prohibition only reform for you and the removal of corruption in your religion and your dealings.

﴿As far as I am able﴾: as far as my capacity reaches and my power is enabled.

﴿And my success is only through Allah﴾: that is, I have not become one granted success, a guide, a prophet, a rightly-guiding one, except by Allah's support, His empowering me to it, and His granting it to me.

﴿Upon Him I rely﴾ in all my affairs, among which is your command and your prohibition.

﴿And to Him I turn penitently﴾: that is, I return in every matter that befalls me and I entrust all my affairs to what He chooses for me of His decree and destiny. It is said the meaning is: and to Him I return in the Hereafter. It is also said that inabah means supplication, and the meaning is: and to Him I supplicate.

His statement: (p-671) ﴿And O my people, let not my opposition cause you to incur [the punishment]﴾.

Az-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, let not my opposition cause you to incur the punishment's striking you, as it struck those before you. It is said the meaning is: let not my opposition move you; and al-shiqaq is enmity, and from it is the saying of al-Akhtal:

"Is there none who will convey from me a message? How did you find the taste of enmity?"

And ﴿that there befall you﴾ is in the position of an accusative as the second object of "yajrimannakum". ﴿Like what befell the people of Nuh﴾ by drowning; ﴿or the people of Hud﴾ by the wind; ﴿or the people of Salih﴾ by the Blast. The explanation of "yajrimannakum" and of shiqaq has already passed. ﴿And the people of Lut are not far from you﴾. It may mean: their place is not far from your place; or their time is not far from your time; or they are not far from you in the cause that brings their punishment, which is absolute disbelief. The word "ba'id" is singular for the same reason as in ﴿and it is not far from the wrongdoers﴾.

Then, after frightening them with punishment, he commanded them to seek forgiveness and repent, saying: ﴿And seek forgiveness of your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance. Indeed, my Lord is Merciful and Loving﴾. The explanation of seeking forgiveness, together with the ordering of repentance after it, has passed at the beginning of the surah, and the explanation of "al-Rahim" has passed. What is meant here is that He is greatly merciful to the penitent. "Al-Wadud" is the one who loves.

In al-Sihah it is said: "waddadtu al-rajul awuddu wuddan": when I loved the man. Al-wadud is the loving one, and al-widd, al-wudd and al-wadd are love. The meaning here is that He does to His servants what one who is most loving does to one he loves: kindness toward him, bringing good to him, and warding off evil from him.

In this is a reason for what preceded it, the command to seek forgiveness and repent.

The sentence ﴿They said: O Shu'ayb, we do not understand much of what you say﴾ is a fresh statement like the preceding sentences. The meaning: you bring us things for which we have no prior knowledge, such as reports of unseen matters like resurrection and rising, and we do not understand that, meaning we do not comprehend it as we comprehend visible, present matters. So the negation of understanding in this case is literal, not figurative. It is also said: they said this turning away from hearing him and holding his speech in contempt, though it was understood by them and known to them; so the negation of understanding is not literal but figurative. It is said: faqiha yafqahu means "he understood, with understanding and comprehension"; and al-Kisa'i related fuqhanan; and it is said faqaha fiqhan means "he became a faqih."

﴿And indeed, we see you among us as weak﴾: that is, you have no strength by which you can prevent yourself from us and by which you can oppose us. It is said the meaning is that he was weak in his body; this was said by Ali ibn Isa. It is also said that he had been afflicted in his sight.

An-Nahhas said: The lexicographers related that Himyar would say to a blind man "da'if" (weak): that is, he has become weak through the loss of his sight, just as he is called "darir" (harmed): that is, he has been harmed by the loss of his sight. It is said that "da'if" means "contemptible," which is close to the first statement.

﴿And had it not been for your clan, we would have stoned you﴾. The clan (rahṭ) of a man is his kinsfolk upon whom he relies and by whom he is strengthened; and from it is "al-rahit," the hole of the jerboa, because it is secured by it and its young is hidden in it. "Al-rahṭ" applies to three up to ten. They made his clan a barrier against inflicting harm upon him, though they were few while the disbelievers were numerous and gathered; because they were upon their religion, they left him out of respect for them, not out of fear of them.

Then they confirmed what they had described him with of weakness by saying: ﴿And you are not mighty against us﴾, so that we would restrain from you for the sake of your might among us; rather, we left stoning you because of the might of your clan over us. The meaning of "we would have stoned you" is that we would have killed you by stoning, for they, when they killed a person, stoned him with stones. It is also said the meaning of "we would have stoned you" is "we would have reviled you." From it is the saying of al-Ja'di:

"We reviled one another with bitter speech, until we became as if we were two horses racing."

The word "rajm" is also applied to cursing, and from it is "al-shaytan al-rajim" (the accursed Satan).

The clause "﴿Qāla yā qawmi a-rahṭī aʿazzu ʿalaykum mina llāh﴾" [He said: "O my people, is my clan more honourable to you than God?"] is a resumed statement (mustaʾnafah), and he said "aʿazzu ʿalaykum mina llāh" and did not say "aʿazzu ʿalaykum minnī" because the negation of honour from himself and its affirmation for his people, as indicated by the placing of the pronoun before the negative particle, is a belittling of him, and belittling the prophets of God is belittling God, Mighty and Majestic. Thus their speech implied that his clan was more honourable to them than God. So he disapproved of this from them, marvelled at it, and obliged them with something from which they had no escape or way out, in the form of a question. In this there is what is not hidden of the strength of argument, clarity of disputation, and silencing of the opponent. For this reason Shuʿayb was named "khaṭīb al-anbiyāʾ" (the orator of the prophets). The pronoun in "wa-ttakhadhtumūhu" refers to God, glorified is He.

The meaning: "You have taken God, Mighty and Majestic, [as something to be cast aside] because of your lack of regard for His prophet whom He sent to you, ﴿and have put Him behind your backs﴾", i.e., cast away and placed behind the back, not caring for Him. It was also said the meaning is: "You have taken the command of God, which He commanded me to convey to you, and which is what I brought you, and put it behind your backs." It is said: "I made his command a back (bi-ẓahr)" when one neglects it. "Ẓihriyyan" is a relative form derived from "ẓahr," and the kasra is to alter the relative form. ﴿Indeed my Lord is encompassing of what you do﴾, nothing of your sayings and deeds is hidden from Him.

﴿And O my people, act according to your position; indeed I am acting. You will soon know﴾: when he saw their persistence in disbelief and their determination upon the religion of their fathers, and that admonition had no effect on them, he threatened them that he would act to the utmost of their ability and the limit of their capacity. It is said: "makuna makānatan" when one becomes firmly established to the utmost degree. He informed them that he was acting according to what is possible for him and what God decrees for him. Then he intensified the threat and warning by saying: ﴿You will soon know﴾, i.e., the outcome of what you are in of worshipping other than God and harming His servants. A similar expression occurred earlier in al-Anʿām. ﴿Who will receive a punishment that disgraces him﴾: "man" is in a position of object of "taʿlamūn" (you will know), i.e., you will soon know who it is that will receive the disgracing punishment that results in humiliation, shame and disgrace. ﴿And who is a liar﴾ is conjoined to "man yaʾtīhi," and the meaning: "You will soon know who is the one punished and who is the liar?" In it there is an allusion to their lying in their saying: ﴿Had it not been for your clan, we would have stoned you, and you are not mighty against us﴾. It was also said: "man" is a subject (mubtadaʾ) and what follows it is its relative clause, and the predicate is omitted, the estimation being: "Whoever is a liar, he will know his lie and taste the evil of his affair."

Al-Farrāʾ said: The reason "huwa" came in "man huwa kādhib" is that they do not say "man qāʾimun" (who is standing); they say "man qāma," "man yaqūmu," and "man al-qāʾim," so they added "huwa" so that it would form a clause standing in place of a verb (faʿala and yafʿalu).

Al-Naḥḥās said: What indicates the opposite of this is the saying of the poet:

*"Man rasūlī ilā al-Thurayyā, fa-innī / ḍiqtu dhar'an bi-hajrihā wa-l-kitābi"*
(Who will be my messenger to the Pleiades? For I have become constricted with distress from her separation and from the letter.)

﴿And wait; indeed I am with you among the watchers﴾, i.e., await, for I am with you awaiting what God will decide between us.

﴿And when Our command came, We saved Shuʿayb and those who believed with him﴾, i.e., when Our punishment came, or Our command to punish them came, We saved Shuʿayb and his followers who believed in him ﴿by a mercy from Us﴾ toward them because of their faith, or by a mercy from Us toward them, which is their guidance to faith. (p-672) ﴿And the cry seized those who wronged﴾, others, for what they took of people's wealth without right, and who wronged themselves by their insistence upon disbelief: the Cry with which Gabriel shouted at them until their souls left their bodies. In al-Aʿrāf it says: ﴿So the quake seized them﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 7:78, 91], and likewise in al-ʿAnkabūt.

We have already stated that the "rajfah" is the earthquake, and that it follows the Cry, due to the agitation of the air that leads to it. ﴿So they became in their homes prostrate﴾, i.e., dead.

Its explanation, and the explanation of ﴿as if they had never dwelt therein﴾, has been given shortly before, and likewise the explanation of ﴿Away with Madyan, as Thamūd were taken away﴾.

Al-Kisāʾī reported that Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī recited "kamā baʿudat Thamūd" with a ḍammah on the ʿayn.

Al-Mahdawī said: Whoever puts a ḍammah on the ʿayn in "baʿudat" has a dialect in which it is used for both good and bad; whereas "baʿidat" with a kasra, according to the reading of the majority, is used specifically for evil, and here it means a curse.

Ibn Jarīr and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed I see you in prosperity﴾, he said: cheap prices; ﴿and indeed I fear for you the punishment of an encompassing day﴾, he said: high prices.

Ibn Jarīr reported from him regarding ﴿baqiyyatu llāh﴾, he said: God's provision.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Qatādah: ﴿The remainder of God is better for you﴾, he says: your portion from your Lord is better for you.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Mujāhid: he said: obedience to God.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from al-Aʿmash regarding His saying: ﴿Does your prayer command you?﴾, he said: your recitation.

Ibn ʿAsākir reported from al-Aḥnaf that Shuʿayb was the most prayerful of the prophets.

Ibn Jarīr and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Zayd regarding His saying: ﴿or that we do with our wealth what we please﴾, he said: He forbade them from clipping these dinars and dirhams, and they said: "They are only our wealth; we do with them what we please. If we wish, we clip them; if we wish, we burn them; if we wish, we throw them away."

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn al-Mundhir reported similar from Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb.

Both reported similarly from Zayd ibn Aslam as well.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Ibn Saʿd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abū al-Shaykh and ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported similarly from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab as well.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed you are the forbearing, the upright﴾, he said: they say, "Indeed you are not forbearing nor upright."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Qatādah: a mockery of him.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk regarding His saying: ﴿and He provided me from Himself with good provision﴾, he said: the lawful.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Qatādah regarding His saying: ﴿And I do not intend to oppose you in what I forbid you from﴾, he said: he says, "I would not forbid you from a matter and then commit it myself."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Mujāhid regarding His saying: ﴿And to Him I turn in repentance﴾, he said: to Him I return.

Abū Nuʿaym in al-Ḥilyah reported "from ʿAlī, who said: I said, 'O Messenger of God, advise me.' He said: 'Say: God is my Lord, then be steadfast.' I said: 'My Lord is God, and my success is only by God; upon Him I rely and to Him I turn in repentance.' He said: 'May knowledge be pleasant for you, Abū al-Ḥasan; you have drunk knowledge in gulps and quaffed it deeply.'" In its chain is Muḥammad ibn Yūsuf al-Kudaymī.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Qatādah: ﴿Let not my opposition lead you to sin﴾: let not my separation from you bring you to it.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Mujāhid: he said: "my opposition" is my enmity.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from al-Suddī: he said: let not my enmity move you.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq and Ibn Jarīr reported from Qatādah regarding His saying: ﴿And the people of Lot are not far from you﴾, he said: they were only recent people, close after Noah and Thamūd.

Abū al-Shaykh and Ibn ʿAsākir reported from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr: ﴿And indeed we see you among us as weak﴾, he said: he was blind, and he became blind from his weeping out of love for God, Mighty and Majestic.

al-Wāḥidī and Ibn ʿAsākir reported from Shaddād ibn Aws, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Shuʿayb (peace be upon him) wept out of love for God until he became blind."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim (who authenticated it), al-Khaṭīb and Ibn ʿAsākir reported through several chains from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His saying: ﴿And indeed we see you among us as weak﴾, he said: he was blind in sight.

Abū al-Shaykh reported similarly from Abū Ṣāliḥ.

Abū al-Shaykh reported from Sufyān regarding His saying: ﴿And indeed we see you among us as weak﴾, he said: he was blind, and he was called "the orator of the prophets."

Abū al-Shaykh reported from al-Suddī: he said: its meaning is, "You are only one."

Abū al-Shaykh reported from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib that he delivered a sermon and recited this verse concerning Shuʿayb, ﴿And indeed we see you among us as weak﴾, and said: he was blind, so they attributed weakness to him. ﴿Had it not been for your clan, we would have stoned you﴾. ʿAlī said: "By God, besides whom there is no god, they did not fear the majesty of their Lord; they feared only the tribe."

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Mujāhid regarding His saying: ﴿And you have taken Him behind your backs as something cast away﴾, he said: you have cast away His command. Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Qatādah, who said regarding the verse: "You do not fear Him."

Abū al-Shaykh reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, who said: "You belittled Him."

And We sent to Madyan their brother Shu'ayb. That is, the people of Shu'ayb, and Shu'ayb was their brother in lineage. They were named Madyan after their father, who was Madyan ibn Ibrahim; and it is said they were named after their city.

An-Nahhas said: Madyan is not declined, because it is the name of a city. This matter has already been discussed in Surat al-A'raf more fully than here. The explanation of ﴿O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him﴾ has already passed at the beginning of the surah. This sentence is a fresh statement, as if it were said: What did Shu'ayb say to them when Allah sent him to them? Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, was called the orator of the prophets for the excellence of his argumentation with his people. He first commanded them to worship Allah, glorified is He, who is the God alone, having no partner. Then he forbade them from diminishing the measure and the balance, because they, along with their disbelief, were people of fraud (tatfif). When the seller came to them with food, they took more by measure; likewise, when what was weighed reached them, they took more by weight. And when they sold, they sold with a lesser measure (p-670) and a lesser weight.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, I see you in prosperity﴾ is a reason for the prohibition: that is, do not diminish the measure and the balance, for indeed I see you in prosperity, meaning in wealth and abundance of provision. So do not change Allah's blessing upon you by disobeying Him and harming His servants. In this blessing there is what suffices you from taking people's wealth without right. Then after this reason he mentioned another reason, saying: ﴿And indeed, I fear for you the punishment of an encompassing day﴾. In this reason there is a reminder to them of the punishment of the Hereafter, just as the first reason contained a reminder of the bounties of this world. The day is described as encompassing, and what is meant is the punishment, because the punishment occurs on the day. The meaning of the encompassing of the day's punishment over them is that none of them will escape it, and they will find no refuge or place of escape from it. The day is the Day of Resurrection; it is also said that it is the day of retribution against them in this world by the Blast.

Then he emphasized the prohibition against diminishing the measure and the weight with his words: ﴿And O my people, give full measure and weight with justice﴾. Al-iyfa' is completion, and al-qist is justice, which is the absence of excess and deficiency. Although exceeding the full measure is virtue and good, it is beyond what the name of justice conveys. The prohibition against deficiency, though it entails giving full measure, combines the two indications into an eloquent emphasis and a fine reinforcement. Then he increased this emphasis, saying: ﴿And do not deprive people of their things﴾. The explanation of this has passed in Surat al-A'raf. It includes a general prohibition against bakhs (defrauding), and "things" is broader than what is measured and weighed; so defrauding by cheating in measure and weight enters into this first and foremost. It is also said that bakhs means only the unjust levy (maks).

Then he said: ﴿And do not act corruptly on the earth, spreading corruption﴾. Its explanation has also passed in al-Baqarah. Acting corruptly on the earth (al-'uthiy) includes everything that causes harm to people in it, so the diminishing of measure and balance in the context enters it. He restricted it by the circumstantial phrase "spreading corruption" in order to exclude what has the form of acting corruptly on the earth but whose aim is reform, as happened with al-Khidr in the ship.

﴿The remainder from Allah is better for you﴾: that is, what Allah leaves for you of lawful provision after giving full rights with justice is more beneficial and blessed than what you leave for yourselves through fraud, defrauding and corruption on the earth. Ibn Jarir and other exegetes mentioned this meaning.

Mujahid said: "The remainder from Allah" is His obedience.
Al-Rabi' said: His counsel.
Al-Farra' said: His watchfulness.

He restricted this by saying ﴿if you are believers﴾, because this benefits only the believer and not the disbeliever; or the intended meaning of "believers" here is those who affirmed Shu'ayb.

﴿And I am not a guardian over you﴾: I do not guard you from falling into sins such as fraud, defrauding and others; or it means I do not keep watch over your deeds, and I will call you to account for them and recompense you for them.

The sentence ﴿They said: O Shu'ayb, does your prayer command you that we abandon what our fathers worshipped, or that we not do with our wealth what we please?﴾ is a fresh statement, an answer to an assumed question, as if it were said: What did they say to Shu'ayb? The reading "ṣalātuka" is in the singular. "An natruka" is in the position of an accusative. Al-Kisa'i said its position is genitive by the implied preposition "bi". Their intent by "what our fathers worshipped" is the idols they worshipped. The interrogation is for denial against him and for mockery of him, because prayers in their view are not among the good things said to one who does them when one wants to soften his heart and tame his harshness, as one says to someone who was very generous in charity when he does something not fitting to right conduct: "Your charity has commanded you to this!" It is said that the prayer here means recitation; it is said it means religion; it is said it means his followers, and from this is the "musalli" who follows the forerunner. This was their answer to Shu'ayb concerning his command to them to worship Allah alone. And their saying: ﴿or that we do with our wealth what we please﴾ is their answer to him concerning his command to them to give full measure and weight, and his prohibition against diminishing them, and against defrauding people and against corruption on the earth. This sentence is conjoined to what is in "what our fathers worshipped."

The meaning is: Does your prayer command you that we abandon what our fathers worshipped, and command you that we abandon doing with our wealth what we will, by taking and giving, increasing and decreasing?

It was read: "naf'ala fi amwalina ma nashā'", with the second-person in both. An-Nahhas said: then "aw" in this reading is for conjunction with the first "an", and the estimate is: "Does your prayer command you that you do with our wealth what you will?"

It was also read: "naf'ala" with a nun and "ma tashā'" with a second-person, and its meaning: Does your prayer command you that we do with our wealth what you will, and that we leave what we will and what is mutually agreed among us?

Then they described him with two great attributes, saying: ﴿Indeed, you are the forbearing, the rightly guided﴾, in the manner of mockery of him, for they believe he is contrary to these two. Or they mean: "Indeed, you are the forbearing, the rightly guided [in yourself and in your own estimation]." Their meaning: this which you forbid us and command us contradicts what you hold in yourself of forbearance and rectitude. It is said they said this not in mockery but that it was truly so in their view, and they denied his command and prohibition to them, as contrary to forbearance and rectitude in their belief.

The explanation of forbearance (ḥilm) and rectitude (rushd) has already passed.

The sentence ﴿He said: O my people, tell me, if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord﴾ is a fresh statement like the sentences before it. The meaning: Inform me, if I am upon a clear proof from my Lord regarding what I have commanded you and forbidden you; ﴿and He has provided me from Himself﴾: that is, from His bounty and the treasuries of His dominion; ﴿with good provision﴾: that is, abundant, wide, lawful, good. He, peace be upon him, was a man of much wealth. It is said he meant by "provision" prophethood; it is said wisdom; it is said knowledge; it is said success (tawfiq). The answer to the condition is omitted, indicated by the context: its estimate is "Shall I abandon your command and your prohibition?" or "Will you say about me what you say, intending by it mockery and derision?"

﴿And I do not intend to oppose you in what I forbid you from﴾: that is, I do not intend by my prohibition to you against defrauding and defrauding people that I oppose you by doing what I forbade you, doing it apart from you. It is said: "khalafahu ila kadha" when one intends it while turning away from it, and "khalaftuhu 'an kadha" in the reverse of that.

﴿I intend only reform﴾: that is, I intend by command and prohibition only reform for you and the removal of corruption in your religion and your dealings.

﴿As far as I am able﴾: as far as my capacity reaches and my power is enabled.

﴿And my success is only through Allah﴾: that is, I have not become one granted success, a guide, a prophet, a rightly-guiding one, except by Allah's support, His empowering me to it, and His granting it to me.

﴿Upon Him I rely﴾ in all my affairs, among which is your command and your prohibition.

﴿And to Him I turn penitently﴾: that is, I return in every matter that befalls me and I entrust all my affairs to what He chooses for me of His decree and destiny. It is said the meaning is: and to Him I return in the Hereafter. It is also said that inabah means supplication, and the meaning is: and to Him I supplicate.

His statement: (p-671) ﴿And O my people, let not my opposition cause you to incur [the punishment]﴾.

Az-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, let not my opposition cause you to incur the punishment's striking you, as it struck those before you. It is said the meaning is: let not my opposition move you; and al-shiqaq is enmity, and from it is the saying of al-Akhtal:

"Is there none who will convey from me a message? How did you find the taste of enmity?"

And ﴿that there befall you﴾ is in the position of an accusative as the second object of "yajrimannakum". ﴿Like what befell the people of Nuh﴾ by drowning; ﴿or the people of Hud﴾ by the wind; ﴿or the people of Salih﴾ by the Blast. The explanation of "yajrimannakum" and of shiqaq has already passed. ﴿And the people of Lut are not far from you﴾. It may mean: their place is not far from your place; or their time is not far from your time; or they are not far from you in the cause that brings their punishment, which is absolute disbelief. The word "ba'id" is singular for the same reason as in ﴿and it is not far from the wrongdoers﴾.

Then, after frightening them with punishment, he commanded them to seek forgiveness and repent, saying: ﴿And seek forgiveness of your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance. Indeed, my Lord is Merciful and Loving﴾. The explanation of seeking forgiveness, together with the ordering of repentance after it, has passed at the beginning of the surah, and the explanation of "al-Rahim" has passed. What is meant here is that He is greatly merciful to the penitent. "Al-Wadud" is the one who loves.

In al-Sihah it is said: "waddadtu al-rajul awuddu wuddan": when I loved the man. Al-wadud is the loving one, and al-widd, al-wudd and al-wadd are love. The meaning here is that He does to His servants what one who is most loving does to one he loves: kindness toward him, bringing good to him, and warding off evil from him.

In this is a reason for what preceded it, the command to seek forgiveness and repent.

The sentence ﴿They said: O Shu'ayb, we do not understand much of what you say﴾ is a fresh statement like the preceding sentences. The meaning: you bring us things for which we have no prior knowledge, such as reports of unseen matters like resurrection and rising, and we do not understand that, meaning we do not comprehend it as we comprehend visible, present matters. So the negation of understanding in this case is literal, not figurative. It is also said: they said this turning away from hearing him and holding his speech in contempt, though it was understood by them and known to them; so the negation of understanding is not literal but figurative. It is said: faqiha yafqahu means "he understood, with understanding and comprehension"; and al-Kisa'i related fuqhanan; and it is said faqaha fiqhan means "he became a faqih."

﴿And indeed, we see you among us as weak﴾: that is, you have no strength by which you can prevent yourself from us and by which you can oppose us. It is said the meaning is that he was weak in his body; this was said by Ali ibn Isa. It is also said that he had been afflicted in his sight.

An-Nahhas said: The lexicographers related that Himyar would say to a blind man "da'if" (weak): that is, he has become weak through the loss of his sight, just as he is called "darir" (harmed): that is, he has been harmed by the loss of his sight. It is said that "da'if" means "contemptible," which is close to the first statement.

﴿And had it not been for your clan, we would have stoned you﴾. The clan (rahṭ) of a man is his kinsfolk upon whom he relies and by whom he is strengthened; and from it is "al-rahit," the hole of the jerboa, because it is secured by it and its young is hidden in it. "Al-rahṭ" applies to three up to ten. They made his clan a barrier against inflicting harm upon him, though they were few while the disbelievers were numerous and gathered; because they were upon their religion, they left him out of respect for them, not out of fear of them.

Then they confirmed what they had described him with of weakness by saying: ﴿And you are not mighty against us﴾, so that we would restrain from you for the sake of your might among us; rather, we left stoning you because of the might of your clan over us. The meaning of "we would have stoned you" is that we would have killed you by stoning, for they, when they killed a person, stoned him with stones. It is also said the meaning of "we would have stoned you" is "we would have reviled you." From it is the saying of al-Ja'di:

"We reviled one another with bitter speech, until we became as if we were two horses racing."

The word "rajm" is also applied to cursing, and from it is "al-shaytan al-rajim" (the accursed Satan).

The clause "﴿Qāla yā qawmi a-rahṭī aʿazzu ʿalaykum mina llāh﴾" [He said: "O my people, is my clan more honourable to you than God?"] is a resumed statement (mustaʾnafah), and he said "aʿazzu ʿalaykum mina llāh" and did not say "aʿazzu ʿalaykum minnī" because the negation of honour from himself and its affirmation for his people, as indicated by the placing of the pronoun before the negative particle, is a belittling of him, and belittling the prophets of God is belittling God, Mighty and Majestic. Thus their speech implied that his clan was more honourable to them than God. So he disapproved of this from them, marvelled at it, and obliged them with something from which they had no escape or way out, in the form of a question. In this there is what is not hidden of the strength of argument, clarity of disputation, and silencing of the opponent. For this reason Shuʿayb was named "khaṭīb al-anbiyāʾ" (the orator of the prophets). The pronoun in "wa-ttakhadhtumūhu" refers to God, glorified is He.

The meaning: "You have taken God, Mighty and Majestic, [as something to be cast aside] because of your lack of regard for His prophet whom He sent to you, ﴿and have put Him behind your backs﴾", i.e., cast away and placed behind the back, not caring for Him. It was also said the meaning is: "You have taken the command of God, which He commanded me to convey to you, and which is what I brought you, and put it behind your backs." It is said: "I made his command a back (bi-ẓahr)" when one neglects it. "Ẓihriyyan" is a relative form derived from "ẓahr," and the kasra is to alter the relative form. ﴿Indeed my Lord is encompassing of what you do﴾, nothing of your sayings and deeds is hidden from Him.

﴿And O my people, act according to your position; indeed I am acting. You will soon know﴾: when he saw their persistence in disbelief and their determination upon the religion of their fathers, and that admonition had no effect on them, he threatened them that he would act to the utmost of their ability and the limit of their capacity. It is said: "makuna makānatan" when one becomes firmly established to the utmost degree. He informed them that he was acting according to what is possible for him and what God decrees for him. Then he intensified the threat and warning by saying: ﴿You will soon know﴾, i.e., the outcome of what you are in of worshipping other than God and harming His servants. A similar expression occurred earlier in al-Anʿām. ﴿Who will receive a punishment that disgraces him﴾: "man" is in a position of object of "taʿlamūn" (you will know), i.e., you will soon know who it is that will receive the disgracing punishment that results in humiliation, shame and disgrace. ﴿And who is a liar﴾ is conjoined to "man yaʾtīhi," and the meaning: "You will soon know who is the one punished and who is the liar?" In it there is an allusion to their lying in their saying: ﴿Had it not been for your clan, we would have stoned you, and you are not mighty against us﴾. It was also said: "man" is a subject (mubtadaʾ) and what follows it is its relative clause, and the predicate is omitted, the estimation being: "Whoever is a liar, he will know his lie and taste the evil of his affair."
