Then He censured the watering place to which he brings them, saying: ﴿And wretched is the watering place to which they are brought﴾, because the one who comes to water, which is called al-wird (the watering place), comes only to quench the heat of thirst and remove his thirst, whereas the Fire is the opposite of that.

Then He censured them after censuring the place they arrive at, saying: ﴿And they are followed in this world by a curse﴾: that is, the people of Pharaoh are followed absolutely, or the chiefs specifically, or they and Pharaoh together in this world by a great curse, that is, expulsion and removal from mercy. ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection﴾: that is, they are followed by a curse on the Day of Resurrection, when the people of the gathering all curse them. Then He made the curse a reward (rifd) for them in a manner of mockery, saying: ﴿Wretched is the reward that is given﴾.

Al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Ubayda said: rafadtu-hu arfiduhu rifdan means I gave him support and gave him something; the name of the gift is rifd, that is, wretched is the gift. Al-i'āna (assistance) is what they were given and what they were assisted with. The object of the censure is omitted, that is, their reward, which is the curse they were followed by in this world and the Hereafter, as though it is a curse after a curse, one extending the first and making it perpetual.

Al-Mawardi reported, on the authority of al-Asma'i, that al-rafd, with a fatha, means a cup, and with a kasra it means what is in it of drink. So it is as though He censured what they are given to drink in the Fire, and this is more fitting to the context. It has also been said that al-rifd means an addition: that is, wretched is what they are given after drowning, which is the addition; this was said by al-Kalbi.

The reference in His words ﴿That is among the reports of the towns; We relate it to you﴾: that is, what Allah, glorified is He, related in this surah of the reports of the earlier nations and what they did with their prophets. That is, it is related to you as one report after another. The meaning of qasas (narrative) has already been established. The pronoun in minhā refers to the towns: that is, among the towns is one still standing, and among them is one mown down. The standing (qā'im) is that which is still standing on its foundations, and the mown down (ḥaṣīd) is that which has no trace left. It has also been said that the standing means the inhabited, and the mown down means the ruined. It has also been said that the standing means the empty towns without their roofs, and the mown down means the uprooted, in the sense of cut down. The towns are compared to a crop that is standing on its stalk and one that has been cut.

The poet said:
"And people in the division of death among them are like crops, some standing and some mown."

﴿And We did not wrong them﴾ by what We did to them of punishment, ﴿but they wronged themselves﴾ through disbelief and sins. ﴿So their gods did not avail them﴾: that is, their idols which they worshipped besides Allah did not ward off from them any of the punishment ﴿when the command of your Lord came﴾: that is, when His punishment came. ﴿And they added nothing to them but ruin﴾: tatbib means destruction and loss: that is, the idols they worshipped added nothing to them but destruction and loss, though they had believed that these would help them obtain benefits.

﴿And such is the seizure of your Lord﴾: al-Jaḥdarī and Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif read akhadha as a verb. The others read akhdh as a verbal noun (maṣdar). ﴿When He seizes the towns while they are wrongdoers﴾: that is, their people, who are wrongdoers. ﴿Indeed His seizure﴾: that is, His punishment of the disbelievers ﴿is painful, severe﴾: that is, painful and harsh.

﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾: that is, in Allah's seizure of the people of the towns, or in the narrative He related to His Messenger, is a lesson and an admonition ﴿for those who fear the punishment of the Hereafter﴾, because they are the ones who take lessons from examples and heed admonitions. The reference in His words ﴿That is a day on which mankind will be gathered﴾ is to the Day of Resurrection, indicated by the mention of the Hereafter, when people will be gathered for reckoning and recompense. ﴿That is a day witnessed﴾: that is, the people of the gathering witness it, or creatures are witnessed in it. He used the expression of a time-adverb in a broad sense, treating it as an object.

﴿And We do not delay it except for a limited term﴾: that is, We do not delay that day except until the end of a limited term, known by number. Allah, glorified is He, has determined that the recompense will occur after it.

﴿On the day it comes﴾: the people of Medina, Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read with the yā' (ya) present in continuous recitation and omitted in pause. Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud read it with the yā' present both in continuous recitation and in pause. Al-A'mash read it with the yā' omitted in both. The reason for omitting the yā' in pause, as al-Kisa'i said, is that the sound verb is paused upon like the jussive, so the yā' is omitted as the ḍamma is omitted. The reason for those who omitted the yā' in continuous recitation is that they saw the written form of the Mushaf that way. Al-Khalil and Sibawayh reported that the Arabs say lā adri (I do not know), omitting the yā' and making do with the kasra. Al-Farra' recited, as evidence for the omission of the yā', the line:
"Your hand, it is no hand that gives a dirham in generosity, and another hand gives blood by the sword."

Al-Zajjaj said: the better grammatical form is to retain the yā'. The meaning is: when it comes, on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿no soul will speak﴾: that is, no soul will speak, one of the two tā's having been dropped for lightness; that is, no soul will speak on it except with what is permitted to it of speech. It has also been said: no soul will speak with argument or intercession except with His permission, glorified is He, for it to speak thus. This is reconciled with His words ﴿This is a day when they will not speak, nor will they be permitted to offer excuses﴾ [al-Mursalat 35–36] by the difference of their states according to the different stations of the Resurrection.

Such a combination has been repeated in several places. ﴿Among them is the wretched and the happy﴾: that is, among the souls is the wretched and among them is the happy. The wretched is the one for whom wretchedness has been written, and the happy is the one for whom happiness has been written. The wretched is mentioned before the happy because the context is one of warning.

﴿As for those who were wretched, they will be in the Fire, for them therein is groaning and sighing﴾: that is, as for those for whom wretchedness has preceded, they will remain in the Fire, and for them therein is groaning and sighing.

Al-Zajjaj said: al-zafīr is from the intensity of moaning, and it is that which is raised very high. He said: the grammarians of Basra and Kufa maintain that al-zafīr is like the beginning of the braying of donkeys, and al-shahīq is like its end. It has also been said: al-zafīr is a loud sound, and al-shahīq a weak sound. It has also been said: al-zafīr is the exhalation of breath, and al-shahīq is the inhalation of breath. It has also been said: al-zafīr is from the chest, and al-shahīq is from the throat. It has also been said: al-zafīr is the repeated drawing of breath from intense fear, and al-shahīq is a long, extended breath. The clause is either a fresh sentence, as though it were said: what is their state therein? or it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

﴿Abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾: that is, for the duration of their continuance.

The scholars have differed in explaining the meaning of this temporal limitation, since it is known from definitive proofs that the punishment of the disbelievers in the Fire is everlasting and never ceases for them, and it is also established that the heavens and the earth will pass away at the end of the days of this world. One group said: this statement follows the custom of the Arabs when they wish to express the intensity of a thing's continuance. He says: "It will last as long as the heavens and the earth endure," and from this is His saying: "I will not come to you as long as night is dark," and "as long as night and day alternate," and "as long as the dove coos," and the like.

So the meaning of the verse is that they will abide therein forever, with no cessation and no end. It has also been said: the intended meaning is the heavens and earth of the Hereafter, for there are reports indicating that the Hereafter has heavens and earth other than those present in this world, which will endure as long as the abode of the Hereafter endures. Also, they must have a place that bears them and another that shades them, and these are earth and sky.

As for His words ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, the people of knowledge have differed about the meaning of this exception, in several opinions:

The first: it relates to His words ﴿so in the Fire﴾, as though He said: except what your Lord wills of delaying a people from that. This was reported by Abu Nadra from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.

The second: the exception applies only to the sinners among the monotheists, who will leave the Fire after a period. On this view, His words ﴿As for those who were wretched﴾ are general to the disbelievers and the sinners, and the exception applies to "abiding" (khalidin), and ma is in the sense of man (who). This was said by Qatada, al-Ḍaḥḥak, Abu Sinan and others.

It has been established by mutawatir (widely transmitted) reports, which yield necessary knowledge, that the people of monotheism will leave the Fire, and this specifies every general statement.

The third: the exception relates to the groaning and sighing: that is, they have therein groaning and sighing, "except what your Lord wills" of kinds of punishment other than groaning and sighing. This was said by Ibn al-Anbari.

The fourth: the meaning of the exception is that they will abide therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, without dying, except what your Lord wills. He will command the Fire, and it will consume them until they perish, then Allah will renew their creation. This was narrated from Ibn Mas'ud.

The fifth: illa (except) means siwā (other than). The meaning is: as long as the heavens and the earth endure, other than what exceeds that of eternity. It is as though He mentioned for their abiding a duration that is not longer in the eyes of the Arabs, then added to it the eternal continuance that has no end. This was related by al-Zajjaj.

The sixth: what was reported from al-Farra', Ibn al-Anbari and Ibn Qutayba, that this does not contradict the non-existence of the will, like your saying: "By Allah, I will strike him, unless I see otherwise." This was objected to on the grounds that the meaning of the verse is the judgement of their abiding, except for the period which Allah willed, so the will has definitely occurred. Al-Zajjaj also related this opinion.

The seventh: the meaning is: abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills of the measure of their standing at their graves and for the reckoning. Related by al-Zajjaj also.

The eighth: the meaning is: abiding therein, except what your Lord wills of an increase of bliss for the people of bliss and an increase of punishment for the people of the blazing Fire. Also related by al-Zajjaj, and chosen by al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi.

The ninth: illa means waw (and). This was said by al-Farra', and the meaning is: "and what your Lord wills of increase." Makki said: this view is far-fetched for the Basrans, that illa should mean waw.

The tenth: illa means ka (like). The estimate is: "as your Lord willed," and from this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women, except what has already passed﴾ [al-Nisa' 22], meaning: as has already passed.

The eleventh: this exception is of the type of exception that the Lawgiver recommends in every speech, and it is like His saying: ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills, in security﴾ [al-Fath 27]. Something similar was reported from Abu 'Ubayd.

These opinions are the entirety of what we have come across of the views of the people of knowledge. Some of them have been objected to with objections, and these have been answered with responses. I have clarified this in an independent treatise that I compiled in answer to a question that came from one of the scholars.

﴿And as for those who were made happy, they will be in the Garden, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 11, verses 96–108 (part 2 of 2):

Al-A'mash, Hafs, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿سُعِدُوا﴾ (su'idu, "they were made happy") with a ḍammah on the sīn. The rest read it with a fatḥah on the sīn (sa'idu). Abu Ubaydah and Abu Hatim preferred this second reading.

Sibawayh said: "One does not say saʿida fulān (فُلانٌ سَعِدَ), just as one does not say shaqiya fulān (شَقِيَ فُلانٌ), because it is among the verbs that do not take an object (intransitive)."

Al-Nahhas said: "I saw ʿAli ibn Sulayman expressing surprise at al-Kisa'i's reading with a ḍammah on the sīn, even though he was knowledgeable in Arabic. This is a grammatical error (laḥn) that is not permissible. The meaning of the verse is as already explained in His words: ﴿Then as for those who are wretched﴾."

As for His words ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾: the preceding statements have already made clear what is suitable for this exception to refer to. ﴿A gift unceasing﴾ means: Allah will give them a gift that is unceasing. Al-majdhudh means "cut off," from jadhdhahu, yajudhdhuhu, when one cuts it. The meaning is that it extends without end.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words ﴿He will lead his people on the Day of Resurrection﴾, that he said: "He will mislead them and bring them down into the Fire."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah regarding the verse that he said: "Pharaoh walks in front of his people until he drives them right into the Fire."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words ﴿and brings them down to the Fire﴾, that he said: "al-wurūd means entering."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words ﴿Wretched is the gift that is given﴾, that he said: "The curse of this world and the Hereafter."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding ﴿Among them are those standing and those harvested﴾, that he meant: "Inhabited towns and extinguished towns."

Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah: "Among them is one standing, whose place is still seen, and one harvested, of which no trace is seen."

Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Juraij: "Among them is one standing, empty upon its roofs, and one harvested, flattened to the ground."

Abu al-Shaykh related from Abu ʿAsim regarding ﴿Their gods did not avail them﴾ that he said: "They did not benefit them."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn ʿUmar, regarding His words ﴿They added nothing to them but ruin﴾, that it means "destruction."

Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Zayd that he said: "Takhsīr" (loss).

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah a similar meaning.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah, glorified and exalted is He, gives respite to the wrongdoer, until when He seizes him, He does not let him go." Then he recited: ﴿And such is the seizure of your Lord when He seizes the towns while they are wrongdoing. Indeed, His seizure is painful and severe.﴾

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Zayd regarding His words ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for whoever fears the punishment of the Hereafter﴾, that he said: "We shall fulfill for them what We promised them in the Hereafter, just as We fulfilled for the prophets that We would help them."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿That is a Day on which mankind will be gathered, and that is a Day witnessed﴾ that he said: "It is the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh related the same from Mujahid.

Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Juraij regarding His words ﴿the Day it comes﴾ that he said: "That Day."

Al-Tirmidhi, who graded it ḥasan, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh related from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, who said: "When the verse ﴿So among them is the wretched and the happy﴾ was revealed, I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, then what are we working for? Is it for something already decided, or for something not yet decided?' He said: 'Rather, it is for something already decided, and the pens have run with it, O ʿUmar. But each is made easy for what he was created for.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "These two are among the hidden matters: Allah's words ﴿So among them is the wretched and the happy﴾ and ﴿On the Day when Allah will gather the messengers and say, 'What was your response?' They will say, 'We have no knowledge.'﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 109]. As for His words ﴿So among them is the wretched and the happy﴾, they are a people from the People of the Book and from the people of this qiblah (the Muslims). Allah will punish them in the Fire for as long as He wills because of their sins. Then He will permit intercession for them, and the believers will intercede for them, and they will be brought out of the Fire and admitted into Paradise. He named them 'wretched' when He punished them in the Fire. ﴿As for those who are wretched, they will be in the Fire, having therein groaning and wailing﴾, ﴿abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾, referring to when He permitted intercession for them, brought them out of the Fire and admitted them into Paradise, and they are the same people. ﴿And as for those who are made happy﴾, meaning after the wretchedness they were in, ﴿they will be in Paradise, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾, meaning those who were in the Fire."

Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh related from Qatadah that he recited this verse: ﴿As for those who are wretched﴾, and said: "Anas told us that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'A people will come out of the Fire.'" And we do not say as the Harurites said, that whoever enters it remains in it forever.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Jabir who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited ﴿As for those who are wretched﴾ up to His words ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, and said to me: 'If Allah wills to bring out some people from among those who were wretched from the Fire and admit them into Paradise, He will do so.'"

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Khalid ibn Ma'dan regarding His words ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾ that he said: "It refers to the people of monotheism (tawḥīd) among the people of the qiblah."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Dhurays, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wal-Sifat related from Abu Nadrah, from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, or from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, or from a man among the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His words ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾ that he said: "This verse overrides the entire Qur'an. Wherever in the Qur'an there is 'abiding therein,' this verse applies to it."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and al-Bayhaqi related from Abu Nadrah who said: "The entire Qur'an ends at this verse: ﴿Indeed your Lord is the Doer of what He intends.﴾"

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾ that he said: "For every Paradise there is a heaven and an earth."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related something similar from al-Suddi.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related something similar also from al-Hasan.

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th wal-Nushur related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾ that he said: "Your Lord has willed that these should abide in the Fire and that those should abide in Paradise."

Ibn Jarir related from him regarding His words ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾ that he said: "Allah excepted from the Fire that it should consume them."

Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi regarding the verse that he said: "Afterwards, there came from Allah's will what abrogated it (nasakha), and it was revealed in Medina: ﴿Indeed those who disbelieved and did wrong, Allah will never forgive them, nor guide them to any path﴾ [al-Nisa': 168], to the end of the verse. So the hope of the people of the Fire to come out of it was removed, and He made eternal abiding obligatory for them."

As for His words ﴿And as for those who are made happy﴾ up to the end of the verse, he said: "Afterwards, there came from Allah's will what abrogated it, and it was revealed in Medina: ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, We will admit them into gardens﴾ up to His words ﴿extended shade﴾ [al-Nisa': 57], and so He made eternal abiding obligatory for them."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from al-Hasan who said: "ʿUmar said: 'If the people of the Fire remained in the Fire for as long as the amount of sand of ʿAlij, there would still be a day for them on which they would come out.'"

Ishaq ibn Rahawayh related from Abu Hurayrah who said: "There will come upon Hell a day when no one will remain in it," and he recited: ﴿As for those who are wretched﴾ up to the end of the verse.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibrahim who said: "There is no verse in the Qur'an more hopeful for the people of the Fire than this verse: ﴿abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾."

He said: "Ibn Mas'ud said: 'There will certainly come upon it a time when its gates will swing (in the wind) because they are empty.'"

Ibn Jarir related from al-Sha'bi who said: "Hell is the swiftest of the two abodes to be inhabited and the swiftest of them to be ruined."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah regarding His words ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾ that he said: "Allah knows best about its exception, in which way it has occurred."

Similar to what ʿUmar, Abu Hurayrah and Ibn Mas'ud mentioned has been related from a group of the early scholars (salaf), such as Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar, Jabir and Abu Sa'id among the Companions, and from Abu Mijlaz, ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam and others among the Successors (tabi'un).

A ḥadīth on this matter occurs in al-Tabarani's al-Mu'jam al-Kabir from Abu Umamah Ṣudayy ibn ʿAjlan al-Bahili, but its chain of narration is weak (ḍaʿīf).

The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) spoke on this point in a way that, for him, had room for omission, and silence about it would have been sufficient. He said: "Let not the statement of the Mujbirah (predestinarians) deceive you, that the intended meaning of the exception is the release of the people of major sins from the Fire. For the second exception calls out against their falsehood and records their fabrication. And what do you think of a people who cast away the Book of Allah when some reliable transmissions were related to them from Ibn ʿAmr: 'There will certainly come upon Hell a day when its gates will be clapped, with no one in it.'" Then he said: "And I say: what did Ibn ʿAmr do with his two swords and his fighting with them against ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that would have preoccupied him from transmitting this ḥadīth? End of quote."

I say: As for the attack on the one who says that people of major sins will come out of the Fire, the one who says so, O wretched one, is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as is authentically established from him in the compilations of Islam, which are the records of the pure Sunnah, and as is authentically established from him in other sources through a group of Companions reaching the number of mass transmission (tawātur). So what concern is it of yours to attack a people who knew what you were ignorant of, and who acted upon what is far from you? And what prevents the exception from being understood in this way, which is what the many sound and numerous proofs have shown, as the majority of scholars, of the early and later generations, went to and said? As for what you supposed, that the second exception calls out against their falsehood and records their fabrication, there is no calling out and no contradiction. And what prevents the exception in both places from being understood as referring to the disobedient ones of this Ummah? The first exception is understood to mean: "except what your Lord wills" of the release of the disobedient of this Ummah from the Fire, and the second exception is understood to mean: "except what your Lord wills" of their not abiding in Paradise as the others abide, because of the delay in their entry into it for the length of time they remained in the Fire. This was said by scholars whom we mentioned earlier, and Ibn ʿAbbas, the scholar of the Ummah (ḥibr al-ummah), also said it.

As for the attack on the Companion of the Messenger of Allah, the guardian of his Sunnah and the worshipper among the Companions, ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr, may Allah be pleased with him: where are you going, O Mahmud? Do you know what you have done, into what valley you have fallen, and on which side you have landed? And who are you, that you climb up to this place and try to reach the stars of the sky with your short hands and your lame leg? Did you not have, among the grammarians and philologists whose works you were trying to break, something that would turn you back from entering into what you do not know and speaking about what you have no understanding of? Glory be to Allah, what a wonder: what deficiency in the knowledge of transmission and distance from knowing it does to a person, leading him to the furthest point of disgrace, for one who does not know his own worth nor halts himself where Allah, glorified is He, has halted him.

The intended meaning of "the signs" is the Torah, and "clear authority" refers to the miracles. It has also been said that "the signs" are the nine signs mentioned elsewhere, and "clear authority" is the staff. Although the staff is one of the nine, it is singled out for mention because it was the most striking of them. It has also been said that "the signs" are what produce conjecture (ẓann), and "clear authority" is what produces certainty regarding what Moses brought. It has also been said that both terms refer to one thing: that is, We sent him with something that combines the quality of being a sign and the quality of being clear authority. It has also been said that "clear authority" is the argument Moses presented to Pharaoh in their dialogue.

﴿To Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾: that is, We sent him with these to them.

It has already been noted that al-mala' (the chiefs, the notables) are the leading people of a nation. He mentioned them specifically rather than the rest of the people because they are followers of Pharaoh in what he issues and what he brings in. He singled out these chiefs, rather than Pharaoh himself, with His words ﴿they followed the command of Pharaoh﴾, because of their command to them to disbelieve. Pharaoh's state of disbelief is a clear matter, since the disbelief of his people, both the notables and others, is based on his disbelief. It is also possible that "the command of Pharaoh" means his affair and his way, so that it includes disbelief and other things. ﴿And the command of Pharaoh was not rightly guided﴾: that is, there was never any right guidance in it; rather, it was error and misguidance. Rashid (rightly guided) here means one who guides, and the attribution is metaphorical; or it means one possessing right guidance, and this implies a contrast: that right guidance lies in the command of Moses.

﴿He will go before his people on the Day of Resurrection﴾: from qadama (to go before), meaning taqaddama (to precede): that is, he will become one who leads them on the Day of Resurrection, going ahead to the punishment of the Fire, just as he used to lead them in the world. ﴿And will bring them to the Fire﴾: that is, he will not cease to lead them while they follow him, until he brings them to the Fire. He expressed this in the past tense to draw attention to the certainty of its occurrence. Then He censured the watering place to which he brings them, saying: ﴿And wretched is the watering place to which they are brought﴾, because the one who comes to water, which is called al-wird (the watering place), comes only to quench the heat of thirst and remove his thirst, whereas the Fire is the opposite of that.

Then He censured them after censuring the place they arrive at, saying: ﴿And they are followed in this world by a curse﴾: that is, the people of Pharaoh are followed absolutely, or the chiefs specifically, or they and Pharaoh together in this world by a great curse, that is, expulsion and removal from mercy. ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection﴾: that is, they are followed by a curse on the Day of Resurrection, when the people of the gathering all curse them. Then He made the curse a reward (rifd) for them in a manner of mockery, saying: ﴿Wretched is the reward that is given﴾.

Al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Ubayda said: rafadtu-hu arfiduhu rifdan means I gave him support and gave him something; the name of the gift is rifd, that is, wretched is the gift. Al-i'āna (assistance) is what they were given and what they were assisted with. The object of the censure is omitted, that is, their reward, which is the curse they were followed by in this world and the Hereafter, as though it is a curse after a curse, one extending the first and making it perpetual.

Al-Mawardi reported, on the authority of al-Asma'i, that al-rafd, with a fatha, means a cup, and with a kasra it means what is in it of drink. So it is as though He censured what they are given to drink in the Fire, and this is more fitting to the context. It has also been said that al-rifd means an addition: that is, wretched is what they are given after drowning, which is the addition; this was said by al-Kalbi.

The reference in His words ﴿That is among the reports of the towns; We relate it to you﴾: that is, what Allah, glorified is He, related in this surah of the reports of the earlier nations and what they did with their prophets. That is, it is related to you as one report after another. The meaning of qasas (narrative) has already been established. The pronoun in minhā refers to the towns: that is, among the towns is one still standing, and among them is one mown down. The standing (qā'im) is that which is still standing on its foundations, and the mown down (ḥaṣīd) is that which has no trace left. It has also been said that the standing means the inhabited, and the mown down means the ruined. It has also been said that the standing means the empty towns without their roofs, and the mown down means the uprooted, in the sense of cut down. The towns are compared to a crop that is standing on its stalk and one that has been cut.

The poet said:
"And people in the division of death among them are like crops, some standing and some mown."

﴿And We did not wrong them﴾ by what We did to them of punishment, ﴿but they wronged themselves﴾ through disbelief and sins. ﴿So their gods did not avail them﴾: that is, their idols which they worshipped besides Allah did not ward off from them any of the punishment ﴿when the command of your Lord came﴾: that is, when His punishment came. ﴿And they added nothing to them but ruin﴾: tatbib means destruction and loss: that is, the idols they worshipped added nothing to them but destruction and loss, though they had believed that these would help them obtain benefits.

﴿And such is the seizure of your Lord﴾: al-Jaḥdarī and Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif read akhadha as a verb. The others read akhdh as a verbal noun (maṣdar). ﴿When He seizes the towns while they are wrongdoers﴾: that is, their people, who are wrongdoers. ﴿Indeed His seizure﴾: that is, His punishment of the disbelievers ﴿is painful, severe﴾: that is, painful and harsh.

﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾: that is, in Allah's seizure of the people of the towns, or in the narrative He related to His Messenger, is a lesson and an admonition ﴿for those who fear the punishment of the Hereafter﴾, because they are the ones who take lessons from examples and heed admonitions. The reference in His words ﴿That is a day on which mankind will be gathered﴾ is to the Day of Resurrection, indicated by the mention of the Hereafter, when people will be gathered for reckoning and recompense. ﴿That is a day witnessed﴾: that is, the people of the gathering witness it, or creatures are witnessed in it. He used the expression of a time-adverb in a broad sense, treating it as an object.

﴿And We do not delay it except for a limited term﴾: that is, We do not delay that day except until the end of a limited term, known by number. Allah, glorified is He, has determined that the recompense will occur after it.

﴿On the day it comes﴾: the people of Medina, Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read with the yā' (ya) present in continuous recitation and omitted in pause. Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud read it with the yā' present both in continuous recitation and in pause. Al-A'mash read it with the yā' omitted in both. The reason for omitting the yā' in pause, as al-Kisa'i said, is that the sound verb is paused upon like the jussive, so the yā' is omitted as the ḍamma is omitted. The reason for those who omitted the yā' in continuous recitation is that they saw the written form of the Mushaf that way. Al-Khalil and Sibawayh reported that the Arabs say lā adri (I do not know), omitting the yā' and making do with the kasra. Al-Farra' recited, as evidence for the omission of the yā', the line:
"Your hand, it is no hand that gives a dirham in generosity, and another hand gives blood by the sword."

Al-Zajjaj said: the better grammatical form is to retain the yā'. The meaning is: when it comes, on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿no soul will speak﴾: that is, no soul will speak, one of the two tā's having been dropped for lightness; that is, no soul will speak on it except with what is permitted to it of speech. It has also been said: no soul will speak with argument or intercession except with His permission, glorified is He, for it to speak thus. This is reconciled with His words ﴿This is a day when they will not speak, nor will they be permitted to offer excuses﴾ [al-Mursalat 35–36] by the difference of their states according to the different stations of the Resurrection.

Such a combination has been repeated in several places. ﴿Among them is the wretched and the happy﴾: that is, among the souls is the wretched and among them is the happy. The wretched is the one for whom wretchedness has been written, and the happy is the one for whom happiness has been written. The wretched is mentioned before the happy because the context is one of warning.

﴿As for those who were wretched, they will be in the Fire, for them therein is groaning and sighing﴾: that is, as for those for whom wretchedness has preceded, they will remain in the Fire, and for them therein is groaning and sighing.

Al-Zajjaj said: al-zafīr is from the intensity of moaning, and it is that which is raised very high. He said: the grammarians of Basra and Kufa maintain that al-zafīr is like the beginning of the braying of donkeys, and al-shahīq is like its end. It has also been said: al-zafīr is a loud sound, and al-shahīq a weak sound. It has also been said: al-zafīr is the exhalation of breath, and al-shahīq is the inhalation of breath. It has also been said: al-zafīr is from the chest, and al-shahīq is from the throat. It has also been said: al-zafīr is the repeated drawing of breath from intense fear, and al-shahīq is a long, extended breath. The clause is either a fresh sentence, as though it were said: what is their state therein? or it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

﴿Abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾: that is, for the duration of their continuance.

The scholars have differed in explaining the meaning of this temporal limitation, since it is known from definitive proofs that the punishment of the disbelievers in the Fire is everlasting and never ceases for them, and it is also established that the heavens and the earth will pass away at the end of the days of this world. One group said: this statement follows the custom of the Arabs when they wish to express the intensity of a thing's continuance. He says: "It will last as long as the heavens and the earth endure," and from this is His saying: "I will not come to you as long as night is dark," and "as long as night and day alternate," and "as long as the dove coos," and the like.

So the meaning of the verse is that they will abide therein forever, with no cessation and no end. It has also been said: the intended meaning is the heavens and earth of the Hereafter, for there are reports indicating that the Hereafter has heavens and earth other than those present in this world, which will endure as long as the abode of the Hereafter endures. Also, they must have a place that bears them and another that shades them, and these are earth and sky.

As for His words ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, the people of knowledge have differed about the meaning of this exception, in several opinions:

The first: it relates to His words ﴿so in the Fire﴾, as though He said: except what your Lord wills of delaying a people from that. This was reported by Abu Nadra from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.

The second: the exception applies only to the sinners among the monotheists, who will leave the Fire after a period. On this view, His words ﴿As for those who were wretched﴾ are general to the disbelievers and the sinners, and the exception applies to "abiding" (khalidin), and ma is in the sense of man (who). This was said by Qatada, al-Ḍaḥḥak, Abu Sinan and others.

It has been established by mutawatir (widely transmitted) reports, which yield necessary knowledge, that the people of monotheism will leave the Fire, and this specifies every general statement.

The third: the exception relates to the groaning and sighing: that is, they have therein groaning and sighing, "except what your Lord wills" of kinds of punishment other than groaning and sighing. This was said by Ibn al-Anbari.

The fourth: the meaning of the exception is that they will abide therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, without dying, except what your Lord wills. He will command the Fire, and it will consume them until they perish, then Allah will renew their creation. This was narrated from Ibn Mas'ud.

The fifth: illa (except) means siwā (other than). The meaning is: as long as the heavens and the earth endure, other than what exceeds that of eternity. It is as though He mentioned for their abiding a duration that is not longer in the eyes of the Arabs, then added to it the eternal continuance that has no end. This was related by al-Zajjaj.

The sixth: what was reported from al-Farra', Ibn al-Anbari and Ibn Qutayba, that this does not contradict the non-existence of the will, like your saying: "By Allah, I will strike him, unless I see otherwise." This was objected to on the grounds that the meaning of the verse is the judgement of their abiding, except for the period which Allah willed, so the will has definitely occurred. Al-Zajjaj also related this opinion.

The seventh: the meaning is: abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills of the measure of their standing at their graves and for the reckoning. Related by al-Zajjaj also.

The eighth: the meaning is: abiding therein, except what your Lord wills of an increase of bliss for the people of bliss and an increase of punishment for the people of the blazing Fire. Also related by al-Zajjaj, and chosen by al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi.

The ninth: illa means waw (and). This was said by al-Farra', and the meaning is: "and what your Lord wills of increase." Makki said: this view is far-fetched for the Basrans, that illa should mean waw.

The tenth: illa means ka (like). The estimate is: "as your Lord willed," and from this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women, except what has already passed﴾ [al-Nisa' 22], meaning: as has already passed.

The eleventh: this exception is of the type of exception that the Lawgiver recommends in every speech, and it is like His saying: ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills, in security﴾ [al-Fath 27]. Something similar was reported from Abu 'Ubayd.

These opinions are the entirety of what we have come across of the views of the people of knowledge. Some of them have been objected to with objections, and these have been answered with responses. I have clarified this in an independent treatise that I compiled in answer to a question that came from one of the scholars.

﴿And as for those who were made happy, they will be in the Garden, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 11, verses 96–108 (part 2 of 2):

Al-A'mash, Hafs, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿سُعِدُوا﴾ (su'idu, "they were made happy") with a ḍammah on the sīn. The rest read it with a fatḥah on the sīn (sa'idu). Abu Ubaydah and Abu Hatim preferred this second reading.

Sibawayh said: "One does not say saʿida fulān (فُلانٌ سَعِدَ), just as one does not say shaqiya fulān (شَقِيَ فُلانٌ), because it is among the verbs that do not take an object (intransitive)."

Al-Nahhas said: "I saw ʿAli ibn Sulayman expressing surprise at al-Kisa'i's reading with a ḍammah on the sīn, even though he was knowledgeable in Arabic. This is a grammatical error (laḥn) that is not permissible. The meaning of the verse is as already explained in His words: ﴿Then as for those who are wretched﴾."

As for His words ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾: the preceding statements have already made clear what is suitable for this exception to refer to. ﴿A gift unceasing﴾ means: Allah will give them a gift that is unceasing. Al-majdhudh means "cut off," from jadhdhahu, yajudhdhuhu, when one cuts it. The meaning is that it extends without end.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words ﴿He will lead his people on the Day of Resurrection﴾, that he said: "He will mislead them and bring them down into the Fire."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah regarding the verse that he said: "Pharaoh walks in front of his people until he drives them right into the Fire."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words ﴿and brings them down to the Fire﴾, that he said: "al-wurūd means entering."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words ﴿Wretched is the gift that is given﴾, that he said: "The curse of this world and the Hereafter."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding ﴿Among them are those standing and those harvested﴾, that he meant: "Inhabited towns and extinguished towns."

Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah: "Among them is one standing, whose place is still seen, and one harvested, of which no trace is seen."

Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Juraij: "Among them is one standing, empty upon its roofs, and one harvested, flattened to the ground."

Abu al-Shaykh related from Abu ʿAsim regarding ﴿Their gods did not avail them﴾ that he said: "They did not benefit them."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn ʿUmar, regarding His words ﴿They added nothing to them but ruin﴾, that it means "destruction."

Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Zayd that he said: "Takhsīr" (loss).

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah a similar meaning.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah, glorified and exalted is He, gives respite to the wrongdoer, until when He seizes him, He does not let him go." Then he recited: ﴿And such is the seizure of your Lord when He seizes the towns while they are wrongdoing. Indeed, His seizure is painful and severe.﴾

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Zayd regarding His words ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for whoever fears the punishment of the Hereafter﴾, that he said: "We shall fulfill for them what We promised them in the Hereafter, just as We fulfilled for the prophets that We would help them."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿That is a Day on which mankind will be gathered, and that is a Day witnessed﴾ that he said: "It is the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh related the same from Mujahid.

Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Juraij regarding His words ﴿the Day it comes﴾ that he said: "That Day."

Al-Tirmidhi, who graded it ḥasan, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh related from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, who said: "When the verse ﴿So among them is the wretched and the happy﴾ was revealed, I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, then what are we working for? Is it for something already decided, or for something not yet decided?' He said: 'Rather, it is for something already decided, and the pens have run with it, O ʿUmar. But each is made easy for what he was created for.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "These two are among the hidden matters: Allah's words ﴿So among them is the wretched and the happy﴾ and ﴿On the Day when Allah will gather the messengers and say, 'What was your response?' They will say, 'We have no knowledge.'﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 109]. As for His words ﴿So among them is the wretched and the happy﴾, they are a people from the People of the Book and from the people of this qiblah (the Muslims). Allah will punish them in the Fire for as long as He wills because of their sins. Then He will permit intercession for them, and the believers will intercede for them, and they will be brought out of the Fire and admitted into Paradise. He named them 'wretched' when He punished them in the Fire. ﴿As for those who are wretched, they will be in the Fire, having therein groaning and wailing﴾, ﴿abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾, referring to when He permitted intercession for them, brought them out of the Fire and admitted them into Paradise, and they are the same people. ﴿And as for those who are made happy﴾, meaning after the wretchedness they were in, ﴿they will be in Paradise, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾, meaning those who were in the Fire."

Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh related from Qatadah that he recited this verse: ﴿As for those who are wretched﴾, and said: "Anas told us that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'A people will come out of the Fire.'" And we do not say as the Harurites said, that whoever enters it remains in it forever.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Jabir who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited ﴿As for those who are wretched﴾ up to His words ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, and said to me: 'If Allah wills to bring out some people from among those who were wretched from the Fire and admit them into Paradise, He will do so.'"

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Khalid ibn Ma'dan regarding His words ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾ that he said: "It refers to the people of monotheism (tawḥīd) among the people of the qiblah."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Dhurays, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wal-Sifat related from Abu Nadrah, from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, or from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, or from a man among the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His words ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾ that he said: "This verse overrides the entire Qur'an. Wherever in the Qur'an there is 'abiding therein,' this verse applies to it."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and al-Bayhaqi related from Abu Nadrah who said: "The entire Qur'an ends at this verse: ﴿Indeed your Lord is the Doer of what He intends.﴾"

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾ that he said: "For every Paradise there is a heaven and an earth."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related something similar from al-Suddi.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related something similar also from al-Hasan.

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th wal-Nushur related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾ that he said: "Your Lord has willed that these should abide in the Fire and that those should abide in Paradise."

Ibn Jarir related from him regarding His words ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾ that he said: "Allah excepted from the Fire that it should consume them."

Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi regarding the verse that he said: "Afterwards, there came from Allah's will what abrogated it (nasakha), and it was revealed in Medina: ﴿Indeed those who disbelieved and did wrong, Allah will never forgive them, nor guide them to any path﴾ [al-Nisa': 168], to the end of the verse. So the hope of the people of the Fire to come out of it was removed, and He made eternal abiding obligatory for them."

As for His words ﴿And as for those who are made happy﴾ up to the end of the verse, he said: "Afterwards, there came from Allah's will what abrogated it, and it was revealed in Medina: ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, We will admit them into gardens﴾ up to His words ﴿extended shade﴾ [al-Nisa': 57], and so He made eternal abiding obligatory for them."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from al-Hasan who said: "ʿUmar said: 'If the people of the Fire remained in the Fire for as long as the amount of sand of ʿAlij, there would still be a day for them on which they would come out.'"

Ishaq ibn Rahawayh related from Abu Hurayrah who said: "There will come upon Hell a day when no one will remain in it," and he recited: ﴿As for those who are wretched﴾ up to the end of the verse.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibrahim who said: "There is no verse in the Qur'an more hopeful for the people of the Fire than this verse: ﴿abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾."

He said: "Ibn Mas'ud said: 'There will certainly come upon it a time when its gates will swing (in the wind) because they are empty.'"

Ibn Jarir related from al-Sha'bi who said: "Hell is the swiftest of the two abodes to be inhabited and the swiftest of them to be ruined."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah regarding His words ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾ that he said: "Allah knows best about its exception, in which way it has occurred."

Similar to what ʿUmar, Abu Hurayrah and Ibn Mas'ud mentioned has been related from a group of the early scholars (salaf), such as Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar, Jabir and Abu Sa'id among the Companions, and from Abu Mijlaz, ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam and others among the Successors (tabi'un).

A ḥadīth on this matter occurs in al-Tabarani's al-Mu'jam al-Kabir from Abu Umamah Ṣudayy ibn ʿAjlan al-Bahili, but its chain of narration is weak (ḍaʿīf).

The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) spoke on this point in a way that, for him, had room for omission, and silence about it would have been sufficient. He said: "Let not the statement of the Mujbirah (predestinarians) deceive you, that the intended meaning of the exception is the release of the people of major sins from the Fire. For the second exception calls out against their falsehood and records their fabrication. And what do you think of a people who cast away the Book of Allah when some reliable transmissions were related to them from Ibn ʿAmr: 'There will certainly come upon Hell a day when its gates will be clapped, with no one in it.'" Then he said: "And I say: what did Ibn ʿAmr do with his two swords and his fighting with them against ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that would have preoccupied him from transmitting this ḥadīth? End of quote."

I say: As for the attack on the one who says that people of major sins will come out of the Fire, the one who says so, O wretched one, is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as is authentically established from him in the compilations of Islam, which are the records of the pure Sunnah, and as is authentically established from him in other sources through a group of Companions reaching the number of mass transmission (tawātur). So what concern is it of yours to attack a people who knew what you were ignorant of, and who acted upon what is far from you? And what prevents the exception from being understood in this way, which is what the many sound and numerous proofs have shown, as the majority of scholars, of the early and later generations, went to and said? As for what you supposed, that the second exception calls out against their falsehood and records their fabrication, there is no calling out and no contradiction. And what prevents the exception in both places from being understood as referring to the disobedient ones of this Ummah? The first exception is understood to mean: "except what your Lord wills" of the release of the disobedient of this Ummah from the Fire, and the second exception is understood to mean: "except what your Lord wills" of their not abiding in Paradise as the others abide, because of the delay in their entry into it for the length of time they remained in the Fire. This was said by scholars whom we mentioned earlier, and Ibn ʿAbbas, the scholar of the Ummah (ḥibr al-ummah), also said it.

As for the attack on the Companion of the Messenger of Allah, the guardian of his Sunnah and the worshipper among the Companions, ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr, may Allah be pleased with him: where are you going, O Mahmud? Do you know what you have done, into what valley you have fallen, and on which side you have landed? And who are you, that you climb up to this place and try to reach the stars of the sky with your short hands and your lame leg? Did you not have, among the grammarians and philologists whose works you were trying to break, something that would turn you back from entering into what you do not know and speaking about what you have no understanding of? Glory be to Allah, what a wonder: what deficiency in the knowledge of transmission and distance from knowing it does to a person, leading him to the furthest point of disgrace, for one who does not know his own worth nor halts himself where Allah, glorified is He, has halted him.

The intended meaning of "the signs" is the Torah, and "clear authority" refers to the miracles. It has also been said that "the signs" are the nine signs mentioned elsewhere, and "clear authority" is the staff. Although the staff is one of the nine, it is singled out for mention because it was the most striking of them. It has also been said that "the signs" are what produce conjecture (ẓann), and "clear authority" is what produces certainty regarding what Moses brought. It has also been said that both terms refer to one thing: that is, We sent him with something that combines the quality of being a sign and the quality of being clear authority. It has also been said that "clear authority" is the argument Moses presented to Pharaoh in their dialogue.

﴿To Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾: that is, We sent him with these to them.

It has already been noted that al-mala' (the chiefs, the notables) are the leading people of a nation. He mentioned them specifically rather than the rest of the people because they are followers of Pharaoh in what he issues and what he brings in. He singled out these chiefs, rather than Pharaoh himself, with His words ﴿they followed the command of Pharaoh﴾, because of their command to them to disbelieve. Pharaoh's state of disbelief is a clear matter, since the disbelief of his people, both the notables and others, is based on his disbelief. It is also possible that "the command of Pharaoh" means his affair and his way, so that it includes disbelief and other things. ﴿And the command of Pharaoh was not rightly guided﴾: that is, there was never any right guidance in it; rather, it was error and misguidance. Rashid (rightly guided) here means one who guides, and the attribution is metaphorical; or it means one possessing right guidance, and this implies a contrast: that right guidance lies in the command of Moses.

﴿He will go before his people on the Day of Resurrection﴾: from qadama (to go before), meaning taqaddama (to precede): that is, he will become one who leads them on the Day of Resurrection, going ahead to the punishment of the Fire, just as he used to lead them in the world. ﴿And will bring them to the Fire﴾: that is, he will not cease to lead them while they follow him, until he brings them to the Fire. He expressed this in the past tense to draw attention to the certainty of its occurrence. Then He censured the watering place to which he brings them, saying: ﴿And wretched is the watering place to which they are brought﴾, because the one who comes to water, which is called al-wird (the watering place), comes only to quench the heat of thirst and remove his thirst, whereas the Fire is the opposite of that.

Then He censured them after censuring the place they arrive at, saying: ﴿And they are followed in this world by a curse﴾: that is, the people of Pharaoh are followed absolutely, or the chiefs specifically, or they and Pharaoh together in this world by a great curse, that is, expulsion and removal from mercy. ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection﴾: that is, they are followed by a curse on the Day of Resurrection, when the people of the gathering all curse them. Then He made the curse a reward (rifd) for them in a manner of mockery, saying: ﴿Wretched is the reward that is given﴾.

Al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Ubayda said: rafadtu-hu arfiduhu rifdan means I gave him support and gave him something; the name of the gift is rifd, that is, wretched is the gift. Al-i'āna (assistance) is what they were given and what they were assisted with. The object of the censure is omitted, that is, their reward, which is the curse they were followed by in this world and the Hereafter, as though it is a curse after a curse, one extending the first and making it perpetual.

Al-Mawardi reported, on the authority of al-Asma'i, that al-rafd, with a fatha, means a cup, and with a kasra it means what is in it of drink. So it is as though He censured what they are given to drink in the Fire, and this is more fitting to the context. It has also been said that al-rifd means an addition: that is, wretched is what they are given after drowning, which is the addition; this was said by al-Kalbi.

The reference in His words ﴿That is among the reports of the towns; We relate it to you﴾: that is, what Allah, glorified is He, related in this surah of the reports of the earlier nations and what they did with their prophets. That is, it is related to you as one report after another. The meaning of qasas (narrative) has already been established. The pronoun in minhā refers to the towns: that is, among the towns is one still standing, and among them is one mown down. The standing (qā'im) is that which is still standing on its foundations, and the mown down (ḥaṣīd) is that which has no trace left. It has also been said that the standing means the inhabited, and the mown down means the ruined. It has also been said that the standing means the empty towns without their roofs, and the mown down means the uprooted, in the sense of cut down. The towns are compared to a crop that is standing on its stalk and one that has been cut.

The poet said:
"And people in the division of death among them are like crops, some standing and some mown."

﴿And We did not wrong them﴾ by what We did to them of punishment, ﴿but they wronged themselves﴾ through disbelief and sins. ﴿So their gods did not avail them﴾: that is, their idols which they worshipped besides Allah did not ward off from them any of the punishment ﴿when the command of your Lord came﴾: that is, when His punishment came. ﴿And they added nothing to them but ruin﴾: tatbib means destruction and loss: that is, the idols they worshipped added nothing to them but destruction and loss, though they had believed that these would help them obtain benefits.

﴿And such is the seizure of your Lord﴾: al-Jaḥdarī and Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif read akhadha as a verb. The others read akhdh as a verbal noun (maṣdar). ﴿When He seizes the towns while they are wrongdoers﴾: that is, their people, who are wrongdoers. ﴿Indeed His seizure﴾: that is, His punishment of the disbelievers ﴿is painful, severe﴾: that is, painful and harsh.

﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾: that is, in Allah's seizure of the people of the towns, or in the narrative He related to His Messenger, is a lesson and an admonition ﴿for those who fear the punishment of the Hereafter﴾, because they are the ones who take lessons from examples and heed admonitions. The reference in His words ﴿That is a day on which mankind will be gathered﴾ is to the Day of Resurrection, indicated by the mention of the Hereafter, when people will be gathered for reckoning and recompense. ﴿That is a day witnessed﴾: that is, the people of the gathering witness it, or creatures are witnessed in it. He used the expression of a time-adverb in a broad sense, treating it as an object.

﴿And We do not delay it except for a limited term﴾: that is, We do not delay that day except until the end of a limited term, known by number. Allah, glorified is He, has determined that the recompense will occur after it.

﴿On the day it comes﴾: the people of Medina, Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read with the yā' (ya) present in continuous recitation and omitted in pause. Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud read it with the yā' present both in continuous recitation and in pause. Al-A'mash read it with the yā' omitted in both. The reason for omitting the yā' in pause, as al-Kisa'i said, is that the sound verb is paused upon like the jussive, so the yā' is omitted as the ḍamma is omitted. The reason for those who omitted the yā' in continuous recitation is that they saw the written form of the Mushaf that way. Al-Khalil and Sibawayh reported that the Arabs say lā adri (I do not know), omitting the yā' and making do with the kasra. Al-Farra' recited, as evidence for the omission of the yā', the line:
"Your hand, it is no hand that gives a dirham in generosity, and another hand gives blood by the sword."

Al-Zajjaj said: the better grammatical form is to retain the yā'. The meaning is: when it comes, on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿no soul will speak﴾: that is, no soul will speak, one of the two tā's having been dropped for lightness; that is, no soul will speak on it except with what is permitted to it of speech. It has also been said: no soul will speak with argument or intercession except with His permission, glorified is He, for it to speak thus. This is reconciled with His words ﴿This is a day when they will not speak, nor will they be permitted to offer excuses﴾ [al-Mursalat 35–36] by the difference of their states according to the different stations of the Resurrection.

Such a combination has been repeated in several places. ﴿Among them is the wretched and the happy﴾: that is, among the souls is the wretched and among them is the happy. The wretched is the one for whom wretchedness has been written, and the happy is the one for whom happiness has been written. The wretched is mentioned before the happy because the context is one of warning.

﴿As for those who were wretched, they will be in the Fire, for them therein is groaning and sighing﴾: that is, as for those for whom wretchedness has preceded, they will remain in the Fire, and for them therein is groaning and sighing.

Al-Zajjaj said: al-zafīr is from the intensity of moaning, and it is that which is raised very high. He said: the grammarians of Basra and Kufa maintain that al-zafīr is like the beginning of the braying of donkeys, and al-shahīq is like its end. It has also been said: al-zafīr is a loud sound, and al-shahīq a weak sound. It has also been said: al-zafīr is the exhalation of breath, and al-shahīq is the inhalation of breath. It has also been said: al-zafīr is from the chest, and al-shahīq is from the throat. It has also been said: al-zafīr is the repeated drawing of breath from intense fear, and al-shahīq is a long, extended breath. The clause is either a fresh sentence, as though it were said: what is their state therein? or it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

﴿Abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾: that is, for the duration of their continuance.

The scholars have differed in explaining the meaning of this temporal limitation, since it is known from definitive proofs that the punishment of the disbelievers in the Fire is everlasting and never ceases for them, and it is also established that the heavens and the earth will pass away at the end of the days of this world. One group said: this statement follows the custom of the Arabs when they wish to express the intensity of a thing's continuance. He says: "It will last as long as the heavens and the earth endure," and from this is His saying: "I will not come to you as long as night is dark," and "as long as night and day alternate," and "as long as the dove coos," and the like.

So the meaning of the verse is that they will abide therein forever, with no cessation and no end. It has also been said: the intended meaning is the heavens and earth of the Hereafter, for there are reports indicating that the Hereafter has heavens and earth other than those present in this world, which will endure as long as the abode of the Hereafter endures. Also, they must have a place that bears them and another that shades them, and these are earth and sky.

As for His words ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, the people of knowledge have differed about the meaning of this exception, in several opinions:

The first: it relates to His words ﴿so in the Fire﴾, as though He said: except what your Lord wills of delaying a people from that. This was reported by Abu Nadra from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.

The second: the exception applies only to the sinners among the monotheists, who will leave the Fire after a period. On this view, His words ﴿As for those who were wretched﴾ are general to the disbelievers and the sinners, and the exception applies to "abiding" (khalidin), and ma is in the sense of man (who). This was said by Qatada, al-Ḍaḥḥak, Abu Sinan and others.

It has been established by mutawatir (widely transmitted) reports, which yield necessary knowledge, that the people of monotheism will leave the Fire, and this specifies every general statement.

The third: the exception relates to the groaning and sighing: that is, they have therein groaning and sighing, "except what your Lord wills" of kinds of punishment other than groaning and sighing. This was said by Ibn al-Anbari.

The fourth: the meaning of the exception is that they will abide therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, without dying, except what your Lord wills. He will command the Fire, and it will consume them until they perish, then Allah will renew their creation. This was narrated from Ibn Mas'ud.

The fifth: illa (except) means siwā (other than). The meaning is: as long as the heavens and the earth endure, other than what exceeds that of eternity. It is as though He mentioned for their abiding a duration that is not longer in the eyes of the Arabs, then added to it the eternal continuance that has no end. This was related by al-Zajjaj.

The sixth: what was reported from al-Farra', Ibn al-Anbari and Ibn Qutayba, that this does not contradict the non-existence of the will, like your saying: "By Allah, I will strike him, unless I see otherwise." This was objected to on the grounds that the meaning of the verse is the judgement of their abiding, except for the period which Allah willed, so the will has definitely occurred. Al-Zajjaj also related this opinion.

The seventh: the meaning is: abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills of the measure of their standing at their graves and for the reckoning. Related by al-Zajjaj also.

The eighth: the meaning is: abiding therein, except what your Lord wills of an increase of bliss for the people of bliss and an increase of punishment for the people of the blazing Fire. Also related by al-Zajjaj, and chosen by al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi.

The ninth: illa means waw (and). This was said by al-Farra', and the meaning is: "and what your Lord wills of increase." Makki said: this view is far-fetched for the Basrans, that illa should mean waw.

The tenth: illa means ka (like). The estimate is: "as your Lord willed," and from this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women, except what has already passed﴾ [al-Nisa' 22], meaning: as has already passed.

The eleventh: this exception is of the type of exception that the Lawgiver recommends in every speech, and it is like His saying: ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills, in security﴾ [al-Fath 27]. Something similar was reported from Abu 'Ubayd.

These opinions are the entirety of what we have come across of the views of the people of knowledge. Some of them have been objected to with objections, and these have been answered with responses. I have clarified this in an independent treatise that I compiled in answer to a question that came from one of the scholars.

﴿And as for those who were made happy, they will be in the Garden, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 11, verses 96–108 (part 2 of 2):

Al-A'mash, Hafs, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿سُعِدُوا﴾ (su'idu, "they were made happy") with a ḍammah on the sīn. The rest read it with a fatḥah on the sīn (sa'idu). Abu Ubaydah and Abu Hatim preferred this second reading.

Sibawayh said: "One does not say saʿida fulān (فُلانٌ سَعِدَ), just as one does not say shaqiya fulān (شَقِيَ فُلانٌ), because it is among the verbs that do not take an object (intransitive)."

Al-Nahhas said: "I saw ʿAli ibn Sulayman expressing surprise at al-Kisa'i's reading with a ḍammah on the sīn, even though he was knowledgeable in Arabic. This is a grammatical error (laḥn) that is not permissible. The meaning of the verse is as already explained in His words: ﴿Then as for those who are wretched﴾."

As for His words ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾: the preceding statements have already made clear what is suitable for this exception to refer to. ﴿A gift unceasing﴾ means: Allah will give them a gift that is unceasing. Al-majdhudh means "cut off," from jadhdhahu, yajudhdhuhu, when one cuts it. The meaning is that it extends without end.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words ﴿He will lead his people on the Day of Resurrection﴾, that he said: "He will mislead them and bring them down into the Fire."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah regarding the verse that he said: "Pharaoh walks in front of his people until he drives them right into the Fire."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words ﴿and brings them down to the Fire﴾, that he said: "al-wurūd means entering."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words ﴿Wretched is the gift that is given﴾, that he said: "The curse of this world and the Hereafter."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him regarding ﴿Among them are those standing and those harvested﴾, that he meant: "Inhabited towns and extinguished towns."

Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah: "Among them is one standing, whose place is still seen, and one harvested, of which no trace is seen."

Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Juraij: "Among them is one standing, empty upon its roofs, and one harvested, flattened to the ground."

Abu al-Shaykh related from Abu ʿAsim regarding ﴿Their gods did not avail them﴾ that he said: "They did not benefit them."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn ʿUmar, regarding His words ﴿They added nothing to them but ruin﴾, that it means "destruction."

Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Zayd that he said: "Takhsīr" (loss).

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah a similar meaning.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah, glorified and exalted is He, gives respite to the wrongdoer, until when He seizes him, He does not let him go." Then he recited: ﴿And such is the seizure of your Lord when He seizes the towns while they are wrongdoing. Indeed, His seizure is painful and severe.﴾

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Zayd regarding His words ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for whoever fears the punishment of the Hereafter﴾, that he said: "We shall fulfill for them what We promised them in the Hereafter, just as We fulfilled for the prophets that We would help them."

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿That is a Day on which mankind will be gathered, and that is a Day witnessed﴾ that he said: "It is the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh related the same from Mujahid.

Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Juraij regarding His words ﴿the Day it comes﴾ that he said: "That Day."

Al-Tirmidhi, who graded it ḥasan, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh related from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, who said: "When the verse ﴿So among them is the wretched and the happy﴾ was revealed, I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, then what are we working for? Is it for something already decided, or for something not yet decided?' He said: 'Rather, it is for something already decided, and the pens have run with it, O ʿUmar. But each is made easy for what he was created for.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "These two are among the hidden matters: Allah's words ﴿So among them is the wretched and the happy﴾ and ﴿On the Day when Allah will gather the messengers and say, 'What was your response?' They will say, 'We have no knowledge.'﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 109]. As for His words ﴿So among them is the wretched and the happy﴾, they are a people from the People of the Book and from the people of this qiblah (the Muslims). Allah will punish them in the Fire for as long as He wills because of their sins. Then He will permit intercession for them, and the believers will intercede for them, and they will be brought out of the Fire and admitted into Paradise. He named them 'wretched' when He punished them in the Fire. ﴿As for those who are wretched, they will be in the Fire, having therein groaning and wailing﴾, ﴿abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾, referring to when He permitted intercession for them, brought them out of the Fire and admitted them into Paradise, and they are the same people. ﴿And as for those who are made happy﴾, meaning after the wretchedness they were in, ﴿they will be in Paradise, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾, meaning those who were in the Fire."

Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh related from Qatadah that he recited this verse: ﴿As for those who are wretched﴾, and said: "Anas told us that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'A people will come out of the Fire.'" And we do not say as the Harurites said, that whoever enters it remains in it forever.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Jabir who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited ﴿As for those who are wretched﴾ up to His words ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, and said to me: 'If Allah wills to bring out some people from among those who were wretched from the Fire and admit them into Paradise, He will do so.'"

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Khalid ibn Ma'dan regarding His words ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾ that he said: "It refers to the people of monotheism (tawḥīd) among the people of the qiblah."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Dhurays, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wal-Sifat related from Abu Nadrah, from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, or from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, or from a man among the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His words ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾ that he said: "This verse overrides the entire Qur'an. Wherever in the Qur'an there is 'abiding therein,' this verse applies to it."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and al-Bayhaqi related from Abu Nadrah who said: "The entire Qur'an ends at this verse: ﴿Indeed your Lord is the Doer of what He intends.﴾"

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾ that he said: "For every Paradise there is a heaven and an earth."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related something similar from al-Suddi.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related something similar also from al-Hasan.

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th wal-Nushur related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾ that he said: "Your Lord has willed that these should abide in the Fire and that those should abide in Paradise."

Ibn Jarir related from him regarding His words ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾ that he said: "Allah excepted from the Fire that it should consume them."

Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi regarding the verse that he said: "Afterwards, there came from Allah's will what abrogated it (nasakha), and it was revealed in Medina: ﴿Indeed those who disbelieved and did wrong, Allah will never forgive them, nor guide them to any path﴾ [al-Nisa': 168], to the end of the verse. So the hope of the people of the Fire to come out of it was removed, and He made eternal abiding obligatory for them."

As for His words ﴿And as for those who are made happy﴾ up to the end of the verse, he said: "Afterwards, there came from Allah's will what abrogated it, and it was revealed in Medina: ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, We will admit them into gardens﴾ up to His words ﴿extended shade﴾ [al-Nisa': 57], and so He made eternal abiding obligatory for them."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from al-Hasan who said: "ʿUmar said: 'If the people of the Fire remained in the Fire for as long as the amount of sand of ʿAlij, there would still be a day for them on which they would come out.'"

Ishaq ibn Rahawayh related from Abu Hurayrah who said: "There will come upon Hell a day when no one will remain in it," and he recited: ﴿As for those who are wretched﴾ up to the end of the verse.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibrahim who said: "There is no verse in the Qur'an more hopeful for the people of the Fire than this verse: ﴿abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾."

He said: "Ibn Mas'ud said: 'There will certainly come upon it a time when its gates will swing (in the wind) because they are empty.'"

Ibn Jarir related from al-Sha'bi who said: "Hell is the swiftest of the two abodes to be inhabited and the swiftest of them to be ruined."
