For steadfastness as Allah commanded it can only be borne by purified souls and sanctified selves. For this reason the Chosen One (ﷺ) said: "Hud has grayed me," as has already been mentioned.

﴿And do not transgress.﴾ *Al-ṭughyān* (الطُّغْيانُ) is exceeding the limit. When Allah, glorified is He, commanded the steadfastness mentioned, He explained that excess in worship and extravagance in obedience, to the extent that one goes beyond the limit He set and the measure He determined, is forbidden and prohibited. This is like one who fasts and never breaks the fast, prays through the night and never sleeps, and abandons the lawful which Allah permitted and encouraged. For this reason the Truthful, the one whose word is confirmed, says in what is authentically related from him: "As for me, I fast and I break the fast, I pray and I sleep, and I marry women. Whoever turns away from my sunnah is not of me." The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) and to his community, giving precedence to their condition over his. Or the prohibition against transgression is specific to the community. ﴿Indeed, He is, of what you do, All-Seeing﴾, He will repay you according to what you deserve. This clause gives the reason for what precedes it.

His saying: ﴿And do not incline toward those who did wrong﴾.

Al-Jumhur (the majority) read *tarkanū* (تَرْكَنُوا) with a fatḥah on the *kāf*. Talhah ibn Musarrif, Qatadah and others read *turkanū* (تُرْكَنُوا) with a ḍammah on the *kāf*.

Al-Farra' said: this is the dialect of Tamim and Qays. Abu ʿAmr said: the reading of the majority is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. He said: the dialect of Tamim is with a kasrah on the *tā'* and a fatḥah on the *kāf*, and they put a kasrah on the vowel of the imperfect prefix in every verb of the pattern *ʿalima yaʿlamu* (عَلِمَ يَعْلَمُ).

Ibn Abi ʿAblah read it with a ḍammah on the *tā'* and a fatḥah on the *kāf*, in the passive form of *arkanahu* (أرْكَنَهُ).

In *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* (the Sihah, a lexicon) it says: *rakana ilayhi yarkunu* with a ḍammah (بِالضَّمِّ). Abu Zayd related *rakina ilayhi* with a kasrah: *yarkinu rukūnan* in both, meaning he inclined toward it and became calm. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not incline toward those who did wrong﴾. As for what Abu Zayd related, *rakana yarkanu* with a fatḥah in both, it is only a combination of the two dialects. End of quotation.

In *Shams al-ʿUlūm* it says: *al-rukūn* is calm, rest. It is said: *rakana ilayhi rukūnan*. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not incline toward those who did wrong﴾. End of quotation.

In *al-Qamus* it says: *rakana ilayhi*, like *naṣara*, *ʿalima* and *manaʿa*, *rukūnan*: he inclined and became calm. End of quotation. These leading authorities of lexicography defined *al-rukūn* by inclination and calm in general, without restriction to what the author of *al-Kashshaf* restricted it to when he said: "*rukūn* is slight inclination." The exegetes likewise explained it by inclination and calm in general without restriction, except those who were among the restrictive ones who follow what *al-Kashshaf* transmits. Some exegetes mentioned conditions in explaining *rukūn* which the lexicographers did not mention.

Al-Qurtubi said in his *Tafsir*: the true meaning of *rukūn* is reliance, dependence, calm toward a thing, and contentment with it.

Among the leading Successors (*tābiʿūn*) there is one who explained *rukūn* by something more specific than its linguistic meaning.

It is related from Qatadah and ʿIkrimah concerning the interpretation of the verse that its meaning is: "Do not love them and do not obey them."

ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said concerning the interpretation of the verse: "*Rukūn* here is *idhān* (flattery/compromise), namely that one does not denounce their disbelief."

Abu al-ʿAliyah said: its meaning is: "Do not be pleased with their deeds."

The leading exegetes have also differed concerning this verse: is it specific to the polytheists, or general? It has been said it is specific, that the meaning of the verse is the prohibition against inclining toward the polytheists, and that they are the ones intended by "those who did wrong." This has been related from Ibn ʿAbbas. It has been said: it is general to wrongdoers without distinction between disbeliever and Muslim, and this is the apparent meaning of the verse. Even if we assume that the cause of revelation was the polytheists, the consideration is by the generality of the wording, not by the specificity of the cause.

If you say: the sound and abundant proofs, reaching the number of mass transmission (*tawātur*), are established from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with an establishment that is not hidden from anyone with even minimal adherence to the pure Sunnah, concerning the obligation to obey the leaders, the rulers and the commanders, to the point that in some wordings of the Sahih it appears: "Obey the ruler even if he is an Abyssinian slave whose head is like a raisin."

And it is related that obeying them is obligatory "as long as they establish the prayer, as long as open disbelief does not appear from them, and as long as they do not command disobedience to Allah."

The apparent meaning of this is that even if they reach the highest degree of wrongdoing and commit the greatest of its kinds, short of going out into manifest disbelief, their obedience is obligatory, provided what they command is not disobedience to Allah. Among what they command is the assumption of government works, and entering religious offices whose entry is not disobedience to Allah. Among what they command is jihad, the collection of obligatory rights from subjects, the establishment of the Shari'ah among litigants among them, and the carrying out of the hudud (legal punishments) upon whoever deserves them. In sum, their obedience is obligatory upon everyone who comes under their command and prohibition, in everything they command which is not disobedience to Allah. In such matters there must be dealings with them, entering upon them, and the like, which cannot be avoided. There is no escape from this that we have mentioned, namely the obligation to obey them under the stated conditions, because of the mass transmission of the proofs that have come. Indeed, the Noble Book has come with it: ﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you﴾ [an-Nisa': 59]. Moreover, it is related that they are given what is due to them of obedience, even if they withhold what is due from them to their subjects, as in some sound hadiths: "Give them what is theirs, and ask Allah for what is yours." Indeed the command to obey the ruler has come, and the Prophet (ﷺ) emphasized this so much that he said: "Even if he takes your wealth and beats your back."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 11, verses 109–115 (part 2 of 2):

If we take the mere inclination and reliance (al-mayl wal-sukun) in its absolute sense, then the bare act of obedience that is commanded, together with the mixing it necessarily entails, is itself an inclination and a reliance. But if we take inclination and reliance as applying to both the outward and the inward, then the prohibition in this verse does not include the one who inclines to them outwardly, for a reason that the Law requires, such as obedience, or out of *taqiyyah* (precautionary dissimulation, i.e. concealing one's true position to avoid harm) and fear of harm from them, or to bring about a general or particular benefit, or to repel a general or particular harm, provided that he has no inward inclination toward them, no love for them, and no approval of their deeds.

I say: As for obedience in its general sense, in all its categories, so long as it is not disobedience to God, then, on the assumption that the name of reliance (*rukun*) applies to it, it specifies the general scope of the prohibition against it by the evidences we have already pointed out. There is no doubt or hesitation in this. Thus, whoever they appoint from the outset to enter into any of the tasks entrusted to them, which are not disobedience to God, such as religious offices and the like, and he is confident of his ability to carry out what is entrusted to him, then this is obligatory for him, let alone being said to be permissible for him.

As for what has been reported of the prohibition against entering into government office (*imarah*), it is restricted to the situation where no command has come from those whose obedience is obligatory, namely the imams, sultans and rulers, reconciling the evidences; or where the one commanded is too weak to carry out what he has been ordered to do. This is how the reason for the prohibition against entering office is given in some authentic hadiths. As for mixing with them and entering upon them to bring about a general or particular benefit or to repel a general or particular harm, while disliking what they are upon of injustice, while the soul has no inclination toward them and no love for them, and while disliking association with them were it not for the bringing about of that benefit or the repelling of that harm, then, on the assumption that the name of reliance applies to this, it is specified by the evidences that indicate the legitimacy of securing benefits and repelling harms, and by the principle that "actions are judged by intentions" and "every person will have only what he intended." Nothing is hidden from God. In sum, whoever is tested with mixing with one who is unjust must weigh his words, his deeds, what he does and what he refrains from by the scale of the Law. If he deviates from that, then "Barraqish has committed a crime against herself" (a proverb). Whoever is able to flee from them before being ordered by them to do something that obliges him to obey is better for him and more fitting for him.

*O Master of the Day of Judgement, You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help* (cf. Qur'an 1:4–5). Make us among Your righteous servants who enjoin what is good and forbid what is evil, who do not fear the blame of any blamer for Your sake. Strengthen us for that, make it easy for us, and help us in it.

Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir: "Companionship with the wrongdoer under taqiyyah is excepted from the prohibition by the condition of necessity." End of quote.

Al-Naysaburi said in his tafsir: The verifying scholars said: the prohibited reliance is approval of what the oppressors are upon, or beautifying their way and adorning it in the eyes of others, and participating with them in any of those matters. As for entering among them to remove harm or to obtain an immediate benefit, this is not included in reliance.

He said: I say this from the perspective of livelihood and dispensation, but the requirement of piety is complete avoidance of them. *"Is not God sufficient for His servant?"* (Qur'an 39:36). End of quote.

His words: *"Then the Fire will touch you"* (Qur'an 11:113), because of reliance upon them. This contains an indication that the oppressors are the people of the Fire, or are like the Fire, and companionship with the Fire necessarily causes it to touch them. The clause *"and you have no protectors other than God"* (Qur'an 11:113) is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from His words *"then the Fire will touch you."*

The meaning is: the Fire will touch you while there is no one to help you or rescue you from it. *"Then you will not be helped"* (Qur'an 11:113) by God, the Glorified, since it has already been decreed in His knowledge that He would punish you for the reliance you were forbidden, and you did not desist out of stubbornness and rebellion.

His words: *"And establish the prayer at the two ends of the day"* (Qur'an 11:114). When God, the Glorified, mentioned uprightness, He specified establishing the prayer among its types, because it is the head of faith. The phrase "the two ends of the day" is in the accusative of time (*zarfiyyah*). What is meant is the dawn prayer and the evening prayer, namely Fajr and 'Asr. It has been said that Zuhr is in the place of 'Asr.

It has also been said that the two ends are Subh and Maghrib, and it has been said that they are Zuhr and 'Asr.

Ibn Jarir preferred that they are Subh and Maghrib. He said: The evidence for this is the consensus of all that one of the two ends is Subh, which indicates that the other end is Maghrib. *"And at intervals of the night"* (Qur'an 11:114), i.e., in parts of the night. *Zulaf* means hours close to one another, and from this the name Muzdalifah is derived, because it is a station after 'Arafah near Makkah.

Ibn al-Qa'qa', Abu Ishaq and others read *zulufan* with a *damma* on the *lam*, the plural of *zalif*, and its singular may be *zulfah*.

Ibn Muhaysin read it with the *lam* sukun.

Mujahid read *zulfa* in the pattern of *fu'la*.

The rest read *zulafan* with a *fatha* on the *lam*, like *ghurfah* and *ghuraf*.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: *zulaf* means hours, its singular being *zulfah*.

Some people said: *zulfah* is the first hour of the night after sunset.

Al-Akhfash said: The meaning of *zulafan min al-layl* is the night prayer. *"Indeed, good deeds remove evil deeds"* (Qur'an 11:114), i.e., good deeds in general, and among them, indeed their pillar, the prayer, remove evil deeds in general. It has been said that what is meant by evil deeds is minor sins, and the meaning of "remove" is that they expiate them until it is as if they had not been. The reference in His words *"That is a reminder for those who remember"* (Qur'an 11:114) is to His words *"so be upright"* and what follows it. It has been said that it refers to the Qur'an: a reminder for those who remember, i.e., an admonition to those who take heed.

*"And be patient"* (Qur'an 11:115) in what you have been commanded of uprightness, and in avoiding transgression and reliance upon those who did wrong. It has been said that what is meant is patience in what one is commanded rather than in what one is forbidden, because there is no hardship in avoiding it. But this is open to question, for there is hardship in avoiding what is forbidden, and even if it is less hardship than carrying out a command, that does not take it out of the category of hardship in general. *"Indeed, God does not waste the reward of the good-doers"* (Qur'an 11:115), i.e., He will pay them their rewards and will not waste any of it; He does not neglect it or diminish it.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words *"And indeed We will pay them their share without diminution"* (Qur'an 11:109): he said, "What has been decreed for them of good or evil."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Zayd concerning the verse, he said: "From the punishment."

Both of them reported from Abu al-'Aliyah, who said: "From the provision."

Both of them also reported from Qatadah concerning His words *"So be upright as you have been commanded"* (Qur'an 11:112), he said: God commanded His Prophet to be upright in His command and not to transgress in His blessing.

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Sufyan concerning the verse, he said: "Be upright in the Qur'an."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from al-Hasan, who said: When this verse *"So be upright as you have been commanded"* was revealed, he said: "Hasten, hasten," and he was never seen laughing.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Juraij concerning *"and those who turned with you"* (Qur'an 11:112), he said: "They believed."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from al-'Ala' ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Badr concerning His words *"and do not transgress"* (Qur'an 11:112), he said: "It does not mean the companions of the Prophet ﷺ; it only means those who come after them."

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, *"and do not transgress"*: he says, "do not wrong."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Zayd, who said: "Transgression is opposition to His command and committing His disobedience."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words *"and do not incline toward those who did wrong"* (Qur'an 11:113), he said: "It means reliance upon polytheism."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him: *"and do not incline"*, he said: "Do not lean toward."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from him, he said: *"and do not incline"*: "Do not be complacent (*tudhinu*)."

Abu al-Shaykh reported from 'Ikrimah concerning the verse, he said: "That you obey them, or show them affection, or cultivate them."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words *"And establish the prayer at the two ends of the day"* (Qur'an 11:114), he said: "The prayer of Maghrib and the morning prayer," *"and at intervals of the night"*: "the prayer of 'Atamah" (i.e., 'Isha).

Both of them reported from al-Hasan, who said: "Fajr and 'Asr." *"And at intervals of the night"*: he said: "They are two intervals: the prayer of Maghrib and the prayer of 'Isha."

He said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "They are the two intervals of the night."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid concerning the two ends, he said: "The dawn prayer and the two evening prayers," meaning Zuhr and 'Asr. *"And at intervals of the night"*: he said: "Maghrib and 'Isha."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid concerning His words *"And at intervals of the night"*, he said: "An hour after an hour," meaning the late 'Isha prayer.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he used to recommend delaying 'Isha, and he would recite *"zulafan min al-layl."*

Ibn Jarir, Muhammad ibn Nasr and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Mas'ud concerning His words *"Indeed, good deeds remove evil deeds"* (Qur'an 11:114), he said: "The five prayers."

Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Muhammad ibn Nasr, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn 'Abbas: *"Indeed, good deeds remove evil deeds"*, he said: "The five prayers, and the enduring good deeds (*al-baqiyat al-salihat*) are the five prayers."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, the authors of the Sunan and others reported from Ibn Mas'ud that a man had kissed a woman, then came to the Prophet ﷺ and mentioned that to him, as if asking about its expiation. So this was revealed to him: *"And establish the prayer at the two ends of the day and at intervals of the night. Indeed, good deeds remove evil deeds"* (Qur'an 11:114). The man said: "O Messenger of God, is this for me?" He said: "It is for whoever acts by it from among my nation."

Ahmad, Muslim, Abu Dawud and others reported from Abu Umamah that a man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of God, establish upon me the prescribed punishment (*hadd*) of God" (he said it once or twice). So he turned away from him. Then the prayer was called, and when he finished, he said: "Where is the man?" He said: "Here I am." He said: "Did you complete your ablution and pray with us just now?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Indeed, you are from your sin as on the day your mother bore you, so do not return to it." Then God revealed to His Messenger at that time *"And establish the prayer at the two ends of the day."*

There are many hadiths on this subject with different wordings, and hadiths have also been transmitted: "Indeed, the five prayers are expiations for what is between them."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Hasan concerning His words *"That is a reminder for those who remember"* (Qur'an 11:114), he said: "They are those who remember God in ease and hardship, in hardship and prosperity, in well-being and affliction."

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Juraij, who said: When the man who kissed the woman was struck with remorse, that is His words *"a reminder for those who remember."*

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 11, verses 116–123 (part 1 of 2)**

This is a return to the conditions of the earlier nations, to show that the reason the annihilating punishment descended upon them was that there was no one among them who forbade corruption and enjoined right guidance.

He says: ﴿Why then were there not﴾, meaning, "Would that there had been," ﴿among the generations﴾ that existed ﴿before you, people of residue﴾ of judgment, intellect and religion ﴿who would forbid﴾ their people ﴿from corruption in the earth﴾, and would prevent them from it, because they were among those whom Allah had gathered to possess both excellence of intellect and strength of religion. In this there is a rebuke to the disbelievers that is not hidden. The word "residue" (baqiyyah) originally refers to what a man keeps back from what he brings out, and he keeps back only its best and finest. Thus the word baqiyyah became a figure of speech for excellence.

The exception in ﴿except a few﴾ is disjunctive (munqati'), meaning: "but a few ﴿of those whom We saved from among them﴾ who forbade corruption in the earth."

It has also been said that the exception is connected (muttasil), because the interrogative particle of urging (hal/lawla) carries the sense of negation. It is as if he said: "There were not among the generations people of residue who forbade corruption in the earth, except a few of those whom We saved from among them." The "min" in "of those whom We saved" is explanatory (bayaniyyah), because only those who forbade were saved. It has been said that these few were the people of Yunus, based on his saying previously: ﴿except the people of Yunus﴾ [Yunus 10:98]. It has also been said that they were the followers of the prophets and the people of truth among the nations in general.

﴿And those who did wrong pursued what they had been given luxury in⁠﴾ is coordinated with an implied element that the context requires, its estimate being: "except a few of those whom We saved from among them, who forbade." The meaning is: they (the wrongdoers) followed, by their direct commission of corruption and their abandonment of forbidding it, what they had been given luxury in.

The mutraf (one given luxury) is the one whom blessing has made insolent. It is said: "a child is mutraf," meaning pampered in body. That is, they became followers of the blessings through which they became luxurious, from abundance of life, comfort of condition, and breadth of provision. They preferred this over occupying themselves with the works of the Hereafter, and they spent their lives absorbed in the appetites of the soul.

It has also been said that the intended meaning of "those who did wrong" is those who abandoned forbidding (wrong).

This is rejected, because it would entail excluding the direct perpetrators of corruption from "those who did wrong," though they are greater wrongdoers than one who did not directly commit it, and their sin was only abandoning the forbidding.

Abu Amr, in one narration from him, read: ﴿And there was pursued those who did wrong⁠﴾ in the passive voice, and its meaning: they were made to pursue the recompense of what they had been given luxury in. The clause ﴿and they were criminals﴾ includes an explanation of the cause of their destruction, and it is coordinated with ﴿had been given luxury﴾: that is, "and these, who were made to pursue what they had been given luxury in, were criminals." Criminality (ijram) is sin (athām).

The meaning: they are people of criminality by reason of their following of appetites and their preoccupation with them over matters that deserve preoccupation. It is also permissible that the clause ﴿and they were criminals﴾ is coordinated with ﴿and those who did wrong pursued⁠﴾: that is, they pursued their appetites and, by that pursuit, were criminals.

﴿And your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people are reformers⁠﴾: that is, it is not correct or proper that Allah, glorified is He, destroy the people of the towns with an injustice they are committing, which is polytheism, while their people are reformers among themselves in the exchange of rights, not wronging people in anything.

The meaning: He does not destroy them merely for polytheism alone, until corruption in the earth is added to it, as He destroyed the people of Shu'ayb by their diminishing the measure and the balance and their depriving people of their things, and as He destroyed the people of Lut because of their commission of the abominable indecency. It has been said that His saying ﴿unjustly⁠﴾ is a circumstantial (hal) clause relating to the subject (the agent).

The meaning: "And Allah would never destroy the towns while being unjust to them, in a state where they are reformers, not corrupters in the earth."

The intended meaning of the verse may be His exaltation, glorified and high is He, above the occurrence of that from Him without a cause that requires it, given the depiction of that in the form of what is impossible for Him. Otherwise, all His acts, whatever they may be, contain no injustice, for He, glorified is He, is not an oppressor of the servants.

Al-Zajjaj said: It is permissible that the meaning be: "And your Lord would never destroy anyone while he is wronging him, even if he were in the utmost state of righteousness, because His disposal is in His own dominion." Its proof is His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong people at all⁠﴾ [Yunus 10:44]. It has also been said the meaning is: "He would not destroy them for their sins while they are reformers," that is, sincere in faith. Injustice, then, on this reading, means sins.

﴿And if your Lord had willed, He would have made mankind one nation⁠﴾, that is, people of one religion, either people of misguidance or people of guidance. It has also been said its meaning is: He would have made them gathered upon the truth, not differing in it, or gathered upon the religion of Islam to the exclusion of all other religions. But He did not will that, so it did not happen. For this reason He said: ﴿And they will never cease to be differing⁠﴾ in their relations with one another, over various religions, or they will never cease to differ concerning the truth or the religion of Islam. It has also been said: they differ concerning provision, this one rich and that one poor.

﴿Except those upon whom your Lord has mercy⁠﴾ by guidance to the true religion, for they do not differ. Or it means: except those among the differing concerning the truth or the religion of Islam upon whom your Lord has mercy, by guiding them to the correct course, which is the judgment of Allah, which is the truth with no truth other than it. Or: except those upon whom your Lord has mercy through contentment.

The better view is to interpret ﴿He would have made mankind one nation⁠﴾ as "gathered upon the truth," so that the meaning of the exception in ﴿except those upon whom your Lord has mercy⁠﴾ is clear, without need for strained interpretation.

﴿And for that⁠﴾, that is, for what has been mentioned of difference, ﴿He created them⁠﴾. Or: "and for His mercy He created them." The reference of the demonstrative "that" to "mercy" is grammatically correct because its feminine gender is not real (metaphorical). The pronoun in "He created them" refers to mankind, or to the one in "those upon whom your Lord has mercy." It has also been said the demonstrative "that" refers to the whole of the difference and the mercy together, and there is no obstacle to using a demonstrative for two things, as in His saying: ﴿neither old nor young, but between that⁠﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:68], ﴿and seek between that a way⁠﴾ [al-Isra' 17:110], and ﴿so let them rejoice in that⁠﴾ [Yunus 10:58].

His saying: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled⁠﴾: the meaning of "has been fulfilled" is "has been established," as He decreed it in His eternal past. When it is fulfilled, it is impossible to change or alter. It has also been said the word is His saying: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind, all together⁠﴾, that is, from among those who deserve it from both groups.

The tanwin in "and each" (wa-kullan) is for compensation for the omitted genitive that was attached to it, and it is in the accusative governed by "We relate" (naqussu).

The meaning: "And each report from the reports of the messengers, of that which is needed, We relate to you," that is, We inform you of it.

Al-Akhfash said: "each" (kullan) is a fronted circumstantial accusative (hal), as in your saying: "Each, I struck the people." The "reports" (anba') are the news.

﴿By which We strengthen your heart⁠﴾, that is, that by which We make your heart firm, through increase in its certainty about what We have related to you and abundance of its tranquility, because the accumulation of proofs is firmer for the heart, more deeply rooted in the soul, and stronger for knowledge. The clause ﴿by which We strengthen⁠﴾ is a substitute for ﴿reports of the messengers⁠﴾, and it is an explanation of "each." It is also permissible that ﴿by which We strengthen⁠﴾ is the object of "We relate," and "each" is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), and the estimate is: "Each method of relating, We relate to you that by which We strengthen your heart."

He says: ﴿Why then were there not﴾, meaning, "Would that there had been," ﴿among the generations﴾ that existed ﴿before you, people of residue﴾ of judgment, intellect and religion ﴿who would forbid﴾ their people ﴿from corruption in the earth﴾, and would prevent them from it, because they were among those whom Allah had gathered to possess both excellence of intellect and strength of religion. In this there is a rebuke to the disbelievers that is not hidden. The word "residue" (baqiyyah) originally refers to what a man keeps back from what he brings out, and he keeps back only its best and finest. Thus the word baqiyyah became a figure of speech for excellence.

The exception in ﴿except a few﴾ is disjunctive (munqati'), meaning: "but a few ﴿of those whom We saved from among them﴾ who forbade corruption in the earth."

It has also been said that the exception is connected (muttasil), because the interrogative particle of urging (hal/lawla) carries the sense of negation. It is as if he said: "There were not among the generations people of residue who forbade corruption in the earth, except a few of those whom We saved from among them." The "min" in "of those whom We saved" is explanatory (bayaniyyah), because only those who forbade were saved. It has been said that these few were the people of Yunus, based on his saying previously: ﴿except the people of Yunus﴾ [Yunus 10:98]. It has also been said that they were the followers of the prophets and the people of truth among the nations in general.

﴿And those who did wrong pursued what they had been given luxury in⁠﴾ is coordinated with an implied element that the context requires, its estimate being: "except a few of those whom We saved from among them, who forbade." The meaning is: they (the wrongdoers) followed, by their direct commission of corruption and their abandonment of forbidding it, what they had been given luxury in.

The mutraf (one given luxury) is the one whom blessing has made insolent. It is said: "a child is mutraf," meaning pampered in body. That is, they became followers of the blessings through which they became luxurious, from abundance of life, comfort of condition, and breadth of provision. They preferred this over occupying themselves with the works of the Hereafter, and they spent their lives absorbed in the appetites of the soul.

It has also been said that the intended meaning of "those who did wrong" is those who abandoned forbidding (wrong).

This is rejected, because it would entail excluding the direct perpetrators of corruption from "those who did wrong," though they are greater wrongdoers than one who did not directly commit it, and their sin was only abandoning the forbidding.

Abu Amr, in one narration from him, read: ﴿And there was pursued those who did wrong⁠﴾ in the passive voice, and its meaning: they were made to pursue the recompense of what they had been given luxury in. The clause ﴿and they were criminals﴾ includes an explanation of the cause of their destruction, and it is coordinated with ﴿had been given luxury﴾: that is, "and these, who were made to pursue what they had been given luxury in, were criminals." Criminality (ijram) is sin (athām).

The meaning: they are people of criminality by reason of their following of appetites and their preoccupation with them over matters that deserve preoccupation. It is also permissible that the clause ﴿and they were criminals﴾ is coordinated with ﴿and those who did wrong pursued⁠﴾: that is, they pursued their appetites and, by that pursuit, were criminals.

﴿And your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people are reformers⁠﴾: that is, it is not correct or proper that Allah, glorified is He, destroy the people of the towns with an injustice they are committing, which is polytheism, while their people are reformers among themselves in the exchange of rights, not wronging people in anything.

The meaning: He does not destroy them merely for polytheism alone, until corruption in the earth is added to it, as He destroyed the people of Shu'ayb by their diminishing the measure and the balance and their depriving people of their things, and as He destroyed the people of Lut because of their commission of the abominable indecency. It has been said that His saying ﴿unjustly⁠﴾ is a circumstantial (hal) clause relating to the subject (the agent).

The meaning: "And Allah would never destroy the towns while being unjust to them, in a state where they are reformers, not corrupters in the earth."

The intended meaning of the verse may be His exaltation, glorified and high is He, above the occurrence of that from Him without a cause that requires it, given the depiction of that in the form of what is impossible for Him. Otherwise, all His acts, whatever they may be, contain no injustice, for He, glorified is He, is not an oppressor of the servants.

Al-Zajjaj said: It is permissible that the meaning be: "And your Lord would never destroy anyone while he is wronging him, even if he were in the utmost state of righteousness, because His disposal is in His own dominion." Its proof is His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong people at all⁠﴾ [Yunus 10:44]. It has also been said the meaning is: "He would not destroy them for their sins while they are reformers," that is, sincere in faith. Injustice, then, on this reading, means sins.

﴿And if your Lord had willed, He would have made mankind one nation⁠﴾, that is, people of one religion, either people of misguidance or people of guidance. It has also been said its meaning is: He would have made them gathered upon the truth, not differing in it, or gathered upon the religion of Islam to the exclusion of all other religions. But He did not will that, so it did not happen. For this reason He said: ﴿And they will never cease to be differing⁠﴾ in their relations with one another, over various religions, or they will never cease to differ concerning the truth or the religion of Islam. It has also been said: they differ concerning provision, this one rich and that one poor.

﴿Except those upon whom your Lord has mercy⁠﴾ by guidance to the true religion, for they do not differ. Or it means: except those among the differing concerning the truth or the religion of Islam upon whom your Lord has mercy, by guiding them to the correct course, which is the judgment of Allah, which is the truth with no truth other than it. The better view is to interpret ﴿He would have made mankind one nation⁠﴾ as "gathered upon the truth," so that the meaning of the exception in ﴿except those upon whom your Lord has mercy⁠﴾ is clear, without need for strained interpretation.

It is as if he said: "There were not among the generations people of residue who forbade corruption in the earth, except a few of those whom We saved from among them." The "min" in "of those whom We saved" is explanatory (bayaniyyah), because only those who forbade were saved. It has been said that these few were the people of Yunus, based on his saying previously: ﴿except the people of Yunus﴾ [Yunus 10:98]. It has also been said that they were the followers of the prophets and the people of truth among the nations in general.

He says: ﴿Why then were there not﴾, meaning, "Would that there had been," ﴿among the generations﴾ that existed ﴿before you, people of residue﴾ of judgment, intellect and religion ﴿who would forbid﴾ their people ﴿from corruption in the earth﴾, and would prevent them from it, because they were among those whom Allah had gathered to possess both excellence of intellect and strength of religion. The word "residue" (baqiyyah) originally refers to what a man keeps back from what he brings out, and he keeps back only its best and finest. Thus the word baqiyyah became a figure of speech for excellence.

The exception in ﴿except a few﴾ is disjunctive (munqati'), meaning: "but a few ﴿of those whom We saved from among them﴾ who forbade corruption in the earth."

It has also been said that the exception is connected (muttasil), because the interrogative particle of urging (hal/lawla) carries the sense of negation. It is as if he said: "There were not among the generations people of residue who forbade corruption in the earth, except a few of those whom We saved from among them." The "min" in "of those whom We saved" is explanatory (bayaniyyah), because only those who forbade were saved. It has been said that these few were the people of Yunus, based on his saying previously: ﴿except the people of Yunus﴾ [Yunus 10:98]. It has also been said that they were the followers of the prophets and the people of truth among the nations in general.

﴿And those who did wrong pursued what they had been given luxury in⁠﴾ is coordinated with an implied element that the context requires, its estimate being: "except a few of those whom We saved from among them, who forbade." The meaning is: they (the wrongdoers) followed, by their direct commission of corruption and their abandonment of forbidding it, what they had been given luxury in.

The mutraf (one given luxury) is the one whom blessing has made insolent. It is said: "a child is mutraf," meaning pampered in body. That is, they became followers of the blessings through which they became luxurious, from abundance of life, comfort of condition, and breadth of provision. They preferred this over occupying themselves with the works of the Hereafter, and they spent their lives absorbed in the appetites of the soul.

It has also been said that the intended meaning of "those who did wrong" is those who abandoned forbidding (wrong).

This is rejected, because it would entail excluding the direct perpetrators of corruption from "those who did wrong," though they are greater wrongdoers than one who did not directly commit it, and their sin was only abandoning the forbidding.

Abu Amr, in one narration from him, read: ﴿And there was pursued those who did wrong⁠﴾ in the passive voice, and its meaning: they were made to pursue the recompense of what they had been given luxury in. The clause ﴿and they were criminals﴾ includes an explanation of the cause of their destruction, and it is coordinated with ﴿had been given luxury﴾: that is, "and these, who were made to pursue what they had been given luxury in, were criminals." Criminality (ijram) is sin (athām).

The meaning: they are people of criminality by reason of their following of appetites and their preoccupation with them over matters that deserve preoccupation. It is also permissible that the clause ﴿and they were criminals﴾ is coordinated with ﴿and those who did wrong pursued⁠﴾: that is, they pursued their appetites and, by that pursuit, were criminals.

﴿And your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people are reformers⁠﴾: that is, it is not correct or proper that Allah, glorified is He, destroy the people of the towns with an injustice they are committing, which is polytheism, while their people are reformers among themselves in the exchange of rights, not wronging people in anything.

The meaning: He does not destroy them merely for polytheism alone, until corruption in the earth is added to it, as He destroyed the people of Shu'ayb by their diminishing the measure and the balance and their depriving people of their things, and as He destroyed the people of Lut because of their commission of the abominable indecency. It has been said that His saying ﴿unjustly⁠﴾ is a circumstantial (hal) clause relating to the subject (the agent).

The meaning: "And Allah would never destroy the towns while being unjust to them, in a state where they are reformers, not corrupters in the earth."

The intended meaning of the verse may be His exaltation, glorified and high is He, above the occurrence of that from Him without a cause that requires it, given the depiction of that in the form of what is impossible for Him. Otherwise, all His acts, whatever they may be, contain no injustice, for He, glorified is He, is not an oppressor of the servants.

Al-Zajjaj said: It is permissible that the meaning be: "And your Lord would never destroy anyone while he is wronging him, even if he were in the utmost state of righteousness, because His disposal is in His own dominion." Its proof is His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong people at all⁠﴾ [Yunus 10:44]. It has also been said the meaning is: "He would not destroy them for their sins while they are reformers," that is, sincere in faith. Injustice, then, on this reading, means sins.

It has also been said its meaning is: He would have made them gathered upon the truth, not differing in it, or gathered upon the religion of Islam to the exclusion of all other religions. But He did not will that, so it did not happen. For this reason He said: ﴿And they will never cease to be differing⁠﴾ in their relations with one another, over various religions, or they will never cease to differ concerning the truth or the religion of Islam. It has also been said: they differ concerning provision, this one rich and that one poor.

Or: except those upon whom your Lord has mercy through contentment.

The pronoun in "He created them" refers to mankind, or to the one in "those upon whom your Lord has mercy." ﴿And there has come to you in this the truth⁠﴾, that is, in this surah has come to you, or in these reports, the decisive proofs indicating the soundness of the origin and the return, and an admonition by which the believer who stands upon it is admonished, and a reminder by which whoever among them reflects upon it is reminded. The believers are specified because they are the qualified ones for being admonished and reminded. It has also been said the meaning is: "And there has come to you in this world the truth, which is prophethood." On the first interpretation, the specifying of this surah with the coming of the truth in it, though it has come in other surahs as well, is for the purpose of showing that it contains that, not to indicate that it exists in it and not in others.

The meaning: "Wait for the outcome of Our affair, for We are waiting for the outcome of your affair and what punishment and chastisement of Allah will befall you."

He specified the unseen, though He knows what is witnessed as He knows what is hidden, because it is of the knowledge that no one else shares in. It has also been said that the unseen of the heavens and the earth is the descent of punishment from the sky and its emergence from the earth. ﴿So worship Him and rely upon Him⁠﴾, for He is sufficient for you against everything you dislike, and gives you everything you love. He says: ﴿Why then were there not﴾, meaning, "Would that there had been," ﴿among the generations﴾ that existed ﴿before you, people of residue﴾ of judgment, intellect and religion ﴿who would forbid﴾ their people ﴿from corruption in the earth﴾, and would prevent them from it, because they were among those whom Allah had gathered to possess both excellence of intellect and strength of religion. In this there is a rebuke to the disbelievers that is not hidden. The word "residue" (baqiyyah) originally refers to what a man keeps back from what he brings out, and he keeps back only its best and finest. Thus the word baqiyyah became a figure of speech for excellence.

The exception in ﴿except a few﴾ is disjunctive (munqati'), meaning: "but a few ﴿of those whom We saved from among them﴾ who forbade corruption in the earth."

It has also been said that the exception is connected (muttasil), because the interrogative particle of urging (hal/lawla) carries the sense of negation. It is as if he said: "There were not among the generations people of residue who forbade corruption in the earth, except a few of those whom We saved from among them." The "min" in "of those whom We saved" is explanatory (bayaniyyah), because only those who forbade were saved. It has been said that these few were the people of Yunus, based on his saying previously: ﴿except the people of Yunus﴾ [Yunus 10:98]. It has also been said that they were the followers of the prophets and the people of truth among the nations in general.

﴿And those who did wrong pursued what they had been given luxury in⁠﴾ is coordinated with an implied element that the context requires, its estimate being: "except a few of those whom We saved from among them, who forbade." The meaning is: they (the wrongdoers) followed, by their direct commission of corruption and their abandonment of forbidding it, what they had been given luxury in.

The mutraf (one given luxury) is the one whom blessing has made insolent. It is said: "a child is mutraf," meaning pampered in body. That is, they became followers of the blessings through which they became luxurious, from abundance of life, comfort of condition, and breadth of provision. They preferred this over occupying themselves with the works of the Hereafter, and they spent their lives absorbed in the appetites of the soul.

It has also been said that the intended meaning of "those who did wrong" is those who abandoned forbidding (wrong).

This is rejected, because it would entail excluding the direct perpetrators of corruption from "those who did wrong," though they are greater wrongdoers than one who did not directly commit it, and their sin was only abandoning the forbidding.

Abu Amr, in one narration from him, read: ﴿And there was pursued those who did wrong⁠﴾ in the passive voice, and its meaning: they were made to pursue the recompense of what they had been given luxury in. The clause ﴿and they were criminals﴾ includes an explanation of the cause of their destruction, and it is coordinated with ﴿had been given luxury﴾: that is, "and these, who were made to pursue what they had been given luxury in, were criminals." Criminality (ijram) is sin (athām).

The meaning: they are people of criminality by reason of their following of appetites and their preoccupation with them over matters that deserve preoccupation. It is also permissible that the clause ﴿and they were criminals﴾ is coordinated with ﴿and those who did wrong pursued⁠﴾: that is, they pursued their appetites and, by that pursuit, were criminals.

﴿And your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people are reformers⁠﴾: that is, it is not correct or proper that Allah, glorified is He, destroy the people of the towns with an injustice they are committing, which is polytheism, while their people are reformers among themselves in the exchange of rights, not wronging people in anything.

The meaning: He does not destroy them merely for polytheism alone, until corruption in the earth is added to it, as He destroyed the people of Shu'ayb by their diminishing the measure and the balance and their depriving people of their things, and as He destroyed the people of Lut because of their commission of the abominable indecency. It has been said that His saying ﴿unjustly⁠﴾ is a circumstantial (hal) clause relating to the subject (the agent).

The meaning: "And Allah would never destroy the towns while being unjust to them, in a state where they are reformers, not corrupters in the earth."

The intended meaning of the verse may be His exaltation, glorified and high is He, above the occurrence of that from Him without a cause that requires it, given the depiction of that in the form of what is impossible for Him. Otherwise, all His acts, whatever they may be, contain no injustice, for He, glorified is He, is not an oppressor of the servants.

Al-Zajjaj said: It is permissible that the meaning be: "And your Lord would never destroy anyone while he is wronging him, even if he were in the utmost state of righteousness, because His disposal is in His own dominion." Its proof is His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong people at all⁠﴾ [Yunus 10:44]. It has also been said the meaning is: "He would not destroy them for their sins while they are reformers," that is, sincere in faith. Injustice, then, on this reading, means sins.

﴿And if your Lord had willed, He would have made mankind one nation⁠﴾, that is, people of one religion, either people of misguidance or people of guidance. It has also been said its meaning is: He would have made them gathered upon the truth, not differing in it, or gathered upon the religion of Islam to the exclusion of all other religions. But He did not will that, so it did not happen. For this reason He said: ﴿And they will never cease to be differing⁠﴾ in their relations with one another, over various religions, or they will never cease to differ concerning the truth or the religion of Islam. It has also been said: they differ concerning provision, this one rich and that one poor.

﴿Except those upon whom your Lord has mercy⁠﴾ by guidance to the true religion, for they do not differ. Or it means: except those among the differing concerning the truth or the religion of Islam upon whom your Lord has mercy, by guiding them to the correct course, which is the judgment of Allah, which is the truth with no truth other than it. Or: except those upon whom your Lord has mercy through contentment.

The better view is to interpret ﴿He would have made mankind one nation⁠﴾ as "gathered upon the truth," so that the meaning of the exception in ﴿except those upon whom your Lord has mercy⁠﴾ is clear, without need for strained interpretation.

﴿And for that⁠﴾, that is, for what has been mentioned of difference, ﴿He created them⁠﴾. Or: "and for His mercy He created them." The pronoun in "He created them" refers to mankind, or to the one in "those upon whom your Lord has mercy." It has also been said the demonstrative "that" refers to the whole of the difference and the mercy together, and there is no obstacle to using a demonstrative for two things, as in His saying: ﴿neither old nor young, but between that⁠﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:68], ﴿and seek between that a way⁠﴾ [al-Isra' 17:110], and ﴿so let them rejoice in that⁠﴾ [Yunus 10:58].

﴿By which We strengthen your heart⁠﴾, that is, that by which We make your heart firm, through increase in its certainty about what We have related to you and abundance of its tranquility, because the accumulation of proofs is firmer for the heart, more deeply rooted in the soul, and stronger for knowledge. ﴿And there has come to you in this the truth⁠﴾, that is, in this surah has come to you, or in these reports, the decisive proofs indicating the soundness of the origin and the return, and an admonition by which the believer who stands upon it is admonished, and a reminder by which whoever among them reflects upon it is reminded. ﴿And your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people are reformers⁠﴾: that is, it is not correct or proper that Allah, glorified is He, destroy the people of the towns with an injustice they are committing, which is polytheism, while their people are reformers among themselves in the exchange of rights, not wronging people in anything.

The meaning: He does not destroy them merely for polytheism alone, until corruption in the earth is added to it, as He destroyed the people of Shu'ayb by their diminishing the measure and the balance and their depriving people of their things, and as He destroyed the people of Lut because of their commission of the abominable indecency. It has been said that His saying ﴿unjustly⁠﴾ is a circumstantial (hal) clause relating to the subject (the agent).

The meaning: "And Allah would never destroy the towns while being unjust to them, in a state where they are reformers, not corrupters in the earth."

The intended meaning of the verse may be His exaltation, glorified and high is He, above the occurrence of that from Him without a cause that requires it, given the depiction of that in the form of what is impossible for Him. Otherwise, all His acts, whatever they may be, contain no injustice, for He, glorified is He, is not an oppressor of the servants.

Al-Zajjaj said: It is permissible that the meaning be: "And your Lord would never destroy anyone while he is wronging him, even if he were in the utmost state of righteousness, because His disposal is in His own dominion." Its proof is His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong people at all⁠﴾ [Yunus 10:44]. It has also been said the meaning is: "He would not destroy them for their sins while they are reformers," that is, sincere in faith. Injustice, then, on this reading, means sins.

﴿And if your Lord had willed, He would have made mankind one nation⁠﴾, that is, people of one religion, either people of misguidance or people of guidance. It has also been said its meaning is: He would have made them gathered upon the truth, not differing in it, or gathered upon the religion of Islam to the exclusion of all other religions. But He did not will that, so it did not happen. For this reason He said: ﴿And they will never cease to be differing⁠﴾ in their relations with one another, over various religions, or they will never cease to differ concerning the truth or the religion of Islam. It has also been said: they differ concerning provision, this one rich and that one poor.

﴿Except those upon whom your Lord has mercy⁠﴾ by guidance to the true religion, for they do not differ. Or it means: except those among the differing concerning the truth or the religion of Islam upon whom your Lord has mercy, by guiding them to the correct course, which is the judgment of Allah, which is the truth with no truth other than it. Or: except those upon whom your Lord has mercy through contentment.

The better view is to interpret ﴿He would have made mankind one nation⁠﴾ as "gathered upon the truth," so that the meaning of the exception in ﴿except those upon whom your Lord has mercy⁠﴾ is clear, without need for strained interpretation.

﴿And for that⁠﴾, that is, for what has been mentioned of difference, ﴿He created them⁠﴾. Or: "and for His mercy He created them." The reference of the demonstrative "that" to "mercy" is grammatically correct because its feminine gender is not real (metaphorical). The pronoun in "He created them" refers to mankind, or to the one in "those upon whom your Lord has mercy." It has also been said the demonstrative "that" refers to the whole of the difference and the mercy together, and there is no obstacle to using a demonstrative for two things, as in His saying: ﴿neither old nor young, but between that⁠﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:68], ﴿and seek between that a way⁠﴾ [al-Isra' 17:110], and ﴿so let them rejoice in that⁠﴾ [Yunus 10:58].

His saying: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled⁠﴾: the meaning of "has been fulfilled" is "has been established," as He decreed it in His eternal past. When it is fulfilled, it is impossible to change or alter. It has also been said the word is His saying: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind, all together⁠﴾, that is, from among those who deserve it from both groups.

The tanwin in "and each" (wa-kullan) is for compensation for the omitted genitive that was attached to it, and it is in the accusative governed by "We relate" (naqussu).

The meaning: "And each report from the reports of the messengers, of that which is needed, We relate to you," that is, We inform you of it.

Al-Akhfash said: "each" (kullan) is a fronted circumstantial accusative (hal), as in your saying: "Each, I struck the people." The "reports" (anba') are the news.

﴿By which We strengthen your heart⁠﴾, that is, that by which We make your heart firm, through increase in its certainty about what We have related to you and abundance of its tranquility, because the accumulation of proofs is firmer for the heart, more deeply rooted in the soul, and stronger for knowledge. The clause ﴿by which We strengthen⁠﴾ is a substitute for ﴿reports of the messengers⁠﴾, and it is an explanation of "each." It is also permissible that ﴿by which We strengthen⁠﴾ is the object of "We relate," and "each" is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), and the estimate is: "Each method of relating, We relate to you that by which We strengthen your heart."

﴿And there has come to you in this the truth⁠﴾, that is, in this surah has come to you, or in these reports, the decisive proofs indicating the soundness of the origin and the return, and an admonition by which the believer who stands upon it is admonished, and a reminder by which whoever among them reflects upon it is reminded. The believers are specified because they are the qualified ones for being admonished and reminded. It has also been said the meaning is: "And there has come to you in this world the truth, which is prophethood." On the first interpretation, the specifying of this surah with the coming of the truth in it, though it has come in other surahs as well, is for the purpose of showing that it contains that, not to indicate that it exists in it and not in others.

﴿And say to those who do not believe⁠﴾ in this truth, and are not admonished and do not remember: ﴿Work according to your position⁠﴾, according to your firmness, your state and your direction. Its verification has already passed. ﴿Indeed, we are working⁠﴾ according to our position, our state and our direction, of belief in the truth and being admonished and reminded. In this there is an intensifying of the threat and the warning to them.

Likewise His saying: ﴿And wait; indeed, we are waiting⁠﴾ contains a warning and threat that is not hidden.

The meaning: "Wait for the outcome of Our affair, for We are waiting for the outcome of your affair and what punishment and chastisement of Allah will befall you."

﴿And to Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth⁠﴾, that is, knowledge of everything that is hidden from the servants in them. He specified the unseen, though He knows what is witnessed as He knows what is hidden, because it is of the knowledge that no one else shares in. It has also been said that the unseen of the heavens and the earth is the descent of punishment from the sky and its emergence from the earth. The first is better, and Abu Ali al-Farisi and others said so. He attributed the unseen to the object (maf'ul) as an expansion of meaning. ﴿And to Him the whole matter is returned⁠﴾, that is, on the Day of Resurrection, and He will recompense each for his deed.

Nafi' and Hafs read "is returned" (yurja'u) in the passive voice. The rest read it in the active voice.

﴿So worship Him and rely upon Him⁠﴾, for He is sufficient for you against everything you dislike, and gives you everything you love. The "fa" is for the arrangement of the command to worship and to rely upon Him on the basis that the return of all matters is to Allah, glorified is He. ﴿And your Lord is not unaware of what you do⁠﴾, but rather He is Knowing of all that and will recompense for it: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil.

The people of Medina, Syria and Hafs read "you do" (ta'malun) with the second-person (ta') form, addressed to them. The rest read it with the third-person (ya') form.

Ibn Abi Hatim has reported from Abu Malik regarding His saying ﴿Why then were there not⁠﴾ that he said: "meaning, would that there had been."

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited to me: ﴿Why then were there not among the generations before you people of residue and wisdom who forbade corruption in the earth⁠﴾."

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Jurayj regarding ﴿except a few of those whom We saved from among them⁠﴾: "Allah reduces them, from every people, to a few."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid regarding ﴿And those who did wrong pursued what they had been given luxury in⁠﴾: "In their dominion and their tyranny and their abandonment of the truth."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh reported through the chain of Ibn Jurayj who said: Ibn Abbas said: "Ut'rifu fihi" means "They were made insolent in it."

al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Daylami reported from Jarir, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) being asked about the interpretation of this verse: ﴿And your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people are reformers⁠﴾. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'And their people help one another to justice.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Kharaʾiti in Masawi' al-Akhlaq reported it as a statement of Jarir (mawquf).

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Dahhak regarding ﴿And if your Lord had willed, He would have made mankind one nation⁠﴾: "The people of one religion, the people of misguidance or the people of guidance."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿And they will never cease to be differing⁠﴾: "The people of truth and the people of falsehood." ﴿Except those upon whom your Lord has mercy⁠﴾: "The people of truth." ﴿And for that He created them⁠﴾: "For mercy."

Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him regarding ﴿Except those upon whom your Lord has mercy⁠﴾: "Except the people of His mercy, for they do not differ."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him, who said: "They will never cease to be differing over desires."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ata' ibn Abi Rabah: ﴿And they will never cease to be differing⁠﴾, that is, the Jews, the Christians, the Magians and the Hanifiyyah, and those whom your Lord has mercy upon are the Hanifiyyah.

These same (compilers) reported from al-Hasan regarding the verse, who said: "People differ over various religions, except those upon whom your Lord has mercy. Whoever your Lord has mercy upon does not differ." ﴿And for that He created them⁠﴾: "For difference."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid regarding ﴿And they will never cease to be differing⁠﴾: "The people of falsehood." ﴿Except those upon whom your Lord has mercy⁠﴾: "The people of truth." ﴿And for that He created them⁠﴾: "For mercy."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported similarly from Ikrimah.

They both reported from al-Hasan who said: "They will never cease to be differing over provision."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿And for that He created them⁠﴾: "He created them as two groups: a group that is shown mercy and so does not differ, and a group that is not shown mercy and so differs. That is His saying: ﴿Among them is the wretched and the blessed⁠﴾ [Hud 11:105]."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Juraij, regarding His saying: ﴿And We relate to you the news of the messengers, by which We strengthen your heart﴾, that it means: so that you, O Muhammad, may know what the messengers before you suffered from their peoples.

Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh related through several chains from Ibn Abbas, who said: regarding ﴿And in this the truth has come to you﴾, he said: "in this surah."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari the like of it.

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr the like of it also.

Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Hasan the like of it.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatada, who said regarding "in this": "in this world."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatada regarding ﴿Act according to your standing﴾, that it means: according to your positions.

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Juraij regarding ﴿So wait; indeed I am with you among the waiting﴾, that he said: it means "Wait for the promises of Satan, which he adorns for you," and regarding His saying ﴿And to Him the whole matter returns﴾, he said: "Then He will judge between them with the judgment of justice."

Abd Allah ibn Ahmad, in the Zawa'id (additions) to al-Musnad, Ibn al-Durays in Fada'il al-Qur'an (Virtues of the Qur'an), Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ka'b, who said: "The opening of the Torah is the opening of al-An'am, and the closing of the Torah is the closing of Hud: ﴿And to Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾" up to the end of the verse.
